title: Fantasy Football: Brock Bowers is back — and he looks ready to break the game
description: Fantasy football analyst Scott Pianowski examines some target trends to note as we head into Week 4.
fullText:
Target data is something we need to consider every week, but it doesn't stop there. Every week we'll jump into the spreadsheets to try to figure out what's going on with pass-catchers — who's popping (or slumping) and some of the reasons why.

Open up those spreadsheets and let's see what we find.

I didn't have a lot of interest in Bowers at his second-round ADP this summer. He was coming off a year ruined by injury, and I didn't like the opportunity cost of selecting him instead of an impact receiver or running back. Kirk Cousins is a back-nine quarterback (that's putting it kindly) and rookie QB Fernando Mendoza has a wide range of outcomes. When Bowers had a meniscus procedure a few weeks back and missed the first two games, I felt further validated by the soft fade.

But Bowers has made a career out of being an outlier. He's the only player to win the Mackey Award (college's best tight end) more than once. His rookie year in 2024 was an unstoppable party (112-1,194-5), and despite missing five games last year, he still scored seven times and averaged 56.7 yards per game.

And then there was Bowers' 2026 debut in Week 3.

A 10-116-1 line speaks for itself — screams for itself — but the genesis of the usage is even more impressive. Bowers received a first-read target on 50% of the Las Vegas pass attempts, an unheard-of number (for context, Jaxon Smith-Njigba logged a 44.6% number last year, the highest in the last five seasons). And the Raiders didn't bog Bowers down with blocking assignments — he ran a route on 94.6% of the Cousins dropbacks (that stat was at 84 and 80% the last two years).

New head coach (and offensive designer) Klint Kubiak is a talent elevator. His fingerprints were all over JSN's monster season last year. And perhaps Cousins, at age 38, has more left than I realized. And heck, bringing this back to the top, Cousins knows how to get production from a tight end — the historical Kyle Pitts Sr. (more on him below) game last December (11-166-3 on a Thursday night) came with Cousins at the controls.

Ranking Trey McBride as the TE1 all summer was reasonable — he still could claim that spot — and I wasn't the only person expecting a big year from Loveland. But I'm prepared to have all the FOMO watching Bowers toy with overmatched linebackers and defensive backs for the next three months. The Raiders look better than expected, and this offense needs Bowers to dominate targets, given the modest talent in the receiver room.

It was exciting to see the Falcons offense show up in Week 3. This was a team that didn't even have a red zone trip in the first two weeks. We're still not sure how good QB Michael Penix Jr. really is, but he's obviously great for Drake London, and a lifter for Bijan Robinson, too.

Penix has made 13 starts as a pro, and played in 17 games overall. The cumulative stats are a little less than what we'd see in a full season. Most of his indexed efficiency stats are below code, though he is better than league average in avoiding negative plays (sacks, interceptions).

When Penix looks downfield, he only has eyes for London. Here's his target distribution over 460 professional passes:

— London: 139 targets, 89-1,341-8

— Robinson: 65 targets, 49-499-2

Even when Pitts draws a Penix target, it's not offering much downfield. His career YPA per quarterback reads like this:

— Matt Ryan, 9.4 (109 attempts)

— Kirk Cousins, 8.4 (132 attempts)

— Taylor Heinicke, 7.6 (19 attempts)

— Desmond Ridder, 7.2 (73 attempts)

— Michael Penix, 6.9 (62 attempts)

I suppose you could look at the Penix/Pitts data and conclude "small sample," but I'm not sure that caveat really applies anymore. They played in nine games together last year and Pitts had a 36-357-1 return. No volume, no splash plays, little goal-line equity. Pitts had just one catch and two targets last week, despite the Falcons rolling up 498 yards of offense and 35 points.

Pitts has been called a unicorn since he came into the league five years ago. But maybe this is a case of a round peg and a square hole.

When the Bears added Raymond before this season, there was no apparent reason for fantasy adjustment. Raymond was entering his age-32 season and he's had a respectable but underwhelming career. He's never had 50 catches in a season. He's never gone past 616 yards receiving. He had all of nine touchdown catches in nine years. He's been a good return man and a depth player; that's about it. And even as his previous time in Detroit had overlap with Ben Johnson, the results were muted.

But the Chicago passing tree isn't as narrow as we suspected — and it's Raymond changing the dynamic. Through three games, he's rocking a 19-214–1 line. He's caught 19 of his 21 targets, an excellent 90.5% catch rate. He's averaging 10.2 yards per target, which is also excellent.

Luther Burden III was active Monday against Philadelphia and now leads the Bears with his 23 targets. But Raymond's 21 looks are coming at the expense of other pieces here — Rome Odunze has just 13 targets (despite a juicy 10.7 yards per target) and Colston Loveland is stuck at nine targets (and 3.8 YPT). It's extra painful for fantasy managers that Odunze (bobble) and Loveland (tackled at the one) both narrowly missed touchdowns in Week 3.

All summer we dreamt of Burden becoming the Amon-Ra St. Brown of the Chicago offense, but it's telling that Raymond has a slightly lower aDOT than Burden (6.0 versus 7.2). Meanwhile, Odunze is almost all shot plays — he's at 17.6 YPT. Fantasy managers have spent the last few days trying to figure out if Raymond has enough fantasy juice to actually be a trustworthy commodity on Sundays, but at minimum, he's trusted enough to muck up the spike seasons we imagined for the rest of this passing game.

Statistics from Fantasy Points and Pro Football Reference were used in the research and composition of this article.

title: Who’s your Uber driver on the phone to? Welcome to the long, long diaspora phone call
description: For those employed in arduous solitary work such as cab driving, a marathon phone call is the perfect place to navigate the dislocations of immigrant...
fullText:
For those employed in arduous solitary work such as cab driving, a marathon phone call is the perfect place to navigate the dislocations of immigrant life

Don’t get The Long Wave delivered to your inbox? 
The question of the week is: “who are Uber drivers always talking to on the phone?” It’s one that regularly surfaces on Reddit threads and social media and even, on a couple of occasions, in the office. It’s not my question (I know who they are talking to), but I think the fact that many people are so baffled by it tells us a lot about the separate worlds we occupy.

When you get a cab on a ride-hailing app, the chances that your driver will be on the phone is high. The conversation is almost always quiet, containing pauses so long that it often seems they are actually no longer on a call. But then comes a rejoinder, a laugh, an interjection, and the marathon continues.

For anyone of an immigrant background, the question of who they are talking to is absolutely no mystery. They are talking to us; their siblings, parents, cousins and friends. Sometimes the person on the end of the line is back home, other times they are in a western city also navigating the dislocations of immigrant life. The long phone call is a regular feature of diaspora lives, and even more so for those employed in long, solitary work such as cab driving. These conversations are about nothing and everything.

This is not an exhaustive list, but based on the calls I constantly field from friends and family, the content I receive in a follow-up call, and familiar themes from chats with drivers in Arabic (which I sometimes get drawn into), the subjects are remarkably consistent. The range includes family gossip, wedding updates, complaints about the cost of living in the west, advice on navigating complex immigration systems, extremely detailed health updates, and political analysis of whatever crisis is unfolding. These conversations can broadly be sorted into one of two categories: “serious technical resolution of a problem” or “shooting the breeze”.

In my experience, these beast mode long phone calls are between someone on a long shift, commute or drive, and a mother cooking in the kitchen. There is a languorous quality to the call. Time and conversational convention shift to accommodate long silences without explanation, as one person or the other breaks away to get on with something – dismount or park or blitz something in the food processor. Because the point is not the actual chat. It is a broadly phatic – that is to say language used for bonding – form of communication, an exercise in yearning and homesickness. It helps us bridge a gap between long distances and absences, and simulate a proximity that is so deeply longed for.

Why talk all through the working day?

The interminable phone call is an immigrant’s lifeline, now made cheap and stable by voice over IP (the ability to make calls on an internet connection). But it is also a feature of broader cultural and economic patterns. Western time is personal, individual, literally “me time”, something that is violated if demanded without permission. This time is parcelled out necessarily for decompression, for work, for leisure. In other cultures, time is social and public.

In Sudan, for example, there is no such thing as calling ahead before a visit. Your home is a drop-in destination from about 11am onwards. A neighbour will pop in for a chat, a relative will be driving home and swing by, and if there are children in the household, their own social lives mean you just never know how many people you are cooking for. The corner shop is a lifeline of last minute provision as numbers swell unexpectedly. If you are an introvert, good luck.

When that physical socialisation is impossible, the phone does the work. Certain conditions make the visit and the call possible. Homes where there is often a homemaker to receive, or work that does not require strict, in-office professional deportment and execution. Highly structured working environments and fast-paced modern lives mean that entire societies are firmly post-casual-phone-call. In these contexts, I find myself so wary of ambushing or alarming people with a call that I send a clear warning beforehand. No, there is nothing to worry about, and are you sure this is a good time to speak? Absolutely no worries if not.

But it is also a mindset, which you can lose over time. I find myself becoming increasingly post-phone call outside work, constantly thinking to myself that I will ring a relative back when I have the time. Generally, I prefer to message or voice note, conscious that when I return the call, it absolutely will not be a quick and efficient catch up. But, in truth, I do have the time, I have just assimilated the same rigid notions of downtime and non-urgent phone calls as an incursion. Fundamentally, this is an extremely capitalist notion of time as purely a function of work, where even if you are not working, you are “re-charging” in anticipation of more work.

Reclaiming the lost art of the ambling phone call

The fact that the long driver call is such a bewildering anomaly is a meeting of those two worlds. In one, a passenger cannot fathom that you might have so much to say to someone over the phone, because everyone you love or want to see is generally within your immediate social reach, and because it is unfathomable to dedicate so much of your precious bandwidth to seemingly aimless conversation. In another, loved ones are in a different country or sprawl all over the world, and without their constant companionship life is just alienation and monotonous work.

But I suspect there is more to the lost art of the phone call in certain societies than just the pressures of modernity. In contemporary life, there are so many ways to feel like you are in touch and in conversation when you are not. So many ways to feel part of some slipstream of humanity, when in fact we are scrolling, meme-ing, seeing news from friends and strangers alike via story updates, while not exchanging anything meaningful or even uttering a single word. Those in exile are acutely aware of alienation, and reach out to remedy it. But for those in their home countries, loneliness still lurks in ways harder to recognise. A phone call is honestly less time consuming and more replenishing than anything else we use our devices for.

Do you have long, aimless phone calls? How do you think your preferred mode of communication connects to your culture? Share your thoughts by replying to this, or emailing us at thelongwave@theguardian.com and we may include your response in a future issue.

Last week, we explored Britain’s fraught relationship with its historical role in enslavement. You shared your thoughts on the publication of the Register of British Slave Traders and the records of enslaved people, and mounting calls for recognition and reparations.

I started to search online for my enslaved ancestors for the first time and discovered that decades of British secrecy means I have no written records of my ancestors to start with. No names no approximate births or death dates. This legacy means I have a family left not literate enough to document their history. Ancient family members that don’t speak English. People who make up their new own names because their family names derived from the slavers. It’s great that we have this info but I wish there was more help in finding the people we want to know about.

Michelle B, based in Stroud, UK

The stories that a country tells itself make a huge difference. Kudos to Germany for making sure that the blot on their journey is never forgotten among their own. Former colonial powers would do well to teach history accurately – otherwise they risk forgetting the past rather than learning from it, and helping to correct the damage that was done while they enriched themselves for generations.

David P.A. Mullings, based in the US and Jamaica

title: How Zach Cregger’s Resident Evil stands out from all other game adaptations
description:
There’s no Leon, Claire or Ada Wong in Cregger’s adaptation. Instead, it re-creates something more fundamental – the strange, terrifying experience of actually playing the game
• Don’t get Pushing Buttons delivered to your inbox? Sign up here
I’ve been surprised by the number of Resident Evil fans complaining on social media about Zach Cregger’s cinematic adaptation of the survival horror series. “It’s not a real Resident Evil movie,” they’ve claimed. Were we watching the same film?
fullText:
There’s no Leon, Claire or Ada Wong in Cregger’s adaptation. Instead, it re-creates something more fundamental – the strange, terrifying experience of actually playing the game

Don’t get Pushing Buttons delivered to your inbox? 
I’ve been surprised by the number of Resident Evil fans complaining on social media about Zach Cregger’s cinematic adaptation of the survival horror series. “It’s not a real Resident Evil movie,” they’ve claimed. Were we watching the same film? Certainly, it doesn’t feature any of the familiar heroes – there’s no Leon, no Claire, no Ada Wong – and there’s a distinct lack of recognisable antagonists and well-known locations. Despite all of this, Cregger’s interpretation is one of the most accurate and interesting video game films ever made.

On the surface, it’s about a zombifying virus that gets accidentally released in Raccoon City by the Umbrella Corporation. These are, of course, the foundations of the Resi mythos. More interestingly, Cregger seeks to replicate and explore the structural and narrative conventions of the series. In the film, the player character, hapless courier Bryan Hodukavich, is thrust into a viral outbreak, with no weapons and no idea what’s going on. He is then submerged into an uncanny shadow world of escalating peril and body horror. The film takes us through a series of locations dragged straight from the games – an abandoned farmhouse, a road tunnel crammed with abandoned cars, a hospital and the obligatory sewer level. As he progresses, Bryan finds increasingly powerful weapons, from a handgun to an assault rifle – but he is always short on ammo. And there are typewriters in at least two scenes!

Bryan’s understanding of the world is shaped, as in any Resident Evil game, through found footage (voice recordings, emails etc) and via short, enigmatic interchanges with non-player characters. There’s a sequence in the road tunnel where a recently infected young girl says to Bryan: “My mom bit me, I don’t know where she went.” This is a classic Resident Evil exchange: in one terse sentence she gives us narrative information and an implied threat – the mother could be lurking anywhere nearby, waiting to pounce …

Aware perhaps of online discourse, Cregger released a video explaining his vision for the movie, and how he has sought to reflect not just the fictitious universe of the games, but also the experience of playing them – that sense of quickly moving through a world of endlessly evolving horror. It’s also been interesting to see theories emerge about Bryan’s role as a sort of NPC precursor to a true lead character, leaving the hints, tips and ammo behind for someone capable to pick up.

I always thought thatthe subsidiary non-playable characters in the early Resident Evil titles had the most interesting stories: affable old Barry Burton from the first game, cowardly helicopter pilot Brad Vickers from Resi 3, Resident Evil 4’s omnipresent merchant. “I’m interested in vulnerable characters, in normal human beings,” series creator Shinji Mikami once told me. “The horror experience is most scary when the player really isn’t sure whether their character is going to live or die – death and survival need to be on a constant see-saw. If there’s a situation where you’re not 100% sure that you can avoid or defeat the enemies, if you feel maybe there’s a chance you’ll make it – that’s where horror lies.” Bryan Hodukavich lives in that space for the whole film.

Cregger’s Resident Evil should perhaps be put alongside Kane Parsons’s Backrooms and Genki Kawamura’s Exit 8 as a movie that is as much an exploration of video game mechanics as it is any sort of translation. These movies make us feel like players, trapped in an unfamiliar nightmare world with its own rules, characters and temporal conventions, which we have to gradually unpeel. Cinema has always deconstructed other media, whether that’s the theatre (Les Enfants du Paradis, The Producers) or superhero comics (Unbreakable, Logan), and it’s fascinating to see video games having the same sort of scrutiny. This is, after all, the most self-reflexive medium – the audience is spectator and participant, the world is naturalistic yet necessarily artificial, with its yellow-painted walls (see: Keza’s newsletter just last week), and its indestructible barriers (to stop a player wandering out of the rendered environment).

So yes, this is definitely a Resident Evil movie – it’s just that the camera pans away from Claire as she blasts another zombie, or Leon as he makes a daft wisecrack. Instead, it takes us just around the corner, to where the huddling masses of Raccoon City await their destiny, with maybe three bullets, two lines of dialogue and a voice recorder.

First appearing as a browser-based game back in 2010, the ragdoll-physics gore-fest Happy Wheels is now on Steam – and it’s just as ridiculous as ever. Your aim is to make it across an obstacle-laden landscape in whatever vehicle you’re given without falling into a chasm or being chainsawed in half, or stabbed or eaten. There are dozens of levels but you can also design your own and share them with the community. I’m not surprised the Steam version has been wishlisted by 750,000 players. This kind of hilarious, awkward, experimental game thrived in the Flash era of the noughties and it’s lovely to see a classic example return in all its blood-drenched, clipart-esque glory.

Available on: PC

 Estimated playtime: Several laughable hours

It’s been weird to watch Microsoft and Sony seemingly trying to find yet more ways to antagonise gamers after concerns over mass redundancies and the death of physical media. Two weeks ago, the gaming site Respawn First discovered a Microsoft patent to serve ads to Xbox players during down times in games, perhaps while loading a level or after a boss battle. Not to be outdone, Sony has filed a US patent for technology allowing players to tap their phone or credit card on a PlayStation controller to pay for digital goods. Call me cynical, but perhaps more convenient advertising and monetisation models are not the best way to win back hearts and minds.

Naughty Dog studio head Neil Druckmann has revealed that there are two Last of Us projects on the go, expanding on the canon of the first two games. Both are in the very early stages of development, and it’s not even known if they are games – they could include a new TV series, movie or graphic novel.

Looking for somewhere nice to visit? Minecraft is getting its first new dimension in 15 years, a particularly lush world named The Sift, filled with pastel-hued meadows, multicolour lakes and bunny-like mobs. It arrives in Minecraft Dungeons II this month, and will be in the main editions of the game next year.

Ace Combat 8: Wings of Theve – brilliant aerial combat game fulfils the Top Gun fantasy | ★★★★★

Playing video games with my 22-year-old son has brought me to tears

Meet the real-life Pokémon professors, the unsung heroes of competitive monster-battling

‘Mum, where did my Robux go?’ :The Roblox scam targeting children

A cosy question from Simon, via email:

“Last year I ended up spending a lot of time supporting my dad during a rough patch with this health, and this led to me playing a lot of Animal Crossing: Pocket Camp Complete on my iPhone. I have found it really soothing during a challenging year but I’ve pretty much exhausted it. [Someone] recommended [playing] Stardew Valley but it doesn’t feel especially suited to playing on a relatively small mobile, nor my limited free time. Any suggestions? Hopefully nothing involving micro transactions?”

Smartphone games can be an amazing tonic during tough times – I’m glad they helped you through them. If you’ve not played Unpacking yet, it’s an extremely relaxing narrative tidying game with lots of subtle emotional touches. I also like the gentle platforming adventure Spiritfarer about shepherding spirits to the afterlife. If you’re looking for more of an Animal Crossing vibe, there’s Wilderness: Meadowfell, a lush exploration game set in a procedurally generated landscape, or try one of the classics from Japanese developer, Kairosoft, such as the Game Dev Story or Jumbo Airport Story. If you can stomach a couple of suggestions with very noninvasive in-app purchases My Leisure Time and Animal Restaurant, have been recommended to me as great life sims with bags of character.

If you have a question for Question Block – or anything else to say about the newsletter – hit reply or email us at pushingbuttons@theguardian.com.

title: Seth Meyers on Trump canceling $1bn in federal funds: ‘Is he adding a waterslide to the reflecting pool?’
description:
Late-night hosts weighed in on Trump’s relationship with tech leaders and the White House’s new AI-powered site
On Tuesday night, late-night hosts discussed a Maha summit in Washington DC, the White House’s new AI-powered website and Donald Trump once again falling asleep on live TV.
 Continue reading...
fullText:
Late-night hosts weighed in on Trump’s relationship with tech leaders and the White House’s new AI-powered site

On Tuesday night, late-night hosts discussed a Maha summit in Washington DC, the White House’s new AI-powered website and Donald Trump once again falling asleep on live TV.

On NBC, Seth Meyers focused on the president’s ill-phrased announcement of the US murder rate declining. “We have the best, uh, murder,” Trump said.

“What are you talking about, ‘We have the best murder’?” Meyers responded. “It’s a murder rate, not a murder rating.”

On Monday, Trump also took issue with the claim by the US ambassador to China, David Perdue, claim that he offered to sell weapons to China, saying: “I think he was probably talking about Taiwan.”

“So wait, are you saying that we have an ambassador to China who doesn’t know the difference between China and Taiwan?” asked Meyers. “That’s like if Mr Met showed up to the stadium wearing a Yankees jersey.”

Meanwhile, health officials in Florida have issued a local state of emergency after an outbreak of dengue fever. “Man, RFK Jr has only had the job two years and Florida is already turning into an episode of House,” the host laughed.

The White House has also rebuked criticism of taxpayer-funded TV ads. They said “they are public service announcements that are ‘reminding Americans to love their country’”, explained Meyers, before quipping: “The clearest sign of a healthy relationship is if you have to remind someone to love you.”

Trump reportedly told congressional leaders on Friday that he was revoking nearly $1bn in federal funding.

“Oh God, what’s he doing to the reflecting pool now?” joked Meyers. “Is he adding a waterslide?”

Meyers closed his monologue with news that the makers of a smart glasses brand have recalled frames after customers reported them overheating and causing burns.

“Well, I hate to break it to you,” he said, “but no matter what smart glasses you’re wearing, you’re gonna get burned.”

On Jimmy Kimmel Live! the host discussed Trump hosting all the top tech executives at the White House for a lunch on Tuesday. The guest list included Elon Musk, Mark Zuckerberg, OpenAI’s Greg Brockman and the House speaker, Mike Johnson, “who was there to ask if there was any way that AI could turn him into a real boy”.

In a press conference, Trump announced that he was “changing the name” of AI from “artificial intelligence” to “superintelligence” “So far, everybody likes it,” he added.

“Yes,” responded Kimmel drily. “I’m sure the guy whose company’s name is OpenAI is very excited about this development.

“The idea that our guardrails against AI are being erected by an addled 80-year-old man … It’s like asking your grandpa to set up a wifi router in your house. You just wouldn’t do it.”

The host moved on to talk about the new AI-powered government website America.gov.

“A White House official called America.gov ‘a new front door for the federal government’,” said Kimmel. “You know, we need a new front door because Trump demolished the old front door to build his ballroom.”

Kimmel added that Trump is still trying to blame all of America’s struggles on his predecessor, again branding former president Joe Biden “sleepy” in Oval Office remarks this week. Ironically, Trump fell asleep shortly after.

“Only a few minutes after invoking the name ‘sleepy Joe Biden’, nappy Don Trump drifted off to dreamland on live TV,” Kimmel said.

This week also saw the second annual Maha summit in DC in an event attended by JD Vance, Robert F Kennedy Jr and Mike Tyson.

“You know we’re screwed when the sanest person in the group has half a face tattoo,” Kimmel said.

title: ‘President of the Unites States’: White House’s AI accord includes spelling error
description:
Donald Trump and six tech executives voluntarily signed the document, which included a misspelling, committing to safely developing AI
The White House misspelled “United States” under the signature of Donald Trump on an accord he signed with AI executives on Tuesday.
At the bottom of the accord on “Super Intelligence”, the term Trump has used to rebrand artificial intelligence, the president’s signature appeared as “President of the Unites States”.
 Continue reading...
fullText:
Donald Trump and six tech executives voluntarily signed the document, which included a misspelling, committing to safely developing AI

The White House misspelled “United States” under the signature of Donald Trump on an accord he signed with AI executives on Tuesday.

At the bottom of the accord on “Super Intelligence”, the term Trump has used to rebrand artificial intelligence, the president’s signature appeared as “President of the Unites States”.

It is unclear how the misspelling occurred or whether it will appear in the Federal Register, the database that contains official presidential actions and other government documents.

Trump and six tech executives signed the document voluntarily committing to safely developing AI to address widespread concerns, sparked by industry leaders who warned the technology is evolving too rapidly to control.

Trump has largely brushed aside concerns about AI harming humans and called for companies to continue developing the technology so the US can become the global leader in AI. Even while signing the accord on safety, the US president praised the business executives for growth.

Trump posted the document containing the misspelling on Truth Social, and the White House Communications Team emailed it out shortly after it was signed.

The Bloomberg News correspondent David Gura appeared to be the first to notice the spelling error.

The Guardian has asked the White House for comment

The accord on artificial intelligence outlined four layers of “controls and audits” that companies will implement to ensure AI capabilities operate as intended. That includes “robust” internal controls and partnering with an “independent external auditor or evaluator”.

Potential internal controls could include empowering a team to monitor and detect that AI is operating correctly and creating monitors to ensure AI technologies will not hack or access technical systems in cybersecurity, biosecurity and chemical threats.

External monitors would also check to make sure the AI is operating as intended and companies could designate a committee of the board of directors to oversee reports from teams operating the controls of the AI.

The accord is the first step in addressing concerns, raised by industry experts in mid-September.

Americans have become increasingly skeptical of AI. A recent New York Times/Siena College poll found that 61% of voters opposed the construction of datacenters, while an SSRS/CNN poll found that 71% of Americans believed the government wasn’t doing enough to regulate the growth and development of AI.

While Tuesday’s document is only an accord, it left open the possibility of codifying the framework into formal regulations or laws – something Trump has repeatedly rejected.

“I think I’m seeing tremendous self-policing,” Trump told reporters outside the White House on Tuesday. “And they understand that they have to self-police.”

The six executives who signed the accord are Dario Amodei from Anthropic; Elon Musk from SpaceXAI; Greg Brockman from OpenAI; Jensen Huang from Nvidia; Mark Zuckerberg from Meta; and Sundar Pichai from Google.

title: Hedge fund CEO gives $3bn to Carnegie Mellon University in historic donation
description:
Unprecedented university donation from Citadel CEO Ken Griffin will go toward building a new Miami campus
Carnegie Mellon University will receive an unprecedented $3bn donation from the billionaire investor Ken Griffin, making it the largest single donation in the history of US education.
Griffin, 57, is the founder and CEO of Citadel, described as the most profitable hedge fund in history. The money is going toward a new Miami campus as well as big investments at the university’s longtime home in Pittsburgh.
 Continue reading...
fullText:
Unprecedented university donation from Citadel CEO Ken Griffin will go toward building a new Miami campus

Carnegie Mellon University will receive an unprecedented $3bn donation from the billionaire investor Ken Griffin, making it the largest single donation in the history of US education.

Griffin, 57, is the founder and CEO of Citadel, described as the most profitable hedge fund in history. The money is going toward a new Miami campus as well as big investments at the university’s longtime home in Pittsburgh.

Part of the funding will be used to develop Carnegie Mellon’s presence in Miami, Florida, where Griffin lives and where Citadel is now headquartered. The rest will support priorities in Pittsburgh, including recruiting prominent academics and making attendance more affordable for students.

The Miami campus will support more than 3,500 undergraduate, master’s and PhD students, nearly 300 faculty and more than 600 staff members, with construction slated to begin in 2027.

$1bn will go toward Carnegie Mellon’s computer science school and other priorities, including financial aid, Griffin and the university president, Farnam Jahanian, said. The school will be renamed the Kenneth C Griffin School of Computer Science.

“Throughout our history, CMU has anticipated moments of profound technological change and responded with new ways of thinking and solving problems,” Jahanian said in a statement. “Artificial intelligence represents one of the defining intellectual developments of our time, and it demands that we rethink how we educate students, conduct research and partner with others.”

Founded by the industrialist Andrew Carnegie, Carnegie Mellon is particularly known for computer science, artificial intelligence, robotics and the performing arts. Its School of Computer Science is ranked as the top undergraduate computer science program in the US.

The planned Miami campus will take a different approach from the traditional academic-major model. According to the university, education there will instead be structured around “societal challenges”.

The campus will concentrate on “challenge areas spanning human health and biological discovery; national security and strategic capabilities; energy and climate resilience; and advanced manufacturing and industrial transformation”.

The expansion also reflects Griffin’s continuing investment in Miami and south Florida. Citadel moved its headquarters from Chicago to Miami in 2022, and Griffin has since increased his commitments to the region to about $2.4bn, according to Reuters. Those contributions include support for a Miami charter school network, the University of Miami, Miami Dade College, public schools and math tutoring.

Griffin, whose net worth Forbes estimated at about $58bn, will also become a member of Carnegie Mellon’s board of trustees. The board already includes hedge fund billionaire David Tepper, a Carnegie Mellon graduate and donor.

The announcement comes one week after Nike co-founder Phil Knight donated $1bn to establish an engineering college at the University of Oregon.

Universities are increasingly seeking wealthy donors to expand science and tech programs as artificial intelligence drives economic changes.

These large donations have generated concerns about how much influence the wealthy class has over higher education.

Griffin has publicly criticized the use of political power for personal enrichment, emerging as one of the most vocal critics of Donald Trump and his administration on Wall Street. Earlier this year, he condemned how the president’s family appear to have made financial gain from their proximity to the White House.

title: Sedum – Playwright tests in English, cheap enough to run on every PR
description: Plain-English browser e2e tests cheap enough to run on every PR. Built on Jev and Playwright, open source, bring your own key. - sedum-dev/sedum
fullText:
Write browser tests in plain English, keep the full power of TypeScript, and
run the whole suite on every pull request for dollars a month instead of
thousands.

Each ai(...) sentence is one step that Sedum resolves on the page, with no
selectors. Everything between steps is ordinary code: Playwright's page and
expect, test data from any library, API calls to seed or skip setup, and
helper functions.

Sedum uses a model for two jobs only: finding the element a sentence refers to,
and judging whether a claim such as "a list of products with prices is shown"
holds on the page. That model is Jev, from TypeSafe. It
returns probabilities, not free text. Everything else is deterministic:
clicking, typing, waiting, verdicts, and exit codes run on Playwright.

Status: pre-alpha. The first alpha is on npm as sedum-cli. The test
format may change before 1.0, and Windows is experimental. Linux and macOS
are verified.

You need Node.js 20.19 or newer and a TypeSafe API key or a compatible provider key.

For a compatible provider, set TYPESAFE_BASE_URL to its API root and
TYPESAFE_API_KEY to that provider's key. Set TYPESAFE_DEFAULT_MODEL if its
model name differs from the default. See
provider configuration.

The example signs in to a demo shop. To see a failure, change its last step to
a false claim, such as verify an error message says the password is incorrect,
and run it again: it fails with exit code 1. If anything is missing,
npx sedum doctor says what and how to fix it.

New to AI browser tests? Read
plain-English browser tests first.

Writing tests in English is not new. Running them on every pull request is
usually too expensive, because hosted tools charge per step. Sedum is open
source, runs on your machine with your own key, and calls a model that is fast
and cheap enough to ask on every step.

The cost row is 50 tests of 10 steps (3 of them AI steps), run about 20 times a
day by a 20-person team, priced at a per-step platform's published
pay-as-you-go rates and at Jev's posted token price ($91 with the cache off).
The speed row is five runs each with every cache off, on one laptop. See
sedum.dev for the full method.

How it compares with other ways to test in a browser:

When a test fails, have Sedum write a report for an agent such as Claude Code
or Cursor:

Then ask the agent to read that file and fix the failure. The report puts the
most urgent problem first, with the sentence and its file and line, the scores,
the page text the model judged, the elements it considered, a screenshot, and a
command to rerun just that test, so the agent can check its own fix. Page text
is fenced and labelled untrusted, so a page cannot inject instructions into the
report.

A test is a test() in a *.test.ts file. Its body gets ai for
plain-English steps, and Playwright's page and context for everything else.

Write {{name}} in a sentence and pass the value separately, so the sentence
stays the same on every run and can be checked before a run. Wrap passwords
and tokens in secret(): they are typed, but never sent to the model or shown
in reports. A file can hold several tests, and each gets a fresh browser
context. See TypeScript tests for the full API, and
examples/saucedemo for a small suite that uses faker,
skips the login form with a cookie, and checks app state behind the UI.

Tests that need no code can also be *.test.yaml files with a list of
sentences. Both formats run side by side in one project.

$VAR reads an environment variable and is treated as a secret. Put shared
steps in a *.module.yaml file and call it with use:. See the
YAML format.

Recently shipped: tests in TypeScript, the first alpha on npm, sedum init to
scaffold a project, parallel runs and sharding, and JUnit reports.

State the outcome and let Sedum work out the actions, then independently verify it:

Goal tests are YAML only for now. Use goal and a required verify claim instead of steps. Supply typing values
through data; before and after hooks remain available. Run and validate the
file with the same CLI commands as authored-step tests. See goal mode
for budgets, reporting, supported operations and recorded limitations.

Issues and pull requests are welcome. See CONTRIBUTING.md
to build from source, and SECURITY.md to report a
vulnerability. Sedum is MIT licensed.

title: Xbox for Sale: Don't Believe Anything Until It Is Officially Denied
description: Xbox is already looking very different than it did a year ago
fullText:
Microsoft’s big Xbox reset looks a lot like what a company might do if it wanted to exit the gaming business or spin off the division into a standalone entity. Amid concerns that mass layoffs and restructuring are a prelude to shopping Xbox around, CEO Asha Sharma remains adamant that’s not the plan.

“Xbox is not for sale,” Sharma told The New York Times in a new profile. “We will do whatever it takes to set the company up for success, and we will look at the right partnerships, the right operating model and everything needed to achieve that.”

The answer, which the interviewer called a “bob and weave,” comes as many analysts are predicting an eventual divestiture of Xbox. The gaming division has always been an awkward fit for Microsoft, whose other businesses, including cloud computing and AI, still dwarf it despite the massive $70 billion acquisition of Activision Blizzard in 2023. As hardware sales have struggled and a big bet on Game Pass failed to materialize, the case for bailing has only grown stronger.

Earlier this year, The Information reported existing discussions within Microsoft around the idea of spinning Xbox off. That could take the form of an outright sale to a separate entity, or it could just consist of Xbox being turned into a standalone subsidiary or joint venture with another company. The reason to do that would be to strip the expensive, high-risk, hit-driven gaming business off of the rest of the company’s books and bolster Microsoft’s financials in the process.

But while killing or selling a number of smaller studios, and shifting others under internal publishing arms like Activision and Bethesda, might seem like the prelude to a potential spin-off, Microsoft’s recent bets can also be viewed as longer-term investments. Gutting Halo Studios and essentially starting over from scratch is a major strategy pivot that might not pay off for five years. The same goes for trying to ramp up quicker sequels to other big franchises like Fallout and Diablo, a new entry for which was announced for 2029.

“We’ve got a long way to go with Microsoft,” Sharma told The New York Times, “and we’re going to take the long-term view.”

title: AI API pricing index -September 2026
description: A reproducible analysis of 80 public AI API pricing records: price distributions, cache and Batch discounts, pricing complexity, and verified September 2026 changes.
fullText:
A reproducible snapshot of 80 public pricing records across 11 providers. Cutoff 2026-09-29; every statistic below is calculated from the same public projection that powers the AICostBudget Dataset.

At least one per-1M-token component

All medians use current public records with a compatible numeric value. Missing values are excluded, never treated as zero.

Across 68 records with a current input-token scalar; observed range $0.10–$30 per 1M tokens.

Across 68 records with a current output-token scalar; observed range $0.10–$180 per 1M tokens.

Across 68 records with both prices. Output generation, not prompt ingestion, is commonly the higher list-price component.

Across 57 comparable records. The observed discount range is 75%–98%.

Across 43 records with a calculation-default Batch input component; observed range 20%–50%.

Document pages, storage, session duration, or time-based units cannot be safely flattened into a token-only price table.

A workload comparison that ignores cache and Batch pricing omits published savings modes for a large share of the tracked records.

14 events: 8 model additions, 3 successor comparisons, 2 lifecycle updates, and 1 time-pricing schedule update.

Time-based pricing schedule updated

The table states the population and method so each result can be independently reproduced.

Provider medians describe the records tracked here; they are not market share or usage-weighted prices.

The source is the AICostBudget public Website projection, generated from canonical provider/model records and linked official provider sources. The population is 80 public pricing records at the 2026-09-29 cutoff.

Comparable text-token scalars are normalized to USD per 1M tokens. Provider and model aliases do not create a second research observation. Null means unavailable or not applicable, never zero.

Cached input and Batch discounts are calculated only when both the standard scalar and a compatible published component exist. Long-context and usage tiers remain separate structured records; thresholds price the whole matching request.

Document pages, per-minute sessions, and token-storage hours keep their native billing units. They count as non-token pricing architecture and are excluded from input/output token medians.

September events use provider-announced or official-changelog effective dates when available. The local snapshot window begins in July 2026, so this page does not claim an industry-wide annual price decline.

Public list prices are planning inputs, not invoices. Regional pricing, negotiated contracts, taxes, routing channels, tokenization, and workload quality can change realized cost.

Full field definitions, official source groups, exclusions, licensing, and downloads are maintained on the AI API Pricing Dataset methodology page.

Link to this dated analysis for the findings; cite the Dataset when reusing the machine-readable records.

Current list prices answer only the first question. Apply them to your own context, output, cache, retry, and routing assumptions before making a model decision.

title: OLAP on GPU
description: Frontier models run on GPUs, and now the database they ask does too. On one GPU, Oliver answers over 6,000 questions a second across 100 million rows, up to 2,529 times faster than asking them one at a time.
fullText:
Zeno of Elea set Achilles a race he could never win. The tortoise starts ahead. By the time Achilles reaches the spot where it was, it has crawled a little farther, and by the time he reaches that spot, it has moved again. There is always one more gap to close, so, Zeno argued, the fastest runner in Greece never catches a tortoise.

He does, of course. The gaps shrink so quickly that all of them together add up to a short, finite stretch of time, and Achilles is past the tortoise before anyone in the crowd notices there was a paradox.

An agent working with a database runs Zeno's race. It asks a question, waits for the answer, and the answer raises three more. Each question is a fresh trip across the data, and by the time the database gets back, the agent has moved on and more data has arrived. A database that answers one question at a time is Achilles on Zeno's terms, forever closing the last gap.

The way out is the same one that settles the paradox. Stop paying for each gap separately. Take every question at once, cross the data once, and the whole endless series of trips comes to one short one.

Frontier models run on accelerators and work in batches. The databases they query were mostly designed for one person asking one question on a CPU. An agent investigating an incident generates dozens to hundreds of questions, a detection pack checks every rule against every event, and a fleet check looks at every series at once. Asked one at a time, each of those questions pays for its own trip through the data.

Oliver is a Frontier Database™. It is built for the way frontier AI asks questions, and it runs on the hardware frontier AI runs on.

A question reaches Oliver as a program rather than a string, so Oliver can take hundreds of them together, work out what they share, and answer all of them in a single pass over the data. On a live tenant, 500 questions over one hour of data took 61.6 seconds asked one at a time and 0.57 seconds asked together. On CPU alone, answering together runs 13 to 262 times faster than answering one at a time.

All of that is on CPU. Then we moved the pass onto a GPU.

A single pass over a lot of data is exactly the work a GPU is built for: one small operation applied to an enormous number of rows at the same time. We put 100 million rows into the memory of one NVIDIA L40S and asked it thousands of questions at a time.

The baseline in every one of those comparisons is Oliver itself, answering one question at a time on the same machine. That is the engine that beat ClickHouse by a median of 3.06×. The GPU runs up to 2,529 times faster than it.

For a sense of scale: a thousand pattern-matching questions take the GPU about a sixth of a second. Asked one at a time, the same thousand take close to seven minutes.

Moving data onto a GPU is the slow part, so Oliver does it once. The 100-million-row window loads into GPU memory and stays there between requests. The next thousand questions start straight away, against data that is already sitting where the work happens.

Detection rules are cheap to write and expensive to run, so teams ration them. On one L40S, a pack of 500 detection rules runs at about 1,300 questions a second, 5.1 times what the same machine manages on its CPU. Every rule can check every event, every time, instead of the dozen someone had time to schedule.

Anomaly detection has the same shape at a larger size. We screened 15 million time series of 128 points each, 1.92 billion points in all, for anomalies on the GPU in 1.66 seconds. That covers every metric in a very large fleet, checked in one go rather than a sample of them on a rota.

A fast answer is only worth having if it is the right one. Every GPU result is checked against what Oliver's CPU engine returns for the same question, and they agree, with sums carried at 128-bit precision. The tier runs on NVIDIA GPUs and on Apple silicon, so it is not tied to one vendor's hardware.

The GPU tier runs in Oliver deployed inside your own cloud account, on your GPUs, next to your data. Tell us what you want to ask of it, and we will set it up with you.

title: The Download: OpenAI's chief research officer explains its hacking response
description: Plus: Trump and tech executives have agreed to “self-regulate” AI.
fullText:
This is today's edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what's going on in the world of technology.

Two months after OpenAI’s agents hacked into the computers of AI company Hugging Face, the company is still dealing with the fallout. Last week brought news of another hack, this time into Australia’s national health-care system, which the government says OpenAI did not report for 84 days.

But OpenAI insists it is not on the back foot. “I do kind of reject the premise that OpenAI is a company with visible impacts in the world and therefore OpenAI is not training safe and aligned models,” says Mark Chen, the company’s chief research officer.

In many ways, the buck stops with Chen. I sat down with him to talk about the fallout from the hacks, what his company is doing about it, and why he thinks things are not as bad as they seem.

Here’s what he told me about making models safer—and why the world is better off with OpenAI in it.

On Monday, MIT Technology Review hosted an exclusive Roundtables conversation about our investigation into the deadly failures of the US’s “virtual wall” of border surveillance towers.

Editor-in-chief Mat Honan, senior AI reporter James O’Donnell, and senior reporter for features and investigations Eileen Guo discussed what the investigation reveals about border surveillance technology and the people who have died in the borderlands.

The full event is now available to watch on demand. 

Read the full “Dying on Camera” investigation here.

When Shubnam saw an Instagram video of a Delhi protest they had attended, they realized a content creator wearing Meta smart glasses had recorded them surreptitiously. The mocking reel drew millions of views, along with transphobic abuse and AI-generated memes.

Experts warn that many others will experience similar ordeals as smart glasses go mainstream. The risks are particularly acute in India, where covert recording and the circulation of images without consent are already pervasive.

The bigger issue is that the smart glasses aren’t just being used to turn ordinary people into targets of viral “pranks.” They’re also becoming a tool of police surveillance.

This is our latest story to become an MIT Technology Review Narrated podcast, which we publish each week on Spotify and Apple Podcasts. Just navigate to MIT Technology Review Narrated on either platform, and follow us to get all our new content as it’s released.

Had he even had a choice about whether to read that article in the first place? How would he ever know if he was truly responsible for making any decisions? “After that, there was no turning back,” says Maoz, now a professor of computational neuroscience at Chapman University.

title: If You Loved 'Furious,' There's One Movie You Need to Watch Next
description: If Emmy Rossum’s tense, twisting story of serial revenge and obsessive police work got you hooked, watch this movie.
fullText:
Furious rocks. Well-written, packed with terrific performances (especially by leads Emmy Rossum, Lola Petticrew, Scoot McNairy, and breakout star Quincy Tyler Bernstine), and offering a nuanced, detailed look at the chain of violence caused by abuse, it landed on a lot of people’s “must-watch” lists this year. One reason it resonated so much is the visceral power of its core stories—the three primary women in Furious are righteously justified in their rage, depressingly limited in what they can do about it, and struggling to keep their heads above water in an unfair world where the smallest bit of respect can feel like the only reason to keep going. If you’re a Furious superfan looking for a movie to watch, there’s an obvious answer: The movie that inspired the show, 1987’s Black Widow.

It’s no secret that Black Widow inspired Elizabeth Meriwether to create Furious, and the connection between the films is pretty clear. The 1987 film stars Debra Winger as a U.S. Justice Department data analyst, Alexandra Barnes, who notices a pattern of suspicious deaths among wealthy men. She eventually realizes that the younger women these men had recently married are all the same person in different disguises—and that this woman (played by Theresa Russell) is seducing, marrying, and murdering these men in order to inherit their wealth.

Black Widow isn’t as complex as Furious. The story is more of a conventional thriller, with Russell’s character more conventionally evil and driven by greed rather than revenge. But the bones of the story offer the same kind of thrill; Alexandra and Russell’s character bond in a weird, subliminally queer way that faintly echoes the complex relationship between Rossum’s broken rookie FBI agent and Petticrew’s broken serial killer. And Alexandra has to battle a sexist, skeptical array of powerful men in order to track a killer and prove that she’s smarter than all of them.

Watching the film, you can see the precise bits of the story that inspired Meriwether to tackle the story from a more modern, more complex perspective. And it’s good to remember how remarkable it was in 1987 to release a major film that not only featured two female lead characters, but two female lead characters who didn’t rely on men to achieve their goals—with one actively treating men as disposable steps toward their own goals (and murdering them). The inversion of traditional sex roles was kind of thrilling forty years ago and still has juice today. If you want to be a Furious completist, check it out. Stream Black Widow on Hoopla or rent it on Prime Video.

Still feeling kind of angry? Don’t worry, there are plenty of other movies that explore the same dark impulses and justified rage against a culture of abuse against women. Here are some that will definitely give you vibes similar to Furious.

If Catherine’s terror campaign against the men who destroyed her before she even had a chance to live resonated with you, Promising Young Woman shares that dark vibe. Carey Mulligan plays Cassie, who dropped out of medical school after the death of her best friend Nina, who was sexually assaulted and eventually committed suicide after the men responsible received no punishment. Cassie now goes to bars at night, feigning intoxication so she can lure and confront men who would take advantage of her, and later embarks on a self-destructive, rage-fueled campaign to punish the people she deems responsible for Nina’s abuse and death. It’s visceral, darkly funny, and Mulligan’s performance will remind you of Catherine in powerful ways. Stream Promising Young Woman on Peacock or rent it on Prime Video.

Catherine is a victim who lets her justifiable rage consume her and drive her to seek violent revenge—and if you love the thrill of seeing a woman turning the tables on the men who seek to destroy her, The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo is your next stop. The novel the film is based on was originally titled “Men Who Hate Women” in the original Swedish, after all, and it introduces the character of Lisbeth Salander, who is Catherine with a little more self-control and tech-savvy. Lisbeth’s story of vengeance against a man who assaults her and tries to impose his power over her is a (thrilling) sub-plot in the book and film, but the investigation into a decades-old murder leads you directly into the same dark, violent places as Furious. Stream The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo on Netflix or rent it on Prime Video.

Furious was both compelling and unsettling because of its unflinching look at cycles of violence and the impact of violence against women. Monster, based on a true story, is a similar exploration. Aileen “Lee” Wuornos (Charlize Theron) is a prostitute who is on the verge of suicide when she meets Selby Wall (Christina Ricci) and falls in love. Determined to make a life with Selby, Lee turns back to prostitution, and after a traumatic, violent encounter, begins murdering her clients and stealing their money and cars to survive. It’s a heartbreaking look at what a lifetime of abuse in a world where women are often valued solely for their bodies can do to a person, and what we do to survive. Rent Monster on Prime Video.

If you found Emmy Rossum’s performance as rookie FBI agent Alice Black the best part of Furious, this classic film from director Jonathan Demme and screenwriter Ted Tally (based on the book by Thomas Harris) is the right choice. Jodie Foster (who won a Best Actress Oscar for her performance) plays Clarice Starling, who is plucked out of training at Quantico to interview the brilliant, insane serial killer Dr. Hannibal Lecter (Anthony Hopkins, offering a performance so good he won a Best Actor Oscar with just 16 minutes of screen time) in the hopes that he’ll offer insight into Buffalo Bill, an active serial killer targeting women. It’s a taut, emotionally rich story anchored by Foster’s performance as a young woman in a male-dominated field forced to confront the violence aimed at women on a daily basis. Rent The Silence of the Lambs on Prime Video.

The character Nicole Kidman plays in Destroyer, Detective Erin Bell, is a kind of amalgamation of Catherine and Alice from Furious—a bent cop who did something horrible in the past and has been punishing herself for it ever since. It’s a searing look at the impact of trauma and guilt that parallels what Catherine and Alice are going through, as Bell initially struggles to cover up her sins and then seeks a kind of absolution, leaving a trail of bodies and bad decisions in her wake. Bell isn’t strictly a victim in the story—she’s the architect of her own misery—but her suffering and rage definitely echo the characters in Furious. Stream Destroyer on Kanopy, Hoopla, Plex, or Tubi.

title: Your Mac Should Be Doing More of the Work. Here's How MacPaw Helps
description: Setapp, CleanMyMac, and Eney take everyday Mac work off your hands without adding one more thing to manage.
fullText:
The work you actually sat down to do rarely gets interrupted by something dramatic. It gets interrupted by housekeeping—a quick fix here, a quick lookup there, each one small enough to feel harmless and just long enough to break your focus.

This is true for freelancers, founders, designers, and developers. But it’s also true for work-from-home employees and busy people in general. And it’s not that any of these tasks are difficult (which almost makes them more annoying); it’s that each one takes just enough time and attention to pull you away from whatever you actually sat down to do. Little interruptions may not seem like much, but they add up to a surprising amount of time spent taking care of your Mac instead of letting your Mac take care of you.

MacPaw has spent 18 years building tools that take everyday work off Mac users' hands by noticing the small stuff you've stopped noticing, and quietly handling it for you. For anyone whose Mac doubles as an office, the files, apps, and projects add up—but the upkeep shouldn't have to.

Here’s how MacPaw’s products help you save time and frustration while using your trusty Mac computer.

When storage starts disappearing, you can open folders one by one, sort through old downloads, track down duplicate files, and try to uncover large files that are eating up space and collecting dust. Or, you can make that maintenance somebody else's problem.

CleanMyMac keeps everyday care in one place, so maintenance takes less of your attention. If you work with video or like to keep many applications open at once, freeing up space can help your Mac work as intended. You’ll spend less time staring at the dreaded spinning color wheel and more time getting things done.

Sometimes you just need an app for one specific task. Maybe you need to compress a video before sending it to a client. The job itself takes two minutes, but first you have to find an app, compare your options, figure out whether you trust it, download it, and possibly even pay for yet another subscription.

Setapp cuts out much of the scavenger hunt by giving you one trusted place to look for the right app, so a two-minute task doesn't start with 15 minutes of searching, comparing, and managing software. It also makes it easy to discover time-savers and cool tricks you didn't even realize were possible on a Mac.

Splitting a PDF or trimming the first few seconds from a video isn't complicated, but if you only do it occasionally, you might still end up digging through menus or Googling it all over again. Eney is MacPaw's on-device helper for handling straightforward tasks like these. Instead of relearning the process every time, ask Eney to take care of it on your Mac.

Go on, then—forget the steps. For straightforward tasks like these, Eney can handle them on your Mac.

There's no shortage of software promising to make you more productive, but finding, installing, learning, and managing all those tools can become another job of its own. The next time a small Mac task pulls you away from what you meant to do, see how MacPaw can help.

And there's more on the way. MacPaw is currently developing its own on-device AI stack for the Mac — an AI runtime called Elix and a memory layer called Mnemos — designed to make its products smarter, keep more of the work and your data on your Mac, and understand what you need before you have to spell it out.

Your Mac should do more for you without giving you more to manage. Explore MacPaw to see how Setapp, CleanMyMac, Eney, and other tools take everyday work off your hands.

Consortium involving ex-Brazil forward Pato seals Northampton takeover
description: The takeover of Northampton Town by a consortium including former AC Milan and Brazil forward Alexandre Pato has been completed.
fullText:
The takeover of Northampton Town by a consortium including former AC Milan, Chelsea and Brazil forward Alexandre Pato has been completed.

Sports Alpha Capital (SAC) had their proposed deal with the Cobblers approved by the Independent Football Regulator (IFR) and English Football League (EFL) earlier this month.

SAC will take a 70% shareholding in Northampton Town Ventures Limited (NTVL) - the company which owns the majority of shares in the League Two club.

Existing owners David Bower, Nigel Le Quesne and Kelvin Thomas will collectively retain a 30% shareholding.

Northampton confirmed the deal would leave them debt-free after announcing a pre-tax loss of just under £3m in April 2026.

The takeover will see Thomas step down as chairman after more than a decade in the role, though he - along with Bower and Le Quesne - will remain as shareholders and directors.

Thomas - who headed the takeover of the Cobblers when they faced a winding-up petition in 2015 - said it had been "an enormous privilege" to lead the club.

SAC's Joao Xavier and Tim Chamberlain will become co-chairmen, with Pato set to join the board as a director.

Chief executive officer James Whiting and supporters' representative Tom Cliffe will also remain on the board, but Jim Rosenthal and Mike Wailing will step down from the board and become associate directors.

In a joint statement, Xavier and Chamberlain said they were "extremely proud to become custodians of a club with such a rich history, passionate supporter base and important place within its community".

"We have ambitious plans for Northampton Town, but ambition must go hand in hand with sustainability and an understanding of what the club means to the people of Northampton and Northamptonshire," the statement added.

"We want the club to continue to be a source of pride within its community and will work closely with the Community Trust, supporters, staff, partners and local stakeholders to ensure that relationship continues to grow.

"We are looking forward to spending much more time in Northampton, listening to supporters and working together to help the club realise its potential both on and off the pitch.

"This is the beginning of a long-term commitment from Sports Alpha Capital to Northampton Town Football Club, and we are incredibly excited about the journey ahead."

Xavier and Chamberlain said that further details of their vision for the club would follow.

Pato was named by SAC, external as one of its investors, along with Gemcorp Capital, a London-based independent investment management firm.

Pato and his fellow investors attended Northampton's 1-0 win over Newport County on 5 September.

The 37-year-old retired from playing last year. He is best known for his five-and-a-half-year spell at AC Milan where he scored 63 goals in 150 matches and won the Serie A title in 2010-11.

Sports Alpha Capital was previously in discussions about taking over Colchester United earlier this year but decided to pull out of a potential deal following initial talks.

The Cobblers suffered relegation to the fourth tier last season, finishing bottom of the League One table, and appointed Chris Hogg as their manager in May.

They brought in 13 players during the summer transfer window, including striker Matty Warhurst from Manchester City.

This feels like a significant moment in the club's history.

A majority takeover by a consortium that appear to have serious capital behind them. This is evident in the club now being 'debt free', a position any club in the country would be envious of.

The debt at the last set of accounts was over £13.5m and is sure to grown prior to today's takeover. That underlines the scale of investment.

There are however still important questions still to be asked.

What is SAC's vision for the club? Just how much finance will be pumped in? How does it improve the footballing side of things in the short to medium term with the Cobblers hovering just outside the League Two relegation zone?

All of these questions require answers.

But for now there is an excitement amongst the fanbase around what this could mean for Northampton Town moving forward.

title: Bahrain GP in Malaysia declared heat-hazard race
description: This weekend's Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia is declared a heat-hazard race, the third time the designation has been used this year.
fullText:
This weekend's Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia has been declared a heat-hazard race, the third time the designation has been used this year.

A heat hazard is an official status for an event where it is forecast that temperatures will be more than 31C at some point during the race.

The Sepang track, near Malaysia's capital Kuala Lumpur, is close to the equator and has long been known as one of the most demanding for drivers.

Temperatures are forecast to be in the 31-33C region across the race weekend, with a high humidity level and chance of rain every day.

This weekend's event is being held in Malaysia as a way of running the Bahrain race, which was postponed from its original April date because of the war in the Middle East.

A number of Bahrain-related activities are being planned across the weekend to emphasise the Gulf kingdom's role in the event.

The heat-hazard ruling means drivers can use an in-car system that flows cooled liquid, such as glycol, through a system of pipes in a fireproof top worn under their overalls.

The cooling kit is not mandatory, but any driver who chooses not to use it has to carry 5kg of ballast in their car to ensure there is no competitive advantage.

Bahrain/Malaysia follows the Austrian and Italian Grands Prix in being declared a heat hazard this year.

The designation was first introduced last year, once the technology for the cooling vest had been developed.

Some drivers prefer not to use the cooling kit because of discomfort, and because there have been issues with the coolant running out before a grand prix is finished.

In that case, the liquid ends up at car temperature, which is considerably higher than ambient.

Temperatures in the cockpit of an F1 car can be more than 40C, and drivers are wearing several layers of fireproof clothing - in addition to a balaclava and helmet - so overheating is a serious concern.

title: Briton Staines' 61-second win earns UFC contract
description: Britain's George Staines stops Loai Abushaar in stunning fashion to earn a UFC contract in Dana White's Contender Series.
fullText:
Britain's George Staines stopped Loai Abushaar in stunning fashion to earn a UFC contract in Dana White's Contender Series.

Staines, 26, took just 61 seconds to rubberstamp his spot in MMA's leading promotion.

The lightweight, who hails from Hull but trains alongside UFC star Paddy Pimblett in Liverpool, slammed Abushaar to the floor before finishing with ground-and-pound.

He was one of four fighters to be handed a contract and was cheered on by Pimblett and fellow UFC fighter Luke Riley as he closed out the show in Las Vegas.

"George, you were up against a massive guy at 155lb and you absolutely destroyed him," UFC president Dana White said.

"It was one of the greatest finishes ever, you made it look easy - congratulations and welcome to the UFC."

Victory extended Staines' perfect professional record to 11 victories, having previously competed under the banner of Oktagon and Cage Warriors.
