title: What will new call-ups bring to Northern Ireland?
description: Before the upcoming 2027 Women's World Cup play-off with Portugal, what will the five new faces bring to Northern Ireland?
fullText:
When Northern Ireland run out to take on Portugal in their 2027 Women's World Cup play-off, they know they will be the underdogs.

That would be the case even if Michael McArdle had a full-strength squad to pick from, but he has had to deal with a lengthy injury list before the first play-off round.

However, disappointment for some leads to opportunities for others, and his 23-strong squad as produced five new names.

Sparta Pargue forward Kess Elmore was a surprise inclusion but her versatility could be key, while Galway United defender Lucy-Jayne Grant is another new face.

McArdle has also rewarded three Women's Premiership players - Naomi McLaughlin, Jane McMaster and Charlotte Havern - with their first call-ups.

But what can they all bring to the international stage?

Elmore and Grant named in Northern Ireland squad

With the absence of key attackers Simone Magill, who is back in training after having her first child, and Danielle Maxwell and Caragh Hamilton, who are injured, the introduction of Elmore to the squad is intriguing.

The 27-year-old Sparta Prague attacker qualifies for Northern Ireland through her father, who is from Lisburn.

Elmore came through Liverpool's academy and made the move to the USA in 2017 to play college football for the UConn Huskies and Oregon Ducks.

Her professional career started with Saint Etienne in France in 2023 and moved to Brooklyn FC for the inaugural USL Super League the following year.

Elmore has Champions League experience with Austrian champions St Polten against the likes of Chelsea and Lyon, and she moved to the Czech Republic in July.

Predominantly an attacking midfielder, Elmore can play right across the forward line and McArdle says "that versatility brings a strength to us".

"The biggest thing for Kess is the attacking prowess she's got as a creative player and an attacking player," said the Scot.

"She's coming in with good experience of playing against high quality opposition, and Portugal's squad is full of players that are at elite European clubs.

"Not speaking on behalf of Kess, but when you get that first call up at the age of 27 it is quite a special moment.

"It's been quite a special few weeks working with Kess in the background, so I'm looking forward to her joining camp and bringing those qualities to the group."

As well as Elmore, another player who has earned their first call-up is Cavan-born left back Lucy-Jayne Grant, who qualifies for Northern Ireland through her father.

The 22-year-old plays for Galway United in the League of Ireland, and she helped the club win the cross-border All-Island Cup in 2024.

McArdle said he had identified Grant for a possible call-up early into this time at the job, and she had earned her chance after he and his staff done their "due diligence".

"Over the summer she's performed well and she has spent time in the environment as a training player, so we have got to know her.

"She has broken through now on the left side of defence, so she'll add to the depth within there with the squad."

As well as her on-pitch ability, Galway's website says that Grant can juggle and is a qualified piano and violin teacher, so should be able to entertain the camp throughout the window.

Women's Premiership players featuring in senior Northern Ireland squads is nothing new.

In fact, before the historic Euro 2022 finals, it was the norm.

While more players have moved to England or Scotland over the past few years, the Irish League still plays a key role for the international team.

In McArdle's squad for the play-off, eight of his players are still based in Northern Ireland, and he has handed three of them first call-ups.

Attacking midfielder McLaughlin, 20, broke through at Sion Swifts before she moved to Cliftonville in 2024.

Her performances at Solitude earned her a move to Aberdeen in January but she returned to Northern Ireland with Glentoran in July, where she has impressed.

"Naomi has had a real purple patch since returning to Glentoran," McArdle said.

"It is exciting for her. She gives us another attacking option and a bit of versatility because she's slightly different to some of the players that are in the squad."

Full back McMaster, 22, has been a stalwart at Linfield and has been a key player in the club's push into title contention this season.

McMaster, who can also play in the centre of defence, has represented Northern Ireland before both at underage level and with the futsal team, but this is her opportunity to win a first senior cap.

"Jane has had a few consistent seasons and come through the international pathway," said McArdle.

"She is having a fantastic season with Linfield and deserves her call-up, which is exciting."

At 16, Havern is the youngest players in McArdle's squad and has earned a call-up after helping Cliftonville to a Premiership and League Cup double, and the Reds are also in the Irish Cup final.

Another underage international, it will be a chance for McArdle to work with the all-action midfielder first hand in the senior squad.

"Charlotte's impressive form with Cliftonville and has been a key part of their performances this season.

"They have helped Charlotte break through into the national team to get this experience."

title: Tom Curry extends Sale Sharks contract
description: England international flanker Tom Curry signs a two-year contract extension with Sale Sharks.
fullText:
England international flanker Tom Curry has signed a two-year contract extension with Sale Sharks.

The 28-year-old has spent his entire career with the Sharks and made his debut aged 18 in October 2016 and his new deal will keep him with the Prem side until the end of the 2027-28 campaign.

Director of rugby Alex Sanderson said Curry, whose identical twin brother Ben also plays for the club, is "fundamental" to the team.

"The terms are a couple of years and that's on Tom's desire to ensure that he's physically in the best spot to be able to honour his contract, to play a load of games for the next two years," Sanderson said.

"Then we both said we'll see where his body's at, at that point, with the want and desire for him to finish his career at Sale.

"He was the one, after some really honest conversations, that said we need to keep this group together, the core group together.

"He's fundamental to us, in terms of being the keystone, really, to that whole group."

Curry added: "Sale Sharks means everything to me and this is the club I have supported my whole life.

"I'm very proud of the hard work we've put in over the last 10 years to get the club to where it is now, but I know how much more we have to give and that's the reason I want to stay. There's no place I would rather be."

Curry, who has been capped 71 times by his country, missed the majority of the 2023-24 season after being diagnosed with femoroacetabular impingement syndrome - a condition that means the ball in the hip joint is not entirely round.

He underwent hip surgery in February 2024 and was warned his career could be over but returned to playing top level rugby just four months later.

In December of that year he had a stem-cell procedure with a view to him being able to play until the 2027 World Cup in Australia.

"He's surpassing expectations, his own medical expectations and what's gone before him in terms of the [hip] injury that he had," Sanderson added.

"We're not seeing any signs of wear and tear at this point and it might come in to factor later down the line but at this point he's as fresh and as mobile as he's ever been."

Meanwhile, Sharks summer signing Courtney Lawes, who made his Prem debut for the side in the 34-24 home defeat by Bristol at the weekend, said earlier this month that players who choose to go abroad should remain eligible for England selection.

Lawes, has won 105 England caps and returned to England this summer, having spent two years at French side Brive where he was ineligible to represent his country.

At present, the Rugby Football Union does not permit players not playing in this country to be picked for Steve Borthwick's national side, other than in exceptional circumstances.

Toulouse back row Jack Willis, who has retained his award as the best player in France's Top 14, has not played for England since 2023 but said this week "it's something I still want to do".

However, Exeter Chiefs director of rugby Rob Baxter has said he does not think the rules should be changed and Sanderson said altering the approach could lead to the Prem being "devastated".

"I just think it would devalue our the Prem, which we know is a really good product with really competitive teams, too much if players were allowed to take the pay cheque, move to France and then get the Eurostar over for training with the international team," he said.

"I think it would devastate the Prem because then players can literally have the cake and eat it, can't they? They can take the pay cheque and there'll be no consequence for playing outside of the country.

"I understand the views of those lads who feel otherwise and we have some in our quarters.

"I'm looking at from a different point of view, from a director of rugby that wants the players and we wouldn't be able to compete to keep them on the books if we had to go against some of the juggernauts of the Top 14."

title: Questions about Wales form not unfair - Bellamy
description: Head coach Craig Bellamy accepts that questions will be asked over Wales' form as they prepare for Thursday's Nations League meeting with Norway in Cardiff.
fullText:
Craig Bellamy says he accepts that questions will be asked about Wales' form as they prepare for Thursday's Nations League game against Norway in Cardiff.

Wales are bottom of League A Group 4 following opening defeats in Portugal and Denmark.

It is now three successive losses in total for Wales - and six games without a win - since they thumped North Macedonia in World Cup qualifying last November.

Bellamy's side will complete what has so far proved a challenging international window by hosting Norway and then Denmark on Sunday.

When asked whether it would be unfair to suggest Wales are under pressure to deliver results in those games given the calibre of opposition, Bellamy said: "No, I don't see it [as] unfair. I see it [as being] as it should be.

"You don't win and you lose a few games in a row, you should be asked questions.

"You'll get some people who maybe will see it and understand a bit, but I don't want anyone to understand. We should always demand and... I'm no different."

Live on BBC iPlayer, BBC Two Wales, BBC Sounds, BBC Radio Wales, Radio Cymru and 5 Live, BBC Sport website and app, plus live text commentary.

This is comfortably the most difficult spell of Bellamy's reign, which began with a nine-game unbeaten run and promotion from Nations League B.

Wales then finished second behind Belgium in World Cup qualifying, but lost at the play-off semi-final stage to Bosnia-Herzegovina.

That was the start of the winless sequence which Wales will attempt to end against Norway at Cardiff City Stadium.

"I knew what I was coming into and I said when I was nine, 10 games unbeaten, there will be moments [like this] - it's inevitable," Bellamy added.

"Now in the moments, you'll see a bit more of me because I think you all thought I'd go crazy but no, I want us as a team to improve and I want to improve as a coach."

Bournemouth midfielder David Brooks, who began the 1-0 loss in Portugal last Thursday, missed Sunday's 2-0 defeat in Denmark and will again be absent through injury against Norway.

Wales were already without a number of players including first-choice goalkeeper Karl Darlow, centre-backs Joe Rodon and Dylan Lawlor and key forward Harry Wilson.

As his side look for inspiration, Bellamy has pointed to his spell as assistant to Vincent Kompany at Burnley as a reason for optimism.

"You never truly get beaten and I'm sorry, it's a cliche saying it, but it's what you learn... how can you improve?" he said.

"I've been there as a player and I've been there as a coach. I went for a whole season only losing two games as a coach [at Burnley] to the next season only winning two games. That coach then [Kompany, who is now Bayern Munich boss], where's he now? What's he doing?

"But it was the moment when he wasn't winning, that's the coach you see now. That's what I got to witness. So for me I'm always, yeah, keep working, keep going."

Norway were beaten 2-1 at home by Portugal on Sunday having begun their Nations League campaign with a 3-2 home victory over Denmark.

That was Norway's first game since the World Cup, when they overcame Brazil in the round of 16 before losing out to England in the quarter-finals.

Norway have fitness concerns over Arsenal captain Martin Odegaard, but Wales can expect to face Erling Haaland, scorer of 65 goals in 57 internationals.

Bellamy dismissed the suggestion that the striker may be affected by news that his club, Manchester City, have been found guilty of breaking the majority of the 115 financial rules they were accused of breaching.

"I don't think he'll be distracted. The guy's a machine – have you seen his record at international level?" Bellamy said.

Bellamy sure Wales belong as Haaland threat looms

Bellamy 'hurting' as Denmark outclass Wales

"He just wants to score - that isn't stopping. He's brilliant. If you love football, you have to appreciate him."

Bellamy, a former striker himself, went on to compare Haaland to former New Zealand rugby superstar Jonah Lomu.

"It's very rare you have a player who's his size and has his mobility," he added.

"When you see certain moments in sporting careers or certain sports, you remember the Jonah Lomu factor, we're coming through the Haaland factor in this present moment.

"Now we will adapt, the game will adapt. How we're able to combat that is going to be another challenge, but an exciting challenge."

title: Olympic champion Muirhead makes curling return with Lammie
description: Olympic champion Eve Muirhead makes her comeback at the Scottish Mixed Curling Championships on Thursday after revoking her retirement.
fullText:
When you've won Olympic gold, you don't enter subsequent events with anything other than winning them in your mind. Eve Muirhead knows that. But she also knows that this is her first curling competition in four years.

The 36-year-old makes her return on Thursday after revoking her retirement when she plays in the Scottish Mixed Doubles Championship in Aberdeen.

Muirhead will reprise her 2022 world title winning partnership with Bobby Lammie - himself a twice Olympic silver medallist - in what the duo hope will be the beginning of a four-year campaign that culminates in the Alpes 2030 Games.

They come into this domestic competition as the big-ticket pairing - having never lost a competitive game - but also as target for the rest of a stacked field.

"We can't put too much pressure on ourselves," Muirhead told BBC Sport Scotland. "I need to remember I've been away for over four years now and I'm just back into it.

"I know our competitive side is going to come out but we need to put things in perspective as well. We've got to remember that it's a long project that we're in."

Scottish Mixed Doubles Championships

Selected matches from Aberdeen streamed live

Muirhead says she has been gripped by a combination of excitement and nerves as she prepares for her comeback.

Six round-robin games across Thursday, Friday and Saturday - and potentially a play-off later that day - will decide if she and Lammie reach Sunday's semis and final, with a selection of their matches live on the BBC.

While the duo know each other's games well, the fact Lammie is Stirling-based and Muirhead trains in Preston has limited their ice time. However, they meet up every couple of weeks and believe they are in a good place for their return.

"We've got pressure on us and eyes on us as a combination but I think we've got to forget about that and just go out and be us," Muirhead said. "That's what we did when we when we won the Scottish Champs in 2022 and went on to win the worlds.

"But the standard of teams in Aberdeen is very, very high - probably one of the strongest ever in a Scottish champs - so it's going to be tough. We just need to curl how we know we can and make sure and do the small parts right and the rest will take take care of itself."

title: English players urged to reconsider Afghan T20 tournament
description: English cricketers aiming to play in a men's T20 franchise tournament organised by the Afghanistan Cricket Board have been urged to think about their "daughters, sisters or mothers".
fullText:
English cricketers aiming to play in a men's T20 franchise tournament organised by the Afghanistan Cricket Board have been urged to think about their "daughters, sisters or mothers".

The inaugural edition of the Afghanistan Premier League (APL) will be staged in the United Arab Emirates later this year.

England players Ollie Pope and Luke Wood have both registered for the tournament draft, held in October, along with fellow Englishmen Moeen Ali, Reece Topley, James Vince, Tom Kohler-Cadmore and Laurie Evans.

Their involvement comes despite the England and Wales Cricket Board's (ECB) refusal to schedule bilateral men's cricket against Afghanistan because of the Taliban's treatment of women and girls.

BBC Sport understands the ECB's policy does not extend to franchise tournaments, meaning players can decide for themselves whether to participate.

The ECB is likely to grant players the No Objection Certificates (NOCs) required to play, provided the tournament is sanctioned by the International Cricket Council (ICC).

The Afghanistan Cricket Board (ACB) has applied to the ICC for approval to stage the tournament and that application is currently being considered.

Last year, ECB chair Richard Thompson used the term "gender apartheid" to describe the Taliban's systematic oppression and restriction of women's and girls' rights in Afghanistan.

When England and Afghanistan last met, at the 2025 Champions Trophy, there were calls for the fixture to be boycotted and a cross-party letter signed by 200 MPs was sent to the ECB.

Tonia Antoniazzi, the Labour MP who led those calls, has told BBC Sport that players considering the APL should think seriously about the consequences of participating.

"Why are we here again? Women and girls in Afghanistan are denied the same rights as those in our country, and the women's team lives in exile," she said.

"Does that not concern the players, especially those with daughters, sisters or mothers?

"I hope the ICC refuses to sanction this event. Continuing to allow Afghanistan full-member status makes a mockery of its own membership criteria."

The five-team APL is due to start on 27 December. A number of Irish and Scottish players, including Jai Moondra and Brandon McMullen, have also registered for the APL draft.

Amnesty International's Felix Jakens told the players to give proper thought to playing in a tournament organised by a cricket board from a country which has "erased women and girls from public life".

"Since 2021, Afghan women have been banned from playing sport, and girls remain barred from education beyond the age of 11," he said.

"Any English player considering the APL, and the ECB weighing their NOCs, should ask what message that sends to those girls.

"And they should use their platform and influence to demand the Taliban reverse its assault on women's rights, not stay silent while it continues."

Afghanistan's women cricketers have been playing as a refugee team since the Taliban took power, funded by the ICC along with the boards of England, India and Australia.

In July, the ICC extended its funding for the Afghan women until 2032 and made a stronger commitment to allowing the team to participate in qualification events in the future.

title: Saints' 'Slim Reaper' on picking up pounds and pointers from Wilkinson
description: Northampton teenager James Pater rose slow and stealthy as a prospest, but his opening-day Prem hat-trick has blown the full-back's cover.
fullText:
Every other year, towards the end of pre-season, Northampton's players are given a pair of smart shoes.

James Pater was handed his first set with his number - 2,110 - inscribed on the sole, earlier this month.

On Friday, he showed how well he can fill a pair of shoes.

With club captain George Furbank having moved to Harlequins, Pater was named at full-back for the Prem opener against Newcastle Red Bulls.

The 19-year-old crossed for his first try inside four minutes, scored his second inside 15 and ended the evening with a hat-trick, and the player of the match award, donated to him by original recipient Fin Smith.

This article contains content provided by Instagram. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. You may want to read Meta’s Instagram cookie policy, external and privacy policy, external before accepting. To view this content choose ‘accept and continue’.

It was a start to spur on the hype. Pater's gliding runs and timely support lines have already been attracting admiration for England Under-20s and Saints age-grade sides.

"James' ceiling is incredibly high," said Northampton boss Phil Dowson earlier this year., external

"He's incredibly fast and dynamic. He always looks like he has time on the ball. He reads space exceptionally well, he's strong under the high ball, his passing is top quality, he's not afraid to carry the ball into contact or take defenders on, and he finds gaps you don't think are there."

Pater made similarly stealthy progress as a teenager.

He only started playing rugby aged 12.

"I always played football growing up," Pater told BBC Sport.

"I didn't start rugby until I went to secondary school and joined Huntingdon Stags.

"Before that it was always football, I played at a high level - Cambridge United's senior development squad. I also played county cricket and some hockey.

"I only got through to Saints academy at 16, which was relatively late. Others were in it from 13 or so. It was coming up to GCSEs and I had to choose to concentrate on something, so I put football to the side."

Around the same time, a star turn helped secure rugby as Pater's priority.

One of the lots in a local charity auction , externalwas a coaching session with England legend Jonny Wilkinson.

"All the parents from our Shelford Under-16s put £50 in and about 15 of us went down to [England's training base] Pennyhill Park to do a kicking session with him," remembers Pater.

"It was really cool, so fun. I wasn't in the Saints academy then, I just loved played rugby and it wasn't something too serious. But to hear his wisdom was unbelievable."

Last season, Pater played his own starring role in a training session. Before January's Champions Cup meeting with Bordeaux-Begles, Dowson gave Pater the task of replicating mercurial France fly-half Matthieu Jalibert.

"He goes for a lot of chip and chase; little kicks through and likes to create opportunities against unstructured defence," remembers Pater.

"I was just trying to challenge our boys and put people into space."

Pater models his own game more on New Zealand's Beauden Barrett, who shares the versatility to switch between 15 and 10, and Australia's maverick stand-off Quade Cooper.

But at Northampton, inspiration is always close at hand.

"I remember being 17 or 18 in the academy, wanting to make it as a professional and watching Furbs [Furbank], George Hendy and Tommy Freeman tear it up," Pater remembers.

Northampton's production line of talent spins at a dizzying rate. Henry Pollock and Archie McParland - both 21 - are a cohort above Pater, and there is always a new crop of academy prospects blossoming at Franklin's Gardens.

"It's quite [remarkable] actually," says Pater. "Before the Prem Cup game against Saracens [in September], we split into two groups for a warm-up game and I was part of the oldies. I am 19, born July 2007.

"You know there's talent coming through. It keeps everyone keen, wanting the shirt and everyone getting better every day. I like it."

Pater's pre-season goal was to come through that competition and feature in half of Northampton's matchday squads up to Christmas.

The other is to lose a nickname. Weighing 13 and a half stone, Pater was dubbed 'the Slim Reaper' by team-mate Chunya Munga.

Over the summer, building that physique to withstand the rough and tumble of the Prem has been a target.

"I want to be more physically robust, win collisions, challenge people at the gainline and be consistent in playing every Saturday," says Pater

"I'm grinding hard in the gym, I probably have licence to eat whatever I want to put on that weight as well.

"It'll just make me stronger and add to my game, so hopefully it looks better out there when I am running faster and beating people."

Pater, who qualifies for Ireland though his parents and was playing in Ireland's IQ programme, external for eligible overseas prospects before being brought into the England pathway, is not looking too far beyond those goals of establishing himself as a Saints regular.

However, it hasn't escaped his notice either that Pollock's breakthrough season, in which the back row earned senior England and British and Irish Lions selection, came, in terms of academic years, in the equivalent campaign he is in now.

Pater has spoken with England A head coach Mark Mapletoft and the second string have a match against an Argentina XV in November which could be a prime opportunity.

"I don't like to get too far ahead of myself and be arrogant, but obviously I've got goals that I want to achieve," he said.

"But it's all based on performance out on the pitch."

So far, so early in the season, that is only counting in his favour.

title: Ex-world champion boxer Liam Smith charged with GBH
description: The 38-year-old was arrested after an alleged attack on an apartment building's night concierge.
fullText:
Former world champion boxer Liam Smith has been charged with causing grievous bodily harm after an alleged attack on a night concierge at a luxury Manchester apartment building.

Smith, who held the WBO light-middleweight title from 2015 to 2016, was arrested after the man suffered serious facial injuries at The Blade on Silvercroft Street in Deansgate on 13 September, police confirmed.

The 38-year-old appeared at Manchester Magistrates Court the following day charged with causing GBH with intent, and was released on bail.

Smith, from Liverpool, is next due to appear at Manchester Crown Court on 19 October, where he will be asked to enter a plea.

The alleged victim reportedly suffered fractures and required surgery.

Smith, nicknamed Beefy, had been due to make a comeback fight against local fighter Ilaru Kujala in Finland on 4 September.

However, he withdrew from the fight a few days earlier after suffering a calf injury, according to reports.

Smith has fought at the highest levels, including against elite champions such as Saul 'Canelo' Alvarez.

More recently he fought British rival Chris Eubank Jr in two memorable bouts, defeating the Brighton man in the first fight in January 2023 before suffering a defeat in the rematch eight months later.

title: 'Business as usual' for Man City Women despite Premier League guilty verdicts
description: Manchester City manager Andree Jeglertz said it was "business as usual" for the women's team despite the Premier League charges against the club.
fullText:
Manchester City manager Andree Jeglertz did not comment on whether he had received assurances that the women's team would not be impacted after the club was found guilty of Premier League financial breaches.

Jeglertz, who joined City last summer, said it was "business as usual" and when asked about how the women's team could be affected, added: "I don't want to comment more around that."

There were seven questions in total posed to Jeglertz relating to the charges before Manchester City's press officer requested the media moved away from it.

The club has been found guilty of all charges related to breaches of Premier League financial rules between the 2009-10 and 2017-18 seasons.

The Premier League said City arranged "sham contracts" with a number of commercial partners as part of a scheme to disguise secret funding of more than £830m.

The club continue to deny any wrongdoing and have until 2 October to submit an appeal.

The women's team were the first representatives of the club to address the media since the guilty charges were confirmed by the Premier League.

It is still unknown what impact the charges could have on the women's team, though BBC Sport understands there is no active investigation taking place from WSL Football.

The charges, which were breaches of Premier League rules, are different financial regulations to the WSL and they came at a time when the women's league was under the governing body of the Football Association.

There is no suggestion so far that any WSL opponents have expressed concern for City's charges, or whether they believe it has helped the women's team progress.

City defender Jade Rose said the women's players had received "the same messaging the public has" from the club.

When asked about the charges raising any concerns for the players, she added: "I'm just here to talk about the football. That's what we're focusing on."

The team took part in an open training session earlier on Wednesday morning and there did not appear to be any changes to their routine or behaviour.

Therese Sjogran, director of women's football at Manchester City, was in attendance for training, as she often is.

There were a few additional media in attendence for Jeglertz and Rose's press conference to preview their Women's Champions League game against Real Madrid.

Jeglertz responded to former men's manager Pep Guardiola's statement on social media, which voiced his support for the club.

Asked whether Jeglertz also stood beside the club, he said: "Definitely. I am working at the club now so that's who I am hired by and working with, so, for sure."

Jeglertz also said he did not find it more challenging to prepare for Thursday's game despite the noise surrounding the club.

"I don't think so. We have been training like normal and doing the work we can do to affect the game," he said.

"We haven't changed anything, we have just kept on doing everything we normally do. Definitely the thing the club has been presented, is the information we have inside of our group.

"We can't talk about anything else and we don't need to talk about anything else at the moment."

Jeglertz added that he was not frustrated by the negative media attention despite City's strong start to their WSL campaign.

The defending champions currently have 12 points from their opening four matches in the WSL and are top of the table.

They face Real Madrid on Thursday (20:00 BST) in their second Women's Champions League league phase match, having drawn their opener against Bayern Munich last week.

title: Football Daily
description: Kieran Maguire & Dale Johnson answer listener questions on the Man City verdict.

title: Criminal investigation? Relegation or expulsion? The key Man City questions
description: BBC Sport takes a look at the key questions following the guilty verdicts handed down to Manchester City.
fullText:
The verdict that football fans around the world had been awaiting for years is in - Manchester City are guilty.

The club still insists it is innocent of the financial rule-breaking charges first brought against it by the Premier League in 2023, and can appeal, so the legal wrangling is far from over.

And the verdict has unleashed some huge questions for both the near and long-term future.

The Independent Football Regulator (IFR) has said the independent commission's decision raises "serious issues".

BBC Sport has taken a look at the key questions in the case and what we know about each of them so far.

The deadline for Man City to make their appeal is Friday.

In previous instances - including the guilty verdicts and punishments handed out when Everton and Nottingham Forest breached spending rules - the appeal was heard and a decision made before the sanctions against the clubs was announced.

The clubs then appealed against the sanctions, too, and had their punishments reduced.

So precedent indicates that City's appeal will be considered and decided upon before punishments are declared. Though that is not guaranteed. And a subsequent appeal against any sanctions could follow.

Exactly how long the process - which will be heard by a new three-person commission - will take is as yet unclear.

One section of the Premier League regulations says that an appeal should conclude no more than 12 weeks after it is filed, and a decision should be made within 30 days of its end.

Procedures can be hurried to meet certain deadlines, like the end of a league season.

Man City cannot make a further appeal to the Court of Arbitration for Sport, but could potentially claim the process was not impartial at the High Court.

The Premier League's statement, formally announcing the guilty verdicts read on Monday, said it wants the process to be "concluded as soon as possible".

The phrasing may not offer any exact insight but the tone - of both the statement, and the strong language used in the independent commission's findings about the length of time the case has taken - is notable.

"It has taken us much longer than we would have wished, and much longer than we had anticipated would be the case when the hearing concluded, to produce our decision," the commission wrote. "That is regrettable."

It is clear that those in charge want the matter wrapped as quickly as can be done.

And it is arguably to the benefit of both Manchester City and all of the other clubs in the Premier League and English Football League to know where they stand sooner rather than later.

City are top of the Premier League, having taken a maximum 15 points from their opening five matches, but whether they are genuinely in a title race will be unclear as long as players, fans, and club owners are in the dark about what their punishment will be.

Were the appeal and sanctions process to drag on beyond the end of the season, it would be possible that legal challenges could be brought by teams who finished below City in the table, or are relegated, or were knocked out by them in the domestic cups, which would be far less viable if the club's 'real' position is known before that point.

There are two key scenarios here.

The first is that one of the sanctions Manchester City are given is so significant a points deduction that they finish this season (or another future campaign, if the process takes longer) in the Premier League's bottom three and are automatically relegated to the Championship.

The second scenario is that they are expelled by the Premier League, which would require 15 of their rival clubs to vote in favour of a motion decreeing so.

Were that to happen, the club's future would be much less clear and would require them to apply to the Football Association for re-entry.

Because the EFL and National League are separate entities from the Premier League, neither would necessarily be obliged to accept an entry request from Manchester City.

And, even if a request were accepted by the EFL, its 72 clubs would have to vote whether or not to accept them.

That is where the possibility of City beginning a reascent in League Two - or potentially even lower - arises from.

There is a huge sporting and financial difference between dropping down to the Championship, with the high possibility of being promoted back to the Premier League after a single season, and starting again far lower down the pyramid.

When Juventus were relegated from Serie A to Serie B in Italy, after being found guilty of match-fixing charges in 2006, they were able to retain some of the world's best players, including Gianluigi Buffon, Pavel Nedved and David Trezeguet.

They were willing to put up with a single season in a lower tier and, when the club returned to Serie A after winning the Serie B title, they immediately finished third and qualified for the Champions League.

If City faced only a single season outside the Premier League, players on long, lucrative contracts would likely be far more inclined to stay, and the economic damage of losing access to the top flight's TV rights income would be hugely reduced.

Guardiola backing Man City after guilty verdicts

Man City Q&A with Kieran Maguire & Dale Johnson

The Fraud Act 2006 states that dishonestly making a false representation with the intention of making a gain or avoiding a loss can lead to individuals being imprisoned for 10 years and facing an unlimited fine, if charges are brought and proven.

"Surely the Man City findings are now a police matter," said Lord Cruddas, a banker and businessman.

"If accounts have been falsified and auditors have been misled then it is potentially a criminal matter. The auditors will call in the police, directors are personally liable for any fraud of a UK company even if it is foreign-owned."

For the case to move from football wrongdoing to something more, there would first need to be an investigation by the relevant authorities.

The bodies who can investigate potential financial crimes in the UK include regional police forces, the National Crime Agency, HMRC and the Serious Fraud Office.

BBC Sport has contacted each of those bodies and been given no indication that any kind of investigation has begun, but some do not routinely confirm investigations owing to confidentiality.

Greater Manchester Police said: "No referral has been made by the relevant authorities in relation to any alleged criminal offences."

But former Manchester City chairman David Bernstein - who left the club five years before its current owners took control - raised the possibility during an interview on BBC Radio 5 Live.

"This is very serious and I wonder whether some of these issues might need to be referred to authorities outside of the league," Bernstein said.

"My immediate thoughts are - can the board of directors continue and should the people involved be suspended immediately?"

Football finance expert Kieran Maguire feels wider investigation may be unlikely.

"HMRC might consider it but there is not a lot for them to go on," he said. "There is certainly no corporation tax to recover. Football clubs lose money and City would have lost more money had it not been for the activities it undertook."

Fans and pundits have been making the point since news of Manchester City's guilt first broke - if they deliberately flounced the rules over the course of nine years, how can their owners possibly be trusted to run the club moving forward?

There is potentially a role to be played by the IFR, which was established in 2025 with the goals of protecting the heritage of English football, ensuring the financial soundness of clubs and promoting resilience in the ownership and spending of clubs.

The IFR awards licences to all 116 clubs in English football's top five tiers, which permits them to operate.

Club owners, directors and senior executives are subject to an enhanced suitability framework - a beefed-up version of the old-school 'fit-and-proper person's test'.

The Football Governance Act 2025 allows the IFR to suspend or revoke licences awarded to clubs as a last resort in cases of wrongdoing.

"The IFR has powers to assess the suitability of owners, directors and executives and we will use these powers where appropriate, in the interests of protecting the sustainability, honesty and integrity of English football where there is clear evidence of wrongdoing by individuals", IFR chairman David Kogan said in a statement.

"This includes taking account of findings made by the Leagues. However, as the proceedings remain ongoing between Manchester City and the Premier League we will await further developments.

"We hope it can be resolved quickly for the sake of fans."

And there is another possible scenario too - government intervention.

In 2022 Roman Abramovich was forced to sell Chelsea by the UK government, following the launch of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Abramovich's background as an oligarch meant the government froze his assets and threatened to conduct a full seizure.

Within three months the club had new owners.

The Manchester City owners are not subject to any action by the UK government, and all that has been formally declared is that the club broke football financial rules.

But the precedent exists that the government can be part of a process in which a football club owner is ousted.

Relations between the UK and UAE - whose royal family controls City's ownership group - were previously strong but have weakened to a degree in recent years.

Any form of ousting would prove a severe test of diplomacy.

title: Djokovic wins first match since Wimbledon in China
description: Novak Djokovic beats Nuno Borges at the China Open to secure his first win since reaching the Wimbledon semi-finals in July.
fullText:
Novak Djokovic maintained his remarkable unbeaten record at the China Open as he beat Nuno Borges to secure his first win since reaching the Wimbledon semi-finals in July.

The 39-year-old former world number one struggled in the second set but came through to win 6-3 7-6 (7-2) for his 30th consecutive victory in Beijing, albeit in his first appearance at the event since 2015.

Djokovic revealed in August that he has been dealing with an underlying health condition that causes particular issues in hot, humid conditions for "the past couple of years" and was far from his best against Portuguese Borges.

During the second set he used his racquet to help stretch his back between games and needed a medical timeout to receive treatment to his right shoulder.

But despite that Djokovic battled to victory in one hour and 50 minutes to set up a second-round match against wildcard Bu Yunchaokete of China.

Playing in the tournament for the first time in 11 years, the Serb, a 24-time Grand Slam champion, is bidding to win the China Open for a record-extending seventh time.

Meanwhile, Great Britain's Katie Boulter is through to the second round in the women's draw with a straight-set victory over Mai Hontama of Japan.

Boulter, 30, claimed a 6-3 6-4 win and will now face Czech seventh seed Karolina Muchova in the next round.

title: Burnham 'really concerned' if Man City owners sell up after rule breaches
description: The prime minister compares the allegations against Manchester City to the plight of his own club Everton.
fullText:
Andy Burnham has said he would be "really concerned" if Manchester City's owners decide to sell up after the club was found guilty of Premier League financial rule breaches.

The prime minister said the situation was "contested by Manchester City" and he praised the club's owners since 2008 - led by Sheikh Mansour, United Arab Emirates deputy prime minister and royal family member - for investing in Manchester.

An independent commission found the club guilty of the majority of the 115 charges they faced, a verdict that City are expected to appeal.

The club continue to deny any wrongdoing and have until 2 October to submit an appeal.

It comes as the Independent Football Regulator – set up by the government in 2025 – said the case had raised "serious issues".

The regulator suggested it would be exploring options – including whether to strip the owners of their licence to own the club – once the disciplinary process was completed.

Among the independent panel's findings were that City arranged "sham contracts" with a number of commercial partners as part of a scheme to disguise secret funding of more than £830m.

The Premier League said City "systematically broke Premier League Rules for nearly a decade".

The independent panel will hold a sanctions hearing – which could take months to convene – to decide the punishment. City can appeal both the guilty verdicts and the sanction, leaving City and the league in a state of chaos and uncertainty.

The punishment could range from a huge fine, being deducted points or ejected from the Premier League, to being stripped of the eight trophies they had won in the affected period.

Some fans and pundits have questioned how the club's owners can carry on if they deliberately breached rules over the course of nine years.

Asked by the BBC's political editor Chris Mason if he was concerned that Manchester City's owners would now sell the club, Burham said on Wednesday: "I would be really concerned to lose them.

"They've been such a huge partner in the building of modern Manchester and obviously the building of Manchester City into the global force that it is."

Burnham, the mayor of Greater Manchester until June, added: "I do actually thank the City Football Group and the wider ownership for the money that they didn't just put into the Etihad [Stadium] and the campus around it but also into the city".

He said he was "of course" confident that his own interactions with City's owners when he was mayor would stand up to scrutiny.

Burnham made his comments amid widespread shock in football about the scale of the independent commission's findings – and the strength of Premier League comments about City's actions.

Burnham was speaking to the BBC from Hill Dickinson Stadium, the home of Everton, the team he supports.

Everton had their own run in with Premier League financial rules when they were charged and deducted 10 points for more minor breaches in November 2023, reduced to six on appeal.

Burnham said: "Everton was in this position a few years ago and you might remember that I fought for Everton in that situation because I still hold the view very firmly that they weren't fairly treated in that process."

Drawing a comparison between that and City's current predicament, he added: "I remember people proclaiming Everton guilty at the time and with hindsight I think more people would say that wasn't fair, the way that was handled.

"So it would be wrong of me to leap to one side given the experience that I'd had before becoming prime minister."

It is "frustrating when people rush to judgement", Burnham said.

He accepted there was "a lot at stake" for City fans, the club and Manchester itself.

But he added it would be wrong for him to intervene.

title: Republic of Ireland will play second Israel game - Hallgrimsson
description: Republic of Ireland head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson says the team's second Uefa Nations League game against Israel will go ahead as planned.
fullText:
Republic of Ireland head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson says the team's second Uefa Nations League game against Israel will go ahead as planned.

Hallgrimsson's side beat Israel 3-0 in Hungary on Sunday after the Republic of Ireland players voted to fulfil the fixture.

They have faced calls to withdraw from the games because of the ongoing Israel-Gaza war, with the 'Stop The Game' campaign - organised by the pressure group Irish Sport for Palestine - issuing an open letter this week calling for the Republic of Ireland to pull out of Sunday's behind-closed-doors match in Serbia.

However, speaking before Thursday's game against Austria in Dublin, Hallgrimsson said the Republic of Ireland will fulfil the second Israel fixture and that he is not aware of a squad meeting to decide whether to play the game.

"The FAI (Football Association of Ireland) has said we are playing both games. That was our intention when we came into the camp and it is still our intention," said Hallgrimsson.

"We are trying to focus on the football. It is already decided we will fulfil the games."

On Saturday, doubts emerged over whether the first Israel game would take place after the Republic of Ireland's pre-match news conference was postponed because of a squad meeting.

When the news conference commenced more than five hours later than planned, FAI chief executive David Courell said a players' vote on whether to play the game passed by a "significant majority".

While fulfilling the game, the Republic of Ireland players did not engage in pre-match formalities, wore black armbands and bowed their heads during Israel's national anthem.

The Republic of Ireland's most recent home game - a friendly against Qatar in May - was interrupted when fans threw tennis balls featuring the Palestine flag on to the pitch.

When asked about potential protests during Thursday's encounter with Austria, Hallgrimsson said: "I must focus on football. I will let others think about security and those things.

"We are playing Austria, the highest-ranked team in the group. I'm not going to allow outside noise to affect me focusing on football."

FAI unclear over possible sanctions if game not played

Republic of Ireland 'raised awareness worldwide' in Israel game - Hallgrimsson

On Saturday, goalkeeper Gavin Bazunu made himself unavailable for both Israel games, saying he felt it "would be wrong to participate".

With Bazunu having returned to training before the Austria match, Hallgrimsson praised the Bolton player and the rest of his squad while hitting out at "lies" that had been reported regarding the goalkeeper's decision.

"Gavin is a great lad. I've always had a good relationship with him and it's probably more tough for him than the other players, but they have really welcomed him," said Hallgrimsson, who confirmed Luton keeper Josh Keeley will take Bazunu's place in the squad for the second Israel game.

"There's been a lot of lies said around all of this, but we welcome him back and he's taken part, amazing.

"I think it shows his character, as well, to be with us, so I want to give him praise for that. I want to give the players praise for how welcome they have been with him.

"Life goes on. He is a part of this group and I think that shows how strong the bond is between these players that even a thing like this is not breaking us."

Later on Wednesday, FAI director of football John Martin confirmed Bazunu was not consulted about his feelings towards the Israel fixtures before he made himself unavailable.

After announcing his squad earlier this month, Hallgrimsson said he had spoken to all players individually, but last weekend clarified that he had only consulted outfield players.

Martin reiterated Hallgrimsson's comment about having spoken to outfield players during the FAI's appearance before the Oireachtas (Irish parliament) Sports Committee in Dublin.

When asked by committee chairman Alan Kelly who spoke to the goalkeepers individually Martin said: "Truthfully, it doesn't appear like anyone spoke to the goalkeepers."

Kelly thanked Martin for his honest response, adding: "That's new information and it's very good information and in fairness that is something that's very transparent."

During his news conference, Hallgrimsson also praised midfielder Finn Azaz, but would not confirm whether he will be selected for the second Israel game after he was an unused substitute in Sunday's 3-0 win.

The Southampton midfielder has family links to Israel on his mother's side, with Hallgrimsson lauding the 26-year-old's "incredible emotional control".

"He's been one of the persons I admire the most in how he conducted himself in all of this," said Hallgrimsson.

"It is about being a member of a team, so you need to listen to all opinions. To do your thing, to do your work with grace and understanding of all opinions.

"Talking about walking the extra mile to being a part of a national team, I don't have words to explain to you and you wouldn't understand because inside camp he has so much respect within this group of players."

title: Trump's tariffs are back in court — again
description: Containers are seen at the container terminal of Nanjing Port, in China's eastern Jiangsu province on September 8, 2026. Most Chinese goods shipped to the United States have faced a minimum 12.5% tax. - AFP/Getty...
fullText:
Here we go again: President Donald Trump's sweeping global tariffs are back under the legal microscope.

On Wednesday, a three-judge panel at the US Court of International Trade is set to hear arguments in a case that could determine whether the president can use a 1970s trade law to impose tariffs on nearly everything the United States imports.

Since late July, goods from 80 countries, including China, India and Japan, have faced tariff rates ranging from 10% to 12.5%. The administration imposed the duties after determining that those countries had allegedly failed to address the use of forced labor in producing goods shipped to the US. The US Trade Representative recommended the tariffs as a remedy, with higher rates applying to countries deemed the "worst offenders."

The rollout of these tariffs coincided with the lapse of a separate 10% near-blanket duty Trump had imposed earlier in the year under a different legal authority. The Supreme Court later ruled that Trump had overstepped his authority, which immediately invalidated the tariffs and triggered $168 billion worth of refunds for importers.

The complaint, filed by the Liberty Justice Center, a libertarian public-interest law firm that successfully won the landmark Supreme Court tariff case, argues that the administration is moving to preserve a predetermined global tariff policy. That, they argue, is an improper use of the trade law commonly referred to as Section 301.

Administration officials, meanwhile, told reporters previously that the timing was to "avoid complexity" that would come from layering the new levies on top of the then-10% duties.

"The real message here that everyone needs to take away is the president is going to always use the tools at his disposal to achieve his trade policy objectives," administration officials said on a briefing call with reporters shortly before the 10%-15% duties took effect.

While Wednesday's arguments may offer clues about how the judges view the case, a ruling could still take weeks — if not months. Either side could then appeal the decision to the US Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit, which could also decide whether to pause enforcement of the tariffs while the case proceeds.

The fight could eventually reach the Supreme Court, extending the legal battle for several months more.

fullText:
Israeli officials alleged the suspect tried to bring down the jet.

Passengers aboard a FlyDubai flight to Tel Aviv on Wednesday sprang into action after a pilot allegedly stabbed another and plunged the plane thousands of feet in an apparent attempt to crash it, in what Israeli officials are saying was an act of terror.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said the intention was to "crash the plane, killing everyone on board" the flight from Dubai.

Passengers described a violent mid-air incident as the unidentified pilot allegedly stabbed the other pilot in the cockpit.

"We just heard screams, and they opened the cockpit and saw amounts of blood from someone who had simply tried to murder the pilot and stabbed him with a pocketknife. Then the plane lost control," a passenger who identified herself as Miriam told Israeli media.

"We felt like we were, like, going to crash. I was already screaming, 'Shema Israel'," she added, referring to the Jewish prayer. "I can't die, I'm my only daughter, I can't do this to my mother."

Netanyahu said in a statement that the plane "went into a spin and began to dive." The passengers were predominantly Israeli citizens, he noted.

The prime minister said that some passengers took a stand, referring to one he said he spoke with after the incident.

"He managed to break into the cockpit with one of the crew members, and together they subdued the pilot who had committed the stabbing while he was attempting to sabotage the aircraft's systems," Netanyahu said.

"Another flight crew member on board entered the cockpit and managed to stabilize the plane," he added.

The flight landed in Tabuk, in northwestern Saudi Arabia, after being diverted.

"I salute the heroes on the flight from Dubai who demonstrated resourcefulness and courage. I have instructed the security establishment to prepare for potential additional threats," Netanyahu said in a statement.

Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz also praised the passengers who stepped up and noted in his statement that investigation is still ongoing.

"According to our preliminary information, the terrorist had a single objective: to crash the plane, killing everyone on board," he said.

Attorney General Todd Blanche and Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told reporters that the U.S. is "closely coordinating with their counterparts overseas," stressing there are "no credible threats."

The flight took off at 7:05 a.m. local time from Dubai, according to Flightradar24.

Tracking data showed the aircraft descended rapidly from 34,000 to 16,000 feet in three minutes.

About 10 minutes after the initial descent, the plane's squawk code -- used by aircraft to communicate with air traffic control -- changed to "general emergency." Seven minutes after that, the squawk code changed again, indicating a hijacking or "unlawful interference."

The aircraft then continued to fly lower at 15,000 feet on average until it landed in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia, about an hour to an hour and a half after the rapid descent began and the emergency signals were sent.

FlyDubai confirmed that the flight "experienced an incident while en route," and landed in Tabuk.

One passenger expressed gratitude to that the incident was resolved.

"We jumped and helped the pilot. Friends, everything is OK now, as you can see we are landing in Saudi Arabia, you can see I am fine. That’s it. We will see in a few minutes what will happen when we land," Itzhak Liber, a passenger, said in a video he posted on Facebook.

An Israeli security source confirmed to ABC News that the Israel Defense Forces recommended that a military aircraft be sent to repatriate Israeli passengers from Saudi Arabia.

However, the Saudi government refused to allow an IDF rescue flight to bring back the Israeli passengers, two Israeli sources familiar with the matter told ABC News.

The repatriation flight landed on Wednesday evening local time, Israeli emergency services said.

"From first assessment, it appears nobody is going to need any medical treatment but we will assess them once more once they're in the terminal," an agency spokesman said.

At the airport, Netanyahu met with one of the passengers who subdued the suspect.

ABC News' Victoria Beaule, David Brennan, Gaby Vinick and Dana Savir contributed to this report.

title: Oil shipments are recovering, but damaged refineries keep fuel prices high
description:
Crude oil is moving through the Strait of Hormuz at a pace that is starting to approach prewar levels, a notable rebound for the world’s most critical oil choke point. 
That restored flow is mainly the result of Iran’s somewhat depleted military capability and a U.S. Navy operation that has secured a portion of the waterway for relatively secure passage. 
Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post.
fullText:
Crude oil is moving through the Strait of Hormuz at a pace that is starting to approach prewar levels, a notable rebound for the world's most critical oil choke point.

That restored flow is mainly the result of Iran's somewhat depleted military capability and a U.S. Navy operation that has secured a portion of the waterway for relatively secure passage.

But the forces driving high fuel prices are not receding along with the development. That will require a lot more than the costly military campaign that is clearing the way for passage of one product at one particular moment in the war.

Most of the refined gasoline and diesel that was moving through the strait before the war is still not getting shipped, a major factor keeping prices elevated.

The rebound of crude shipments "is good news, but we are far from out of the woods," said Bob McNally, founder of the research firm Rapidan Energy Group. "The market realizes that. We have dug ourselves into a deep deficit over the last several months, and this only reduces it. It does not get us back to where we were."

Crude oil prices dipped Tuesday - largely as a response to Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline resuming limited operations. The price of Brent crude, the global benchmark for oil, remained above $100 a barrel Wednesday morning, roughly 40 percent higher than it was when the Iran war began in February.

The outlook for the war and for oil was further clouded on Wednesday, when the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations Centre reported that three vessels carrying fuel through a corridor of the strait the U.S. military has been trying to protect had been attacked the day before.

Meanwhile, the price of a gallon of regular gas in the United States is averaging $4.43, and diesel is at $6.41, according to AAA.

Analysts warn that even sustained deliveries of crude through the Strait of Hormuz at prewar levels would not do much to meaningfully bring down global prices in the coming weeks.

They note that oil inventories are depleted and need to be replenished. Refining infrastructure in the Middle East has been badly damaged and will take time to repair - all the while remaining vulnerable to further attacks.

As a result of that constrained capacity, gasoline and diesel shipments through the strait - crucial to bringing prices down for consumers - remain just a fraction of what they were before the war.

"Nobody consumes crude oil directly," said Mark Finley, an oil markets scholar at Rice University's Baker Institute for Public Policy. "It has to be made into something useful, like diesel or jet fuel or gasoline. The world's refining system that turns crude oil into useful products is severely strained."

As if to punctuate the point that the emergency is not over and inventories of everything are running low, the U.S. Energy Department on Tuesday announced it would release another 40 million barrels from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve, which is already at its lowest level since 1983.

"We have dug ourselves into a big hole," Finley said.

There is general agreement in the oil industry that most of the crude still getting blocked in the Strait of Hormuz is Iranian, and that is by design. The U.S. is trying to put economic pressure on the regime and choke off its funding stream for its military activities.

As far as how much non-Iranian crude is getting through, ship tracking firms offer somewhat different estimates.

According to Kpler, the week ending Sept. 27 averaged nearly 12.5 million barrels per day, just 1 million barrels below the "pre-war baseline."

Windward, another ship tracking platform, estimated closer to 10 million barrels per day.

"This is not trivial," said Ami Daniel, Windward's co-founder and CEO. "The U.S. military has done a fantastic job facilitating consistent shipments."

The amount of oil getting through, though, does continue to swing wildly. There were days in September where only a few million barrels transited the strait, according to ship tracking data.

The restored flows depend on extremely costly U.S. Navy assistance and dark-fleet work-arounds that could unravel with a renewed Iranian military campaign.

Markets remain skeptical that the shipments of crude can continue at prewar levels absent a major diplomatic breakthrough between the U.S. and Iran.

"Maintaining the American military presence required to keep significant volumes of oil moving through the Strait comes at an enormous financial and operational cost," Danny Citrinowicz, a Middle East security scholar at the Atlantic Council, posted Tuesday on X.

"The real test is whether Washington can turn its military advantage into a durable situation in which oil flows normally, insurance and transportation costs decline, the extraordinary U.S. military deployment can be reduced, and Iran effectively loses Hormuz as a tool of strategic coercion," Citrinowicz wrote. "We are not there yet."

Even full restoration of shipping through the strait, McNally warned, would not bring markets back to where they were at the beginning of the year.

Iran has shifted its attacks away from the strait toward oil infrastructure on land, which in some cases can be even more damaging. One such recent attack disabled Saudi Arabia's key East-West pipeline, which had been delivering 7 million barrels of crude each day. The pipeline has been only partially restored, and analysts say it remains extremely vulnerable to further targeting.

"Iran may be losing control of Hormuz, but it retains the ability to disable critical infrastructure," McNally said. "This progress can be quickly offset by the Iranians and their allies hitting those fixed assets."

Karen DeYoung contributed to this report.

fullText:
NASHVILLE, Tenn. (AP) — Tennessee's execution of Christa Gail Pike for a murder she committed at age 18 was halted Wednesday about an hour before it was set to begin, as a federal appeals court sought to review whether her allegations of childhood sexual abuse and rape were fully considered at her sentencing.

Pike, now 50, and her boyfriend were convicted of the 1995 stabbing and beating of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, their classmate at a job training facility in Knoxville. She would have been the first woman executed in Tennessee in at least 200 years.

The 6th Circuit U.S. Court of Appeals halted the execution on a 2-1 vote after execution witnesses and others gathered at the Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville.

Tennessee's attorney general immediately appealed the stay to the U.S. Supreme Court. Witnesses and media remained at the prison in case the high court allows the execution to proceed. Media witnesses were brought into the prison about 10:15 a.m. to wait.

More than 30 people, some wearing shirts that said "Love Heals," gathered in a fenced-in area outside the prison while police on horses watched nearby.

The case garnered widespread attention at the time of the killing in part because a pentagram that was carved on Slemmer's body and other elements of the crime stoked fears of Satan worship during the "satanic panic" of the 1980s and 1990s.

As the execution date drew near, it renewed debate over the death penalty for young offenders.

Pike does not deny committing the killing, but her supporters argue the state should consider Pike's age at the time, mental illness and a history of severe sexual abuse that included being raped from the time she was a toddler. Assistant Federal Defender Stephen Ferrell said Pike's death sentence is an outlier because other 18-year-olds in Tennessee have had such sentences vacated.

After the killing, Pike was diagnosed with bipolar disorder and post-traumatic stress disorder. In her clemency petition she said she only wanted to fight Slemmer but killed her in a frenzied attack when she couldn't "put the brakes on."

"I was a mentally ill 18-year-old kid. It took me numerous years to even realize the gravity of what I'd done. Even more to accept how many lives I affected. I took the life of someone's child, sister, friend. It sickens me now to think I had the ability to commit such a crime," Pike said in a statement.

Slemmer's mother wants the lethal injection to go forward, saying she has waited decades to see Pike's sentence carried out.

"Every time I think about it, I think about Colleen feeling that pain and trying to get up and run," May Martinez told The Associated Press in a telephone interview on Saturday.

Martinez said a group helped raise money so she and her husband could travel from Florida to witness the execution. She didn't respond to a message Wednesday after the execution was halted.

Martinez said her daughter's age should matter too in deciding Pike's fate.

"Not a day goes by, or a minute goes by that I do not think about Colleen. Holidays are the worst," she said, noting that her daughter would have turned 51 earlier in September.

The killing rocked the city of Knoxville. Prosecutors said Pike, fearing Slemmer was trying to steal her boyfriend, lured her to a wooded area on Jan. 12, 1995. Pike cut Slemmer with a box cutter and beat her with a large chunk of asphalt. Shipp, Pike's boyfriend, has admitted that he was the one who carved a pentagram, a star-shaped symbol associated with Satan, into her body.

Shipp was 17 when the crime happened and received a sentence of life in prison with the possibility of parole. Pike was the only one sentenced to death.

Tennessee has not executed a woman for at least 200 years, according to Robin M. Maher, executive director of the Death Penalty Information Center. Older records can be spotty, though, so it's difficult to know precise details about the last woman who was put to death there.

It's a rarity across the U.S. Since 1976, 18 women have been put to death in the country, representing about 1% of all executions, according to the center.

Most recently, Missouri in 2023 executed Amber McLaughlin for a 2003 killing, in what is believed to be the first execution of a transgender woman in the U.S. In 2021, the federal government executed Lisa Montgomery, marking the first time in nearly seven decades that the U.S. government put a female inmate to death.

Pike would be the 30th person executed in the U.S. this year. Florida carried out its 16th execution of 2026 on Tuesday.

title: Johnny Walker ready to reveal full potential in UFC 332 heavyweight debut: ‘I suffered a lot’
description: Johnny Walker arrived at the UFC in 2019 with a lot of hype, winning his first three fights in spectacular fashion: all via wild knockout, all earning him a Performance of the Night bonus. But things got wobbly from there. He’d win some, he’d lose some. He’d injure himself performing the worm. Now he’s 1-3-1 […]
fullText:
Johnny Walker arrived at the UFC in 2019 with a lot of hype, winning his first three fights in spectacular fashion: all via wild knockout, all earning him a Performance of the Night bonus. But things got wobbly from there. He'd win some, he'd lose some. He'd injure himself performing the worm.

Now he's 1-3-1 over his last five and relegated to the early prelims of UFC 332 this Saturday, October 3rd where he faces 10-1 U.K. heavyweight Mick Parkin. Walker expects the move from light heavyweight to heavyweight to make a big difference, based on how hard the cut was affecting his life and training camp.

"It's weird because I usually suffer a lot," Walker told MMA Fighting's Jose Youngs. "It's not hard, but it's a lot of work that I have to do for light heavyweight. And now it's just normal life."

Johnny Walker is thriving at heavyweight during #UFC332 fight week:

"[At light heavyweight], in the middle of a spar, I would have to wait. It's not my heart or my breath. Everything would get dark and dizzy. … I was a heavyweight cutting to 205."

(🎥 @JoseYoungs) pic.twitter.com/Vk8p8hIQSl

"When I was light heavyweight, one month before the fight, like the last three weeks where you can train, I couldn't," Walker revealed. "I'd have when you feel everything [going] dark, like 'Wait, wait, wait.' In the middle of a spar, we'd have to wait. It's not my heart and it's not my breath. It's just everything's getting dark. Like [buzzing noise in ears] and dizzy. And then let's go, back to sparring. It's crazy, no?"

"Now I can train strong until the last week. Even this week I can train with somebody. I don't need [to wait] any more. I'm ready, just technique. I do the strategy, the technique. Nothing hurts and nothing is depleted. Without glycogen. I have full glycogen in my body. I'm ready to perform, so I'm really excited to put the show on."

Walker's heavyweight debut was originally set to go down August 1st in Belgrade, but an injury to his opponent has given him two more months to settle into the weight class. We'll see how the new division looks on him when he faces Parkin this Saturday in Salt Lake City, Utah.

title: Could Trent Alexander-Arnold Ever Return To Liverpool?
description: Trent Alexander-Arnold's Real Madrid career continues to confuse with the right back back in Thomas Tuchel's good graces for England.
fullText:
Handed an opportunity from the start for England against Czechia on Tuesday, Trent Alexander-Arnold demonstrated why he remains a big part of The Three Lions' future. Indeed, the 27-year-old was one of the best players on the pitch as Thomas Tuchel's team claimed a 2-0 win in the UEFA Nations League.

Alexander-Arnold set up Anthony Gordon for the opening goal of the game and was a constant source of creativity down the right side as England controlled matters. One wonders if it was a performance that made Tuchel rue not taking the Real Madrid full back to the 2026 World Cup.

"We never doubted that he can produce these kind of assists," said Tuchel afterwards."I think the second half the position, a bit of a deeper position, suited him more than the higher position in the first half. Overall, I think we had a good and professional performance. Of course the red card is such a heavy influence in the game.

"We need to keep focused, and Trent was a big help in this, because he's very secure on the ball and can be decisive with his crosses. He did this solid defending and one decisive action that helped us score, so a good performance overall."

Watching Alexander-Arnold start on his personal road to redemption as an England player might have raised fresh questions in the minds of Liverpool supporters. The Anfield club has yet to truly replace the 27-year-old who is struggling to hold down a starting spot at Real Madrid. Jose Mourinho seems to favour Denzel Dumfries at right back.

And yet his personal situation at Real Madrid and Liverpool's failure to move on from Alexander-Arnold means all parties should consider a reunion, as difficult as that would be for some supporters to accept. Everyone would be better off for recognising the mistakes that were made in the past.

Tuchel has given Alexander-Arnold a second chance in the England team and is reaping the rewards of that decision. Liverpool should consider doing something similar by offering the 27-year-old a route back to his boyhood club. Alexander-Arnold certainly still has the quality to perform at the elite level.

This article was originally published on Forbes.com

title: Yankees' Cam Schlittler sends message after dominant playoff performance vs. Red Sox
description: Great start to the AL playoffs for the Yankees ace.
fullText:
Yankees' Cam Schlittler sends message after dominant playoff performance vs. Red Sox originally appeared on The Sporting News. Add The Sporting News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.

The Yankees couldn't have asked for much more from Cam Schlittler.

With New York opening its postseason against its biggest rival and Aaron Judge unavailable, Schlittler delivered one of the biggest performances of his young career Tuesday night. The right-hander struck out 10 over 6 1/3 scoreless innings as New York hammered Boston 9-0 in Game 1 of the American League Wild Card Series at Yankee Stadium.

Schlittler allowed only three hits while walking two. More importantly, he never allowed the Red Sox to generate the kind of momentum that can quickly change a short postseason series. And afterward, Schlittler made sure to acknowledge the missing Yankees captain.

Judge wasn't available for the Wild Card Series because of a strained right calf, creating an enormous hole in New York's lineup. Schlittler helped make that absence much easier to handle.

The Yankees starter attacked Boston from the beginning, giving New York's offense plenty of time to build a lead.

Ben Rice eventually made sure it became a blowout. Rice homered twice and drove in six runs, including a grand slam, providing more than enough offense for Schlittler and the New York bullpen.

It was exactly the kind of complementary baseball teams hope to find in October.

MORE: Yankees-Red Sox again, a White Sox shocker and a Dodgers three-peat chase: 10 MLB playoff storylines to watch

The victory completely changes the complexion of the best-of-three series. Instead of facing pressure entering Wednesday, New York now has an opportunity to eliminate Boston and advance without needing a deciding Game 3.

Schlittler's performance also carries implications beyond Tuesday.

If New York advances, knowing it can receive that kind of outing from Schlittler gives manager Aaron Boone another legitimate postseason weapon. The Yankees entered October without Judge available for this round, creating obvious questions about whether they could compensate for the loss of their biggest offensive star.

For at least one night, the answer was emphatic.

Schlittler supplied the pitching.

And the Yankees are suddenly one victory away from moving on.

Five games remained, but Goldson has now admitted he already believed the title race was over.

Speaking to Open Goal, Goldson was asked whether he knew after the Dundee draw that Rangers had lost the league.

Goldson replied: "I felt like I was in a good place then all of a sudden it's like a train hits you 100 miles per hour. Do you know what I mean? You feel the whole thing.

"Yeah. Done. And like physically then it hits you mentally. So even though like physically you don't feel great in the season but mentally you're winning, you're winning, you've won the cup, you're going for the league, you keep yourself going.

"But then after it when you lose at Ross County then you're going up to Dundee. Mentally you're finished, physically my body was in pieces."
