title: From future number one to top of Dortmund’s wishlist: Nine Germany players who could debut against Serbia
description: Jürgen Klopp’s Germany era started with underwhelming results and performances against the Netherlands and Greece, but the extended international break is mainly used to experiment, with five playe...
fullText:
Jürgen Klopp's Germany era started with underwhelming results and performances against the Netherlands and Greece, but the extended international break is mainly used to experiment, with five players already making their senior international debuts.

That number will certainly increase when the four-time World Cup winners face Serbia and Greece in the first week of October. Here is the list of players who could follow in the footsteps of Philipp Treu, Younes Ebnoutalib, Yannik Engelhardt, Bambasé Conté and Hennes Behrens.

Jonas Urbig (23, GK, FC Bayern)

Including his selection to accompany the 59-year-old in the pre-match press conference, all signs are pointing towards Urbig making his debut in Germany's goal against Serbia. FC Bayern's shot-stopper is touted to be Manuel Neuer's long-term replacement at both club and country level.

With the 41-year-old facing multiple setbacks, Urbig has already featured 34 times for the Rekordmeister, including 20 Bundesliga starts. Klopp confirmed that he'll be behind Marc-André ter Stegen in the pecking order, but the former Köln goalie will be expected to make his international debut on Thursday at Allianz Arena.

Köln prodigy El Mala was in the headlines throughout the entire summer transfer market. Both Brentford and Borussia Dortmund were very close to agreeing to a deal with Köln, but the 20-year-old attacker eventually extended his contract.

However, like Köln's legendary number ten Lukas Podolski, he'll surely leave the club in the near future if he maintains his current performance level. Julian Nagelsmann did nominate El Mala for the national team during the World Cup qualifiers, but he was only an unused substitute in the win over Luxembourg.

Finn Jeltsch (20, CB, Stuttgart)

Another uncapped 20-year-old in Klopp's second squad, Jeltsch is on FC Bayern's wishlist for quite some time. The 2024/25 DFB-Pokal winner started all six games for Stuttgart at the start of the season.

The Nürnberg academy product could return to Bavaria if the move to the German giants finally materialized, although recent reports added Real Madrid and Arsenal to the race. Including captaining the U21 side, Jeltsch played a total of 43 games for Germany youth national teams.

The central midfielder is one of the surprise inclusions in Klopp's extended squad for his first four games in charge of Germany. From the previous six Germans in Celtic's history, only the right-back Andreas Hinkel played for the national team while he was still at the club.

Baur joined the Scottish champions after helping Paderborn to a Bundesliga promotion. While Celtic's start to the campaign left plenty to ponder with yet another Champions League elimination and defeats to fierce rivals Rangers, he personally settled well at his first club outside Germany.

Vitaly Janelt (28, CM, Brentford)

If he gets his chance either against Serbia or Greece, Janelt will be Klopp's oldest debutant among the outfield players. The 28-year-old conceded that he was very close to giving up on waiting for his first international call.

In addition to the extended squad list, Brentford's unbeaten start to the Premier League campaign certainly helped the Hamburg-born midfielder in ending that wait. Janelt played every minute so far this season as he scored in the first two home games before captaining his side against Bournemouth and Chelsea before the international break.

Felix Keidel (23, DM, Elversberg)

The all-rounder was playing 3. Liga football with Ingolstadt in the 2024/25 season. When he left his childhood club in a move that cost Elversberg €400k, there was no way he'd expect such a quick turnaround in his career.

After helping the minnows to their first-ever promotion to the Bundesliga, Keidel scored against Borussia Mönchengladbach with a spectacular free-kick. The 23-year-old has never played for Germany youth national teams before receiving Klopp's surprising call.

Derry Scherhant (23, LW, Freiburg)

After Treu's excellent debut, Scherhant could be the next Freiburg star to make his first appearance for Germany. The former Hertha BSC winger displaced Freiburg's legend Vincenzo Grifo from the starting lineup with his strong start to the campaign.

The 23-year-old attacker already registered nine direct goal contributions across three competitions for Julian Schuster's overachieving side. Florian Wirtz was Nagelsmann's preferred option on the left wing during the World Cup, while Scherhant will now compete with El Mala, Kevin Schade and Chris Führich for regular squad spots.

Finn Dahmen (28, GK, Augsburg) and Noah Atubolu (24, GK, Freiburg)

Although it's highly unlikely that they will play against Serbia, either Dahmen or Atubolu could get a chance away in Greece. Both Marc ter Stegen and Alexander Nübel left the squad after playing a game each in the first two fixtures of the UEFA Nations League campaign.

Dahmen and Atubolu are now ahead of Oliver Baumann, who was Germany's number one before Neuer's return from retirement for the World Cup, but they will most likely miss out when Klopp announces his 23-man squad for the next international break in November.

title: Brandt Snedeker criticised for making ‘infuriating’ mistake with Scottie Scheffler at the Presidents Cup
description: Johnson Wagner has suggested that he cannot understand why Brandt Snedeker decided to sit Scottie Scheffler out on Saturday afternoon at the Presidents Cup given how perfect his game is for foursomes. Scheffler had an odd week at Medinah.
fullText:
Johnson Wagner has suggested that he cannot understand why Brandt Snedeker decided to sit Scottie Scheffler out on Saturday afternoon at the Presidents Cup given how perfect his game is for foursomes.

Scheffler had an odd week at Medinah. The world number one has struggled to find anything like his best form when representing his country in team events. And while he did end the Presidents Cup with a record of three wins from four matches, it is fair to say that Team USA do not appear to be any closer to working out just how to get the best out of him.

Scheffler was paired with Sam Burns for each of the first three sessions in Illinois. They won both of their fourball matches, but were beaten by Corey Conners and Nick Taylor in the foursomes on Friday.

Burns had arguably been the better performer within their partnership, so it was not entirely shocking to see Scheffler sit out Saturday afternoon. It certainly says a lot that there was not huge uproar even with Brandt Snedeker's team going into the penultimate session three points behind.

Interestingly, Johnson Wagner did have a problem with Snedeker's decision. Speaking on CBS Sports, he criticised when the captain decided to rest Scheffler. He also questioned only using Jacob Bridgeman in the foursomes.

"Scottie Scheffler is the best driver of the golf ball in the world. He's the best iron player in the world. He's got one of the best short games in the world, and he's become a great putter. The fact that you're going to sit him once is fine. Sit him in best ball, don't sit him in foursomes! He's built to play alternate shot. You could pair him with anybody on that team and they would go out and win foursomes. It's infuriating," he said.

"The way he handled Jackson Koivun, not putting him out in foursomes was brilliant. Let him go play best ball with Justin Thomas. Why he did that to Jacob Bridgeman, it befuddles me."

There is a real problem with Wagner's comments about Scheffler.

Of course, few are coming away from the Presidents Cup claiming that Snedeker did a good job. Ultimately, the American team bailed themselves out in the singles after looking set to suffer an embarrassing defeat on home soil.

However, there was very good reason to rest Scheffler, particularly if the alternative was sending him out with Burns for a fourth time.

Scheffler now has a record of 1-8-0 in foursomes for Team USA. That would be a humiliating record for the last man in on the International Team, let alone a four-time major champion.

Given that he ended up going up against Nico Echavarria in singles – something that was always likely to happen once Snedeker put Scheffler's name forward first – there was an opportunity to put the 30-year-old out on Saturday afternoon alongside a brand new partner.

Perhaps they would have lost again, but it could have provided helpful information ahead of the Ryder Cup next year.

This year's Presidents Cup confirmed that Jim Furyk must use Chris Gotterup and Cameron Young together at Adare Manor, with the pair stealing the show on Saturday.

Had Scheffler played well alongside someone new on Saturday afternoon, that would have built at least some excitement.

title: Ben Rice explodes for historic Yankees playoff performance against Red Sox
description: Rice stepped up in Game 1, putting rival Red Sox on the brink.
fullText:
Ben Rice explodes for historic Yankees playoff performance against Red Sox originally appeared on The Sporting News. Add The Sporting News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.

Aaron Judge wasn't in the Yankees lineup Tuesday night.Ben Rice made sure New York still had plenty of power.

Rice delivered the offensive performance of the night in the Yankees' 9-0 victory over the Boston Red Sox in Game 1 of their American League Wild Card Series, homering twice and driving in six runs.

One of those swings was a grand slam. On a night when much of the attention surrounding New York centered on who wasn't playing, Rice gave Yankees fans a different story.

Rice's emergence has been anything but conventional. The former Dartmouth standout has developed into an important part of New York's offense, and Tuesday provided his biggest opportunity yet to introduce himself to a national postseason audience.

Rice's two home runs gave starter Cam Schlittler more than enough breathing room. Schlittler struck out 10 while working 6 1/3 scoreless innings, combining with Rice to turn what could have been a tense rivalry game into a comfortable New York victory.

The performance was particularly important considering Judge was unavailable because of a calf injury. Replacing Judge's production isn't realistic for any one player.

Rice didn't need to replace him.

For one night, he simply became the most dangerous hitter in the ballpark.

MORE: Yankees' Cam Schlittler sends message after dominant playoff performance vs. Red Sox

The beauty and cruelty of the Wild Card Series is how quickly everything changes.

Boston entered Tuesday needing two wins to advance. After one night, the Red Sox are one loss from elimination. New York can finish the series Wednesday and avoid exposing itself to the randomness of a deciding Game 3.

October often creates unexpected stars. Players who spend much of the regular season outside the national spotlight can suddenly become synonymous with one postseason moment.

Two home runs. Six RBIs. A grand slam. And one enormous Yankees victory.

Not bad for a first impression on one of baseball's biggest stages.

title: On Texas' lack of offense, bad SEC refs and running steps for bad behavior | Bohls' nine things
description: The Texas offense remains inconsistent. The SEC refs had a bad game vs. Tennessee. And running steps for bad behavior. Kirk Bohls' nine things
fullText:
AUSTIN - While I got ya, here are nine things and one crazy prediction:

Anyone who has spotted the Texas offense, please call Bellmont Hall. It's been missing since the fourth quarter of the Ohio State game. It sure wasn't seen in Knoxville last Saturday. Steve Sarkisian praised Texas' offense for its fast start with a touchdown drive on its first series of the Tennessee game and for its next-to-last series with a game-sealing touchdown but didn't see a whole lot of continuity in between. The Longhorns now rank 83rd in offense nationally and an even worse 92nd in rushing as the defense carries this team. It's probably the worst a Texas offense has looked since Sarkisian's first season in 2021 when it went 5-7. He said Monday he doesn't anticipate making any changes in the starting lineup and didn't sound as if newly eligible Cole Hutson figures to get any playing time soon. … But one wonders when this inefficient offense catches up with Texas. When I asked if Texas can win a championship with this lackluster offense, he said, "I don't know because I don't know all the teams that we're going to play yet. What I do know is we need to play better offensively." Seems to me the problem remains the offensive line, all of whom got poor grades in run blocking from Pro Football Focus from between 54.3 (right guard Brandon Baker) and 63.2 (left tackle Trevor Goosby), but Arch Manning hasn't shown as much progress as expected. Sarkisian, however, disagreed and said he though Manning "played a pretty good game." … Manning still has accuracy issues, completing just 63.5% of his passes. Consider that 25 fellow quarterbacks are connecting on 70% or more of their throws, including Miami's Darian Mensah, who is 89% accurate and has thrown just 11 incompletions with 14 touchdowns and zero interceptions. Arch has seven touchdowns and three interceptions, one the bizarre ricochet off Cam Coleman. … Penalties also continue to be alarming. Texas ranks as the 90th worst team in that category after being whistled for 11 penalties for 115 yards on Saturday. Notre Dame, by point of comparison, ranks the most-disciplined team with only 10 penalties all year. The last two games alone, refs have stepped off 19 penalties for 203 yards. … Sarkisian said Texas needs to do better on first and second downs to minimize the third-and-long situations. Well, of course. But how? Eleven of the 30 called runs went for losses or no more than 1 yard. That's unacceptable. … Manning has to get the ball to Coleman than once a game. … I loved the ingenuity of the twin punt return set where Ryan Niblett ran to his right as a decoy for the Volunteers' punt coverage team but the ruse was foiled when Niblett waved for a fair catch and negated a long punt return by Jermaine Bishop Jr. … Sarkisian said injured running back Hollywood Smothers could have played in an "emergency," and should be healthy enough to play against OU on Oct. 10 after recovering from an ankle injury.

When it's illegal. Or should have been when Tennessee tried the ploy near the end of its 20-17 loss to Texas on Saturday. The officials blew it. The league office clarified that ruling Monday when it stated the Volunteers should have been flagged on the play, penalized 5 yards and made to re-kick. That kind of missed call that very well could have impacted the outcome of the game is inexcusable. The refs didn't know the rule. Quite frankly, I thought this was the worst officiating crew I've ever seen. I thought they were horrible from the outset when they ruled Texas was short of a first down on two third-and-1 attempts although it looked to me the Longhorn runner made it on each try. It took a ruling from the replay booth to learn Texas had successfully made the first down. I believe this crew should be suspended from doing SEC games for a minimum of one week. The league does not comment on crew's game assignments. … The SEC is off to an impressive 10-2 start against other Power 4 schools, the best in the nation. The Big Ten, meanwhile, is only 4-10 after winning the last three national championships. The ACC has a 6-9 mark, and the Big 12 5-7. … Sarkisian said he's not at all surprised by the strong starts of Florida and Mississippi State, to name two teams on his schedule. When a reporter said they weren't on many's dance card at the start of the season, Sarkisian said, "They were on my card. I tried to tell you guys about Florida last year. No one wanted to believe me. They've got real players in Gainesville, and they've kind of figured it out. This league is no joke." Funny how Texas fans were more worried about Oklahoma and Texas A&M during preseason than the Gators and Bulldogs. After OU, Texas' next five opponents are all ranked, giving the Longhorns the No. 2 toughest schedule. … Since the start of 2023, Texas has five road wins over ranked teams, more than any other team in college football. It also has 16 wins over Top 25 teams, six of them in the Top 10. It's also gone unnoticed that the Longhorns are 11-1 in their last 12 games with only a road loss to College Football Playoff-bound Georgia. That's pretty impressive. The Bulldogs are 13-1 in their last 14. Alabama is 7-3 in its last 10. Ohio State is 3-3 in its last six. Oregon is 11-3. Indiana, of course, leads all teams with a 20-game win streak.

The Texas baseball team, fresh off its first College World Series appearance under Jim Schlossnagle, has finished a month of practice and will play Houston at Dell Diamond on noon Saturday in an exhibition game. Texas will also move to Dell Diamond, the Disch-Falk batting cages and even Royal-Memorial Stadium for the remainder of its fall workouts. That's because the school is ripping up the turf at Disch-Falk and replacing it with a new FieldTurf that will be flatter and play a bit faster than its slower pace. Also, the dimensions in left field will move in 8 to 10 feet. "I would say the ballpark is definitely going to become more offensive because our turf is really the slowest that we play on all year, and you hit uphill and run uphill. You're going to have to be a better defender." … Shortstop Adrian Rodriguez, who hit for the cycle in Omaha, will give up switch-hitting and bat only from the left side as he continues his recovery from two hand procedures. Second baseman Ethan Mendoza is about to start swinging a bat after his summer shoulder surgery. … All-SEC closer Sam Cozart is probably going to transition to a starting role. Asked if any of the 23 new players were confused when they met the fully bearded and mustachioed Cozart, he said, "Yeah, a few of the younger ones thought I was a coach." Cozart has already become a leader. "Leading by example isn't really leading. So I lean toward vocal leadership. … I think for pretty much every freshman coming to college, especially to the University of Texas, this big of an atmosphere, you can be scared and so it's just getting them over the fear of being new? Was I scared? For about a week." He said winning a national title next summer brings "a major sense of urgency from the returners." … Schlossnagle is blown away by the maturity of freshman catcher Jax Robinson from Waxahachie. "Jax has frankly been the best hitter on the team this fall. Not just the best new hitter, but the best hitter on our team to this point.." He and fellow freshman Brady Murrietta of Yorba Linda, Calif., are competing with Saint Mary's transfer Ian Armstrong for the starting catcher position. … All-American Anthony Pack Jr. is the likely starting center fielder, a position last year's left fielder played for 10 games on the USA national team this summer without an error. He smacked 12 home runs last year but said Monday, "I still say I'm not a power hitter, to be honest. All my home runs came by accident."

Texas has pointed out that schools are not legally allowed to fine athletes like Colin Simmons for his vulgar celebration because they are technically not employees under labor law and there is no collective bargaining agreement because these athletes are unfairly not represented. So unless there is language stating moral clauses in Simmons' and his teammates' NIL contract, Texas doesn't have any financial recourse. … That doesn't mean Sarkisian can't punish his players in other ways like suspensions or punishments like getting Simmons and Raleek Brown up at 5 a.m. to run 500 stadium steps at DKR after their lewd celebrations. Better yet, I'd get the entire defense up that early every morning to run those steps with him. Call it team bonding. That's what Darrell Royal would have done. The Texas administration has chosen not to comment publicly on the issue. … It should be mentioned that no one is saying Simmons is a bad person. He moved his mother and 11-year-old autistic brother Clayton to Austin so he could receive better medical treatment. He's also held football camps for special needs kids and raised money through his foundation Clay's Color Crew for autism awareness. I just think he always plays with an edge, and his emotions got the better of him for the over-the-top celebration. I can't help but think of the days when Earl Campbell handed the ball to the ref after he scored touchdowns. … That wasn't the only shameful play of the week. I don't know what was worse, USC's Desman Stephens II's cheap shot on Oregon quarterback Dante Moore that sent him to the hospital or his celebration of the textbook targeting play afterward and the congratulations his fellow Trojans were showering on him. … On the other side, did you see Mississippi quarterback Trinidad Chambliss waiting until after Jon Sumrall's interview to hug and congratulate the Gators' coach? So classy. … Texas defensive tackle Hero Kanu was named a semifinalist for the 2026 William V. Campbell Trophy, the National Football Foundation announced. In its 37th year, the Campbell Trophy is a scholar-athlete award that annually recognizes an individual as the absolute best in the nation for his combined academic success, football performance and exemplary leadership.

It's always amusing to me how much hate mail I get over my Associated Press Top 25 ballot each week. This ain't Russia. We're not all going to pick our teams the same way. People love to shoot the messenger. And the criticism comes from the same haters who say the poll doesn't matter. So which is it? It's just entertainment, folks. I've often stated I have a very fluid ballot, especially in September, when teams are sorting themselves out. I've been very impressed with Wake Forest for its competitive loss to Miami and upset of Louisville and put the Demon Deacons at No. 17, one spot ahead of the Cardinals. The same goes for unbeaten UCLA at No. 20. I also bumped Iowa up five spots to 13th after beating Michigan. Ranking the final five of the Top 25 is the most difficult exercise of all. … As for keeping Texas No. 1, I still believe the Longhorns have the two best wins of the season over Ohio State and No. 14 Tennessee. However, I do struggle to understand ESPN's Football Power Index that has Ohio State at No. 3 and Texas at No. 4. If that's the case, why even play the game?

I think Kamario Taylor is the new favorite to win the Heisman now that Trinidad Chambliss fell to Florida. He could be the first to go from invisible to Heisman winner since Barry Sanders went from a kick returner to a star tailback at Oklahoma State. …  I think I love Justin Verlander's sweet, poignant goodbye in the final game of his career when his 7-year-old daughter, Genevieve, came to the mound to take him out and embraced her dad in a big hug. So touching. … I think karma has its way of evening things out. Right, Michigan? … I think Georgia is the most untested team in college football. The Bulldogs' schedule is ranked 123rd out of 136 teams. … I think Notre Dame might be second in the untested category. The Irish rank 99th nationally in plays from scrimmage of 10 yards or more. … I think Indiana can be had. Northwestern is much improved and gave the Hoosiers fits Friday night. … I think Lincoln Riley is an average coach. He did very little with Caleb Williams and not that much more with Jaiden Maiava. … I think Brent Venables, the ultimate good guy, could be the first coach to get a contract extension and a pink slip in the same year. Georgia covering the two-touchdown spread against OU was my lock of the week bet last Saturday. … I think it's very sad that former Texas forward Justice Carlton, now with the Houston women's basketball team, tore an ACL in her knee and will miss the season. … I think people are sleeping on Alabama's football team, as incredible as that sounds. The Tide catch Mississippi State next, one of four road games in its next six opponents.

Texas senior Farah O'Keefe has climbed to the No. 1 spot on the World Amateur Golf Ranking list after earning her sixth career victory as the co-medalist at the Jackson T. Stephens Cup. O'Keefe was the 2026 NCAA individual Champion and also won the 2026 ANNIKA Award, 2026 WGCA Player of the Year, 2026 Golfweek Player of the Year and 2026 Honda Award for golf and pretty much every award there is. O'Keefe set an NCAA record with 12 top-10 finishes in the 2025-26 season and set a Texas single season career for stroke average at 69.84. She won four events in the 2025-26 season and her six total victories are tied for second all-time at Texas with Sherri Steinhauer, who played from 1981-85. The all-time record for career victories for a Longhorn woman is held by Michiko Hattori, who played from 1987-91 and recorded 10 victories.

While wondering whatever happened to former Oklahoma quarterback Sam Bradford.

It was Scary Movie Night at the Bohls casa Monday night. We watched "Passenger," a legitimately scary horror movie on Apple Plus that, well, jumps out at you throughout the 92-minute film. It's about a young couple on a perpetual road trip that encounters a relentless demon. I'll never take a cross-country trip in a van ever again. I gave it 7½ 1/2 ducks.

Colin Simmons will have three sacks of John Mateer next week and carry the Sooners quarterback to the OU bench, prop him up with a pillow and get him a Gatorade.

There's more to Houston with the Chronicle.

title: GOP Sen. Mike Lee blocks effort to bar Trump from demolishing Kennedy Center
description:
A Republican senator squashed a bipartisan push to prohibit the Trump administration from demolishing the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts.
Sen. Jeff Merkley, D-Oregon, and Sen. Lisa Murkowski, R-Alaska, who lead the Senate panel that oversees funding for the Kennedy Center, tried to pass a bill that would require an act of Congress to demolish any national memorials that honor a president.
fullText:
A Republican senator squashed a bipartisan push to prohibit the Trump administration from demolishing the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts.

Sen. Jeff Merkley, D-Oregon, and Sen. Lisa Murkowski, R-Alaska, who lead the Senate panel that oversees funding for the Kennedy Center, tried to pass a bill that would require an act of Congress to demolish any national memorials that honor a president. An objection from a single senator can block a bill from being passed by unanimous consent.

Sen. Mike Lee, R-Utah, objected.

The bill – dubbed the "Protecting Presidential Memorials Act" – would also apply to Lincoln Memorial and Washington Monument. But Merkley and Murkowski made their immediate goal clear.

"This has of course to do with the president planning to demolish the Kennedy Center," Merkley said on the Senate floor late Monday evening, Sept. 28, after the passing of the Protect College Sports Act, a major overhaul to college athletics related to NIL (name, image and likeliness) payment for student athletes.

Lee's office said in a statement to USA TODAY that this effort should go through "the appropriate committee process."

"Democrats should join us in lowering the cost of living and securing American elections instead of wasting the Senate’s time with partisan scaremongering," Lee said in the statement shared by communications director Billy Gribbin.

The Senate vote is the latest chapter in a year of legal wrangling and congressional wrangling over the Kennedy Center.

The Kennedy Center added Trump's name to the building's facade in December 2025 after the board – which was handpicked by Trump – voted to rename the center. In June 2026, a judge ordered that his name be taken down, saying that an act of Congress was needed to change the name of the memorial to the assassinated president.

Trump's name has since been removed, but a tarp remains covering the building's name where Trump's name used to be.

Earlier in September, the Kennedy Center closed after part of the ceiling collapsed, and on Sept. 15 the center's board voted to close the center for two years.

That came after a federal judge's second ruling that Trump's name could not be added to the building in September 2026, the culmination of months of legal disputes as the president contended that the center needed to be renovated, that only he could raise the money for it and that his administration should be recognized for it.

Trump has continued to defend his stance about his name being on the building, saying on Sept. 18 that the center had "been a dump" and "lost money" for years. He said that he would subsidize the necessary repairs but said that his administration should be recognized.

Merkley accused the president of wanting to demolish the center, pointing to an image captured of Trump inside Air Force One reading a poster that appears to say "Kennedy Center DEMOLISHED." The photo was taken hours after Trump told reporters that the memorial will "end up being ripped down" unless major renovations are undertaken.

title: Last U.S. troops leave Iraq after 12-year fight against ISIS
description: — The U.S. military announced on Wednesday that it has completed the withdrawal of all American troops from Iraq, ending a 12-year mission to fight the Islamic State group. The last U.S.
fullText:
BAGHDAD (AP) — The U.S. military announced on Wednesday that it has completed the withdrawal of all American troops from Iraq, ending a 12-year mission to fight the Islamic State group. The last U.S. troops left an air base in northern Iraq under a deal between Baghdad and Washington.

The withdrawal, agreed on two years ago, comes against the backdrop of the ongoing war between the United States and Iran that has also sometimes spilled over into Iraq, with Iran-backed militias firing on U.S. troops and the U.S. striking the groups' strongholds.

Baghdad touted the end of the U.S. mission as a sign of the country's increasing strength and sovereignty.

The withdrawal was also celebrated by Iran-backed groups but raised concerns among some other Iraqis, particularly in the Kurdish region. Meanwhile, questions loom around the future of the Iraqi militias, which the Baghdad government has sought — with little success so far — to disarm.

Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell said in a statement that U.S. troops and equipment had completed an "orderly departure" from the air base in Irbil, in northern Iraq's semi-autonomous Kurdish region.

"This milestone reflects the success of a 12-year campaign that defeated ISIS as an organized military threat in Iraq and across the region," he said. "It also marks a transition from a wartime coalition mission to an Iraqi-led security effort supported by a more normal bilateral security relationship."

Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi presided over the handover ceremony and described the U.S. withdrawal as the beginning of a "new phase, one defined by Iraq's sovereignty, the strength of its institutions, the readiness of its forces, the unity of its decision-making, and balanced partnerships with its friends."

He said Iraqi security forces will continue the fight against IS and the government will ensure that non-state groups no longer hold weapons.

U.S. troops invaded Iraq in 2003 to topple Saddam Hussein. They departed in 2011, but three years later, Iraqi authorities invited a smaller U.S.-led mission to fight the Islamic State group, which had rampaged across Iraq, seizing large swaths of territory.

With the extremist group reduced to scattered sleeper cells, Washington and Baghdad agreed in 2024 to wind the mission down.

U.S. troops pulled out of bases in most areas of Iraq last year but maintained a small presence of hundreds of troops in the semiautonomous northern Kurdish region. Bases there have regularly come under attack since the U.S. and Israel launched their war against Iran on Feb. 28. Iran-backed Iraqi militias also have coordinated with Yemen's Houthi rebels to attack Saudi Arabia.

The Iraqi government initially linked the Sept. 30 deadline for U.S. withdrawal to the disarmament of non-state armed groups by that date.

While a handful of less-influential militias have agreed to turn over their weapons, powerful groups close to Iran rejected the prospect or set conditions for disarming that the government would be unlikely to meet.

Al-Zaidi has since walked back the deadline. He told The New York Times earlier this month that the deadline for militia disarmament has been pushed to June 2027.

The effects of the U.S. withdrawal may not be immediately visible, particularly since the U.S. military presence had already been scaled down. But officials in Iraq's Kurdish region have expressed anxiety about the departure and particularly about the removal of U.S. air defense systems.

The Kurdish regional government's Peshmerga Ministry said the Kurdish region had faced more than 1,000 drone and ballistic-missile attacks during the recent U.S.-Iran conflict.

"The departure of the United States from the Kurdistan Region under these complex regional circumstances, without the provision of a defense system, is a matter of concern," the statement said.

Iran-allied groups in Iraq, meanwhile, have celebrated the U.S. withdrawal.

"The expulsion of the occupation forces, defeated, from the land of Iraq is the beginning of full sovereignty," Abu Mujahid al-Assaf, a security official with the powerful Kataib Hezbollah militia, said in a statement.

He added a warning to al-Zaidi and his government not to carry out American plans, threatening that "any government that does not work for the benefit of the people will be overthrown by all means."

title: Israel-bound flight diverts to Saudi Arabia after reported fight between pilots

fullText:
A FlyDubai flight from Dubai to Israel was forced to make an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia on Wednesday after an apparent altercation in the cockpit, raising concerns about a possible hijacking and prompting Israel to scramble fighter jets.

Israeli media outlets, citing security officials, said the incident stemmed from a fight between the commercial plane's two pilots and that everyone on board was safe after it landed in Tabuk, where there is a civilian airport adjacent to a Saudi military base.

The Jerusalem Post reported that one pilot tried to hijack the plane but was subdued by other members of the flight crew and passengers, citing an unnamed Israeli official who told the newspaper that a "major disaster was narrowly avoided."

A female passenger told Israel Hayom that one pilot was stabbed during the brawl, and Israeli passengers intervened to stop the fighting.

"There are people here with shirts covered in blood," she said, describing the incident as "very stressful." Videos shared on social media corroborated her account, showing at two men laying down with blood smeared on and around them.

A passenger speaking to the Jerusalem Post said one pilot stabbed the other and tried to force him out of the cockpit as the plane began to plummet. The passenger told the newspaper a group of Israeli passengers near the front of the aircraft rushed to fight the attacker as the plane lost altitude.

The witness said the intervening passengers shouted at two off-duty pilots at the back of the plane "to run and take control" of it, and one of them did so after the passengers managed to remove the attacker from the cockpit.

Israeli sources told the Post the would-be hijacker was an Omani national. There was no immediate confirmation of the details from Israeli or Saudi officials.

The crew of FlyDubai flight 1073, a Boeing 737 Max 8 aircraft, transmitted an emergency alert shortly after takeoff on Wednesday, according to publicly available flight tracking information.

CBS News' British partner network BBC News said flight tracking data showed the aircraft plummeted more than 17,000 feet in two minutes around 8:21 a.m. local time.

Yasmin Abukasis, whose daughter was on the flight, told journalists at Tel Aviv's Ben Gurion Airport, where the plane had been due to land, that her daughter heard screaming as a pilot called for help.

"The plane start to lose control. So all the people, they scream," she said.

A regional official briefed on the incident told the Associated Press a fight broke out in the cockpit apparently involving the pilots, but the official did not say what had caused the altercation. The AP cited a second official confirming that Israel had scrambled warplanes, fearing a possible hijacking of the plane carrying dozens of Israeli citizens.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has warned in recent days of unspecified, escalating security threats to Israel and its interests.

Netanyahu's office later issued a statement saying the situation was under control and Israel was working to bring the passengers home.

The BBC reported that a recovery flight was on its way to Tabuk to pick up the passengers from the diverted plane.

Emergency landings for personnel reasons are rare but not unheard of. In 2022, two Air France pilots were suspended after fighting in the cockpit on a Geneva-to-Paris flight, though the plane landed as scheduled in the French capital.

FlyDubai is the lower-cost sister carrier of the United Arab Emirates state-owned flagship carrier Emirates airlines. The UAE has become a popular vacation destination for Israeli tourists since the two nations normalized ties in 2020.

Israel has not experienced a plane hijacking in decades, but it maintains some of the strictest airport security in the world.

U.S. Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee posted about the incident Wednesday on X, saying: "Well this had everyone in the Middle East (esp Israel) on FULL ALERT this morning."

"Glad it wasn't more serious," he added, "but having pilots inflight detouring to 'fist city' not your ordinary experience."

Israeli politician Benny Gantz, who is running in upcoming Israeli elections but polling badly, wrote on X: "It's still too early to know what the sequence of events was in this morning's Flydubai flight to Israel, but it's already clear that Israelis are a rare breed."

"The resourcefulness and courage displayed by the passengers on this flight, in the face of clear mortal danger, are exactly the stuff our people are made of," he said.

title: DNA evidence from Thomas Jefferson's hair reveals truth about Sally Hemings relationship
description:
Thomas Jefferson has long been rumored to have fathered children with Sally Hemings. New genetic evidence strengthens that connection. (Photo by Burstein Collection/Corbis/VCG via Getty Images) - Burstein Collection/Corbis/Getty Images
Opening a Bible that once belonged to Thomas Jefferson, staff at the Smithsonian National Museum of American History in 2011 discovered a reddish-blond hair pressed between the pages. That hair, suspected to have belonged to Jefferson himself, launched a DNA investigation spanning more than a decade that’s now providing a long-missing puzzle piece regarding Jefferson’s relationship with Sally Hemings, an enslaved woman in his household.
After spending years reconstructing DNA fragments, scientists have revealed the most compelling evidence to date that Jefferson, a founding father of the United States, also fathered children with Hemings — a relationship that has been long rumored but never definitively proven.
fullText:
Opening a Bible that once belonged to Thomas Jefferson, staff at the Smithsonian National Museum of American History in 2011 discovered a reddish-blond hair pressed between the pages. That hair, suspected to have belonged to Jefferson himself, launched a DNA investigation spanning more than a decade that’s now providing a long-missing puzzle piece regarding Jefferson’s relationship with Sally Hemings, an enslaved woman in his household.

After spending years reconstructing DNA fragments, scientists have revealed the most compelling evidence to date that Jefferson, a founding father of the United States, also fathered children with Hemings — a relationship that has been long rumored but never definitively proven. How that investigation unfolded is documented in the book “History by a Hair: Thomas Jefferson, Sally Hemings & Solving a 200-Year-Old Mystery,” written by Richard Kurin, a distinguished scholar and ambassador-at-large at the Smithsonian, and published on September 22.

Kurin is also senior author of a paper describing the methods that connected the former US president to Hemings’ descendants, which involved delving deep into the genetics of the Jefferson and Hemings family trees. The paper, published September 21 on the preprint platform bioRXiv, has not yet been peer-reviewed.

In addition to testing the hair found in the Bible, the researchers also collected genetic material from multiple confirmed samples of Jefferson’s hair, held in the collection of the Smithsonian. They compared that with DNA from descendants of multiple lineages: Jefferson and his wife Martha, Jefferson’s brother Randolph, and two of Hemings’ sons, Eston and Madison. (Hemings had four children who lived to adulthood, but only Eston and Madison claimed Jefferson as their father).

Matches in the DNA suggest the chance that Thomas Jefferson fathered at least one of Sally Hemings’ children was 99.96%.

Previously, a genetic study from 1998 led by the late Eugene Foster, a retired pathology professor at Tufts University and the University of Virginia, claimed to prove Jefferson’s parentage of Hemings’ children. That study found a rare haplotype — a combination of genes — in the Y chromosomes of males descended from Thomas Jefferson’s uncle. That same haplotype existed in descendants of Hemings, too. However, many experts questioned Foster’s claim for one very important reason, Kurin told CNN.

“He didn’t have Thomas Jefferson’s DNA,” Kurin said. “He didn’t have something to directly compare living descendants of the Jefferson family to Madison Hemings and Eston Hemings and others that might have been the descendants of Thomas Jefferson.” Critics of that the 1998 study said Foster’s evidence merely connected Hemings’ descendants to a male in the Jefferson lineage, and not necessarily to the former president.

“I thought, if we can get Thomas Jefferson’s DNA, we could use that as the source of comparison to various descendants, and really firmly solve the question,” Kurin said.

Kurin and his team were initially disappointed to find that the Bible hair wasn’t the smoking gun that they thought it would be. To check whether the hair was Jefferson’s, they compared its DNA with that of a living woman who was a direct descendant of Thomas Jefferson’s mother along the family’s female lineage. They expected to find identical mitochondrial DNA, which is genetic material specifically inherited from the maternal side. But their hopes were dashed when the two samples didn’t match.

Still, they were able to access other hair samples that records attributed to Thomas Jefferson. These hairs, including a lock clipped at his deathbed, were in a packet provided by the Thomas Jefferson Foundation at Monticello, and had not previously been available for analysis. The scientists reconstructed and compared historic genome sequences of Jefferson and Hemings with DNA collected from 16 living individuals, including multiple descendants of Eston and Madison Hemings. These analyses found matches across genomes that linked Hemings descendants to Thomas Jefferson.

“What made this study so powerful is that researchers weren’t just comparing two genomes,” said Éadaoin Harney, a senior population geneticist at the 23andMe Research Institute. “Instead, they collected DNA samples from multiple people from different branches of the family tree.”

In genetic analysis, larger sample pools provide more robust conclusions, said Harney, who was not involved in the new research. “By studying the patterns of DNA sharing across all of these individuals, it became possible to disambiguate exactly how the descendants of Sally Hemings were related to Thomas Jefferson,” she told CNN in an email.

While the new book and paper focus on genomic data of well-known historical figures, these methods are also broadly useful for illuminating the obscured history of enslaved people, which has been a focus of Harney’s own research. In a 2023 study of enslaved and free African Americans from Maryland, Harney used DNA analysis combined with other biomolecular and archaeological techniques to uncover individuals’ ancestry and places of origin. The data also suggested links to people who still live in Maryland.

“Historical records are full of gaps, particularly when it comes to documenting the lives of people who occupied less privileged places in society,” she said. “This is particularly true for enslaved Africans and African Americans, who are often only described in historical records as property.”

Genetic analyses, such as those used in the new Jefferson study, can help restore connections that were lost because of slavery, Harney added. “The same tools can be applied to study the many enslaved people whose lives were never well documented, and help reconnect them with their descendants.”

Whispers about Jefferson’s sexual relationship with Hemings — who was 30 years his junior and a half-sister to his wife — have endured for more than 200 years. Initial rumors were fueled by local innuendo and supported by records aligning Hemings’ pregnancies with Jefferson’s presence at his plantation home of Monticello in Virginia. An article published in 1902 in the Richmond Recorder stated that “there is not an individual in the neighbourhood of Charlottesville who does not believe the story,” regarding Jefferson fathering children with Hemings.

Though the conclusions of Foster’s 1998 study were not universally accepted, that genetic evidence was compelling enough for the Thomas Jefferson Foundation to issue a statement two years later acknowledging “the strong likelihood that Thomas Jefferson and Sally Hemings had a relationship over time that led to the birth of one, and perhaps all, of the known children of Sally Hemings.”

Finally laying that uncertainty to rest was enough of a motivation to keep Kurin and the other researchers going for more than a decade, despite their initial disappointment that the hair found in the Bible did not belong to Thomas Jefferson, he said.

“We had hit a dead end, but scientists are always looking for alternatives,” he said. “I think we were propelled still by scientific and historical curiosity.”

While the question of Jefferson’s ancestry in Hemings’ descendants may finally have been answered, another remains: Whose hair was pressed in Jefferson’s bible? The researchers had collected enough of its fragmentary genetic data to know that it belonged to a female member of the Jefferson family, but that was all the information the team could learn, Kurin said.

“It’s like a partial fingerprint,” he explained. “That is still a lingering mystery.”

Mindy Weisberger is a science writer and media producer whose work has appeared in Live Science, Scientific American and How It Works magazine. She is the author of “Rise of the Zombie Bugs: The Surprising Science of Parasitic Mind-Control” (Hopkins Press).

title: Rape case at Cornell turns spotlight on campus sexual assault
description:
The Chi Phi fraternity house at Cornell University in Ithaca, New York, on September 28, 2026. - Heather Ainsworth/AP
It was 7:05 p.m. on a Wednesday in mid-September when Jane Doe’s lawsuit hit the New York County Supreme Court docket. Within days, the 101-page, double-spaced filing had captured the nation’s attention, sparking outrage and controversy and refocusing attention on a longstanding issue: sexual assault on college campus.
fullText:
It was 7:05 p.m. on a Wednesday in mid-September when Jane Doe’s lawsuit hit the New York County Supreme Court docket. Within days, the 101-page, double-spaced filing had captured the nation’s attention, sparking outrage and controversy and refocusing attention on a longstanding issue: sexual assault on college campus.

The complaint was explosive, claiming that seven members of a Cornell University fraternity took part in the sexual assault of a 20-year-old sorority member during a drug-fueled, hours-long encounter in the fall of 2024. Included in the filing was a screenshot of a Snapchat message where one of the men wrote that there was “free p*ssy” and others responded gleefully, with comments like “CHI PHIII.”

Soon after the lawsuit’s filing on Sept. 16, a familiar pattern played out. Furious onlookers took to social media to demand accountability, flooded the district attorney’s office with complaints and shared photos and other identifying details of the fraternity members many have taken to calling “the Cornell 7.” Others, meanwhile, condemned the rush to judgment or urged caution in drawing conclusions from the allegations in the lawsuit, which a prosecutor said differ from what the alleged victim reported in 2024. Some hurried to try to unmask the anonymous woman behind the accusations.

There were flashes of politics and victim blaming, judgment and shame in a case that’s rife with unanswered questions and likely to evolve as more details come to light.

The issue of sexual assault on campus – and how allegations should be handled – has resurfaced again and again. An individual case grabs the attention of the nation and sets off a debate over where we are as a country and whether change is needed: Columbia University student Emma Sulkowicz carrying a mattress to protest how her report was handled; Chanel Miller delivering a fiery victim impact statement at the sentencing of a former Stanford University swimmer convicted of assaulting her; Summer Willis crawling to the Texas state capitol on her hands and knees to secure a change to the legal loophole that allowed her assault to go unprosecuted.

Social media posts by actresses Florence Pugh and Mariska Hargitay helped move the Cornell conversation forward, gathering steam as commentary about the case flooded feeds.

Sasha Pieterse, an actress known for her starring role in the hit show “Pretty Little Liars,” told CNN she herself is a survivor of sexual assault. It’s something she has not publicly spoken about until now.

Pieterse said she does not think people “understand the gravity of what happens around the aftermath: the fear, the shame, the level of physical and mental recovery.”

She said she hopes the spotlight on the Cornell allegations will help other victims feel less alone and show why consent laws should be standardized.

“I never want anything like what just happened at Cornell to happen to any other person,” Pieterse said.

Laura L. Dunn, a victims’ rights attorney with a specialization in campus assault cases, heard about the Cornell case almost immediately after the complaint was filed. People across her life sent it to her, reminded not only of her efforts to address the issue but also of her own personal connection to it: As a student athlete on the University of Wisconsin at Madison’s crew team in 2004, she reported being assaulted by two male teammates. No charges were filed.

“It’s a very painful moment in time, on many levels, to see a case that I could have read about 20 years ago happening again,” said Dunn, 41.

Attorneys for two of the seven alleged assailants at Cornell have denied the allegations and some observers have argued that what happened that night in 2024 did not qualify as a crime under New York law – a comment that has also been made by Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten in defending his decision not to file criminal charges when the incident was reported. He said the alleged victim at the time described “her participation in drug use and sexual conduct as voluntary, conscious and consensual.”

Van Houten said this week he will reopen the case, adding that he recognizes “the reality that it can take years of therapy and healing for victims of sexual assaults to fully process and understand what happened to them.”

Others online have tried to tie the Cornell case to high profile incidents that were determined to be unfounded and the alleged perpetrators wrongly accused, such as cases involving Duke University lacrosse players and a fraternity at the University of Virginia that was the subject of a retracted Rolling Stone article.

Research has found that false allegations are rare, estimated to represent 2 to 10 percent of reports, according to one analysis.

After her own assault, Dunn vowed to push for change – and felt in the 2010s that major progress was being made. A high point for her came in 2011, when the Obama administration reminded higher education institutions of their obligation under Title IX to address sexual violence and directed them to step up their investigations into reports.

Colleges and universities responded, she said, by doing more meaningful educational efforts and boosting their Title IX offices.

“There were all these efforts during that era to really turn the tide,” Dunn said.

More people began speaking out, and by 2014 several high-profile incidents – including Emma Sulkowicz’s – held the public’s interest and drove a desire for change. At the same time, some critics worried that the Obama-era guidance had gone too far, tasking college bureaucrats with investigating criminal allegations and diluting due process.

The first Trump administration withdrew it in 2017, citing concerns about due process. Title IX protections were expanded again under rules set by the Biden administration’s Department of Education, which survivor advocates said removed some of the barriers faced by victims of sexual assault. Those changes were again undone this week by Trump officials.

The move cements a change the Trump administration had informally enacted last year to the federal law banning discrimination based on sex and governs how schools respond to complaints of sexual misconduct. The 2020 guidance narrowed the definition of sexual harassment, extended protections for students accused of sexual misconduct and added requirements like live hearings with the potential for cross-examination.

Emma Grasso Levine, a grad student and senior manager of Title IX policy and programs at Advocates for Youth, told CNN the move “sends a message that it’s not safe to speak out.”

Activists say recent years have seen a backlash to the Me Too movement, coupled with the rise of the “manosphere,” both of which have contributed to the climate around sexual assault on college campuses. National Organization for Women president Kim Villanueva described the content as often promoting women as objects and encouraging or glorifying rape culture.

Her team has been having conversations with college students about the Cornell investigation and the meaning of consent. She said it’s important to have conversations with young men about consent and how they view women in society.

“It will involve a lot of social change,” Villanueva said.

Saanya Agarwal was a sophomore at Cornell in 2024 when the university sent an alert about a reported sexual assault on campus. She remembers it mentioned several men allegedly being involved but that it was otherwise scarce on details – something she found unnerving as a female student sharing a campus with them.

Now a senior, she told CNN that her anger at what she considered a lack of transparency fueled her run for a student assembly position representing women. She was elected and spent last year talking to university administrators and Greek life representatives to try to advocate for more transparency.

“I think if you talk to people, especially women on campus, this question is always in the back of your head: What if that was me?” said Agarwal, who is a sorority member.

Reyes Almeida, a junior at Boston University, said the Cornell incident is appalling, but didn’t surprise her because of how “pervasive” sexual assault is on college campuses.

Almeida is president of BU’s chapter of ‘It’s On Us,’ an organization that supports sexual assault survivors on college campuses and tries to prevent assaults from happening through intervention training.

Many of the survivors their organization works with have chosen not to report their sexual assault to the university, Almeida said. CNN has reached out to BU about survivors choosing not to report assault.

Her opinion is that some universities prioritize image over safety. “The only thing they want to do is keep their pristine image,” Almeida said.

At Rowan University, like others around the country, students receive notification when there is a reported sexual assault on campus in compliance with the federal Clery Act.

Tamyah Crafton, a college senior who founded Rowan University’s chapter of the National Council of Negro Women, appreciates these notifications, but wants more information surrounding them and town hall meetings to discuss the details.

“Like, what are you doing to make the campus safer?” Crafton asked.

At Cornell, administrators barred Chi Phi from campus and launched a task force on sexual assault, which issued recommendations earlier this year.

But Agarwal, the Cornell student, said the perceived lack of transparency from Cornell leaves students to wonder about exactly what happened – and whether someone involved might be sitting next to them in class or across from them at the local bar.

“There’s so much distrust and that also creates fear, understandably so, because we don’t know what’s going on,” she said.

CNN’s Jason Carroll and Linh Tran contributed to this report.

title: Supreme Court clears way for Christa Pike's execution after final appeal
description:
Christa Pike, Tennessee's only female death row inmate, has lost her final appeal after the U.S. Supreme Court declined to intervene in her imminent execution.
The nation's highest court denied Pike's request for a stay of execution on Sept. 29, less than 24 hours before Pike is set to be executed by lethal injection on Sept.
fullText:
Christa Pike, Tennessee's only female death row inmate, has lost her final appeal after the U.S. Supreme Court declined to intervene in her imminent execution.

The nation's highest court denied Pike's request for a stay of execution on Sept. 29, less than 24 hours before Pike is set to be executed by lethal injection on Sept. 30. The court joins Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee and lower courts in rejecting arguments from Pike's attorneys that she should be spared because of her exceptionally traumatic childhood.

Also on Sept. 29, Amnesty International joined more than 100 women's advocacy groups and sex abuse experts in continuing to argue for a reprieve for Pike.

"It is unthinkable that Governor Lee would even consider moving forward with this execution," Justin Mazzola, deputy director of research at Amnesty International USA, said in a statement. "In this moment, people around the world are asking Governor Lee to grant clemency to Ms. Pike, and we add our voice to theirs."

Lee announced on Sept. 28 that he upheld Christa Pike's death sentence and was not planning to intervene in her execution. He did not provide an explanation.

If Pike's execution moves forward, she will become the first woman executed in Tennessee in more than 200 years and only the 19th in the U.S. in the last 50 years. She was sentenced to death for the brutal and prolonged 1995 murder of her romantic rival, 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer.

Pike's attorneys and more than 100 women's advocacy groups and sex abuse experts have been imploring the governor and courts to commute Pike's sentence to life in prison. They argued that Pike is so traumatized by repeated rapes throughout her girlhood, that the process of being executed by lethal injection will make her feel like she's being raped all over again.

They argue that amounts to cruel and unusual punishment in violation of the U.S. Constitution.

"She will relive the sounds, the smells, and the pain," wrote a dozen women's advocacy organizations in what's known as a friend-of-the court brief filed in the Tennessee Supreme Court on Sept. 10 and in the U.S. Supreme Court on Sept. 26. "She will feel it now as she did then. And it will be as horrific for her now as it was then."

While the Tennessee Attorney General's Office acknowledges that Pike had a childhood that involved repeated rapes, they have been arguing that her death sentence is a just punishment for her crime.

"Pike’s prior abuse and mental struggles are tragic to say the least," the state wrote in arguments to the Supreme Court this week. "But they are no cause to insulate her from a lawfully imposed and exhaustively reviewed death sentence that a jury of her peers imposed purely because of her own horrific conduct."

Here's what else you need to know about the case, including how Colleen Slemmer's mother feels more than 30 years after her daughter's murder.

On Jan. 12, 1995, 18-year-old Pike, her boyfriend, and another young woman lured Slemmer to the woods in Knoxville. Pike and her boyfriend, then-17-year-old Tadaryl Shipp, tortured and murdered Slemmer in a crime that made international headlines both for its brutality and because of Pike's gender and youth.

"Armed with a box cutter and meat cleaver, Pike and two accomplices lured Slemmer to an isolated area. There, Pike kneed Slemmer’s head, threw her to the ground, and repeatedly kicked her," the Tennessee Attorney General's Office wrote in court documents. "When Slemmer tried to flee, Pike sliced her stomach with the box cutter. ... As Slemmer begged for her life, Pike repeatedly kicked her in the face. Pike then cut Slemmer’s throat as she begged for mercy."

After Slemmer made one final attempt to escape, Pike smashed the back of her head with a rock, they wrote. Shipp also carved a pentagram into Slemmer's chest, and Pike later showed off a piece of Slemmer's skull to a friend.

Pike was sentenced to death and Shipp got a life sentence because at 17, he wasn't eligible for the death penalty.

For Slemmer's mother, May Martinez, Pike's execution more than 30 years after her daughter's murder represents long-awaited justice.

"I just want Christa down so I can end it, relieve my daughter, so she finally can be resting," Martinez told WBIR-TV in 2021. "There's not a day goes by that I don't think about Colleen or how she died and how rough it was."

Martinez recently told WBIR-TV that she plans to attend Pike's execution this week.

"I'll hold Colleen's picture up to remind her of what she did," Martinez told the station. "She never apologized − never even tried − or her family."

She said she remembers her daughter as a playful and compassionate young woman who loved roller skating, computers, and playing old games with her family. She laments that her daughter has been so overshadowed by Pike over the years.

"It's never about the victims," she said. "It's like Colleen was never there."

Court records show that Pike became a rape victim before she was even in preschool. Her grandmother's boyfriend targeted her for years, sexually assaulting her until she was in kindergarten, according to court documents obtained by USA TODAY.

At the age of 11, a neighbor raped Pike in an attack that caused an infection and preceded a suicide attempt at the age of 12. And at 17, a stranger attacked Pike while she was out walking, forced her into the woods, and raped her, court records say.

Pike's execution is certain to take her back to that trauma, the women's advocacy organizations wrote in the friend-of-the-court brief. The experience, which involves being strapped down, is likely to be so visceral to Pike, that it will be unconstitutionally cruel, they argue.

"There is a substantial risk she will feel and believe that she is being raped to death," argue the groups, which include the Coalition Against Trafficking in Women, Rights4Girls and Survivors Justice Project.

The groups, joined by dozens more sex assault experts and women's advocates, also appealed directly to Lee and urged him to commute Pike's sentence to life in prison.

"It is not just that she was a toddler when she was sexually abused for the first time, or that she was raped by three more men before her 18th birthday," they wrote in a letter to Lee on Sept. 10. "It is that Christa was forced to cope with her sexual abuse and rape virtually alone, without any of the victim support services that we know are so vital to recovery."

During a recent three-day hearing in a Knoxville courtroom, prosecutors said they would try to keep men away from Pike during the two-week period known as death watch, when guards closely monitor inmates in part to prevent them from dying by suicide.

David Wickenheiser, an assistant attorney general, quoted from a psychologist's report at the hearing that though "Christa will always carry that history of trauma with her ... she now has the tools and emotions to deal with life stressors."

Senior Judge Mark Ward, the special master appointed by the Tennessee Supreme Court who presided over the hearing, concluded that the Tennessee Department of Corrections has "minimized the potential" for Pike to experience significant triggering and that mental suffering alone is not enough to violate the Constitution's protections against cruel and unusual punishment.

Pike's attorneys requested a stay of execution in the Supreme Court on Sept. 25, arguing that it was an open question whether mental suffering during an execution can be considered a constitutional violation.

"This case presents uniquely compelling circumstances where this Court is likely to consider such an important constitutional question," they wrote. "While the public may have an interest in seeing judgments carried out, it also has an interest that its citizens not be tortured to death in the name of the people."

The court denied the stay without issuing a written opinion.

Pike's attorneys didn't pin all their hopes on the arguments about her past trauma. They also argue that a lethal injection would be unconstitutionally painful for Pike because of her unusually small veins and a condition known as thrombocytosis.

Further, they say that at 18 years old when she killed Slemmer, Pike was "more impulsive and emotional, more susceptible to peer pressure, and less able to make rational decisions." They point out that it's unusual for Tennessee to execute anyone who was so young when they committed murder.

Of more they 200 people sentenced to death in Tennessee in the last 50 years, they say only seven others were 18 at the time of their crimes. All of their death sentences have since been vacated, they say.

As for Pike, she now takes mood-stabilizing medications for her bipolar and PTSD, goes to therapy, and has found an outlet both in painting and in "helping new women to the prison," her attorneys said in a clemency petition.

"After years of psychotherapy and medications to treat her mental illness, Christa is thoughtful, even-tempered, bright, funny, and hopeful," they said.

Though Slemmer's mother says she's never gotten a personal apology about her daughter's murder, Pike expressed remorse in her clemency petition.

"Think back to the worst mistake you made as a reckless teenager. Well, mine happened to be huge, unforgettable and ruined countless lives," she wrote. "I was a mentally ill 18-year-old kid. ... I took the life of someone’s child, sister, friend. It sickens me now to think I had the ability to commit such a crime."

Amanda Lee Myers is a senior crime and courts reporter who covers the death penalty, cold cases and breaking news for USA TODAY. Follow her on X at @amandaleeusat.

title: Reanimated AI Greta Garbo stars again … in a ball-bearing advert

fullText:
Relatives of Hollywood legend say her doppelganger could now be used for more glamorous roles

She shimmered in Hollywood’s silent movie era and lit up the first talkies – now Greta Garbo may be about to star in cinema’s new AI age.

More than a century after her screen debut and decades after her ashes were laid to rest in a Swedish woodland cemetery, the Hollywood superstar’s descendants are ready to consider an AI version of her taking a 21st-century film role.

Her likeness has already been reanimated for an advert for a Swedish industrial company, using AI generation technology. The practice some critics call “ghostploitation” has also been used in the case of the actor Val Kilmer, who died last year.

Asked if the AI Garbo could be cast in other roles, Craig Reisfield, one of three relatives who manage her legacy, told the Guardian: “I won’t say no, especially having seen what I’ve seen. It’s pretty incredible and lifelike. So what’s to say that you can’t bring Greta Garbo back in some kind of fashion in a film role?”

Reisfield said he was “flabbergasted” when he saw the AI version of his great-aunt created for publicity for the ball-bearings giant SKF. The connection comes because Garbo’s second-ever screen role was in a 1921 promotional film involving the Gothenburg-based company.

While Garbo was the definition of glamour in Hollywood’s golden age, appearing as a famous ballerina in Grand Hotel (1932) and as a doomed courtesan in Camille (1936), the 99-second AI performance for SKF is intercut with shots of ball-bearings.

However, the quality of the AI production has prompted the possibility, at least, of a greater digital comeback.

“I was totally impressed: the mannerisms that they could capture and manipulate, her dress, facial images and even her voice,” said Reisfield, a Swedish-American who used to drive for Garbo and saw her often for family occasions when she lived in New York.

“It was startling what they could do and very impactful. And it was touching, from my perspective having known her.”

A far cry from the hand-cranked cameras that captured Garbo’s early work, the SKF performance was conjured by humans prompting AI models including China’s Seedream and Google’s Nano Banana Pro.

Unusually for AI film-making, the creators did not feed moving or still images of Garbo into the AI because the material was protected by copyright. Instead, they used text prompts to create her likeness, including her ice-blue eyes and wavy blond bob. A human actor then played her role with her AI-generated appearance overlaid. Her voice was recreated from a recording from an early film.

The resulting version of Garbo appears to have gone beyond the “uncanny valley” – the problem for AI film-makers in which the closer to an actual likeness an AI rendering becomes, the more strangely implausible it seems.

AI Garbo’s lines, however, are not perhaps quite up to the standards of those given to her by MGM studio writers. At one point, she sounds like Liz Truss complaining about the “disgrace” of Britain’s cheese imports, when she says “around 20% of all global energy is lost to friction: a terrible waste”.

Several big film studios are investing in AI startups or collaborating with new AI studios. Veteran directors including Ron Howard and Paul Schrader are working on AI-enabled films, while a new generation of AI-native film-makers such as Kavan the Kid and Gossip Goblin are using AI to build huge audiences outside the conventional studio system.

Asked whether the real Garbo would have wanted to continue performing as an AI-enabled actor, Reisfield said: “She was at the forefront of cinema in the silent film era. She made the transition to ‘talkies’ and dominated box office receipts.

“So to imagine her as an AI-enabled actor given her track record and ability to captivate and connect with audiences of both men and women isn’t inconceivable.”

Reisfield said the custodians of the rights to Garbo’s voice, name, image and publicity aimed to “preserve, protect, and enhance” her legacy and were “very discerning” on partnerships. Her likeness has been posthumously used by the fashion houses Ferragamo, Gucci and Louis Vuitton but the AI performance for SKF is her first in moving images.

Whatever the future holds for AI Garbo, it kept to the true spirit of the actor by signing off the ball-bearing advert with her immortal line from Grand Hotel: “I want to be alone.”

title: We need ‘right to intervene’ in AI amid growing threat, says Bank of England boss
description: Andrew Bailey’s comments come as fears grow that rogue models could take financial system...
fullText:
Andrew Bailey’s comments come as fears grow that rogue models could take financial system hostage

The governor of the Bank of England has said authorities must retain the “right to intervene” in the AI industry amid growing fears that rogue models could take the financial system hostage.

Andrew Bailey said the risks posed by the rapid advancement of frontier AI models – a number of which have gone rogue in recent months – were “real and increasingly significant” and reduced the ability of society to supervise and intervene when things went wrong.

That had implications for financial stability, with the new technology having increased the “scale and sophistication of cyber threats to the financial system”. That could threaten daily card payment, bank transactions, and stock and bond trading across financial markets, he said.

The comments came as the Bank’s financial policy committee (FPC) warned that the growing mountain of AI debt was increasing financial stability risks.

The potential benefits of AI “are immense”, Bailey said but he added that authorities needed to be ready to step in.

In an inaugural opinion piece penned for the Bank of England’s Insight series, he said: “If we are to realise those benefits safely, we must answer one critical question. Should society retain the ability to intervene, to establish the boundaries within which these systems operate and to revise those boundaries as the technology evolves? To my mind the answer is unequivocally yes.”

However, the governor stopped short of calling for a regulatory clampdown. “Regulation is not, in my view, the right place to start. In the excitement surrounding AI development, there is a risk that we move too quickly to debates about regulatory architecture before establishing where the failure exists in the first place.”

Instead, he said a “sensible starting point” would be rigorous testing of new models, to understanding the behaviour of increasingly complex systems, in order to figure out “credible points” where authorities could intervene.

Warning on the ballooning AI debt pile, the FPC said large players in the sector have taken on $450bn (£339bn) worth of debt between January and September this year, already overtaking the $333bn worth of gilts due to be issued by the UK government for the whole of 2026.

That has tied investors – including hedge funds, asset managers and private credit firms – to AI companies’ fortunes at a time when those tech businesses have yet to turn a profit.

“The rapid increase in artificial intelligence-related debt issuance broadens the exposure of capital markets to development in AI,” minutes of the recent FPC meeting on 25 September said.

“The committee underscores the importance of timely and careful management of these intensifying, interconnected risks.”

title: AI tool that copied actor’s ‘lustrous’ voice violated his rights, says Tokyo court

fullText:
Kenjiro Tsuda wins case against TikTok account in landmark Japanese verdict to protect publicity rights

A court in Japan has ruled that the human voice has legal protection after a landmark case involving a well-known actor and a TikTok account that he claimed had cloned his “lustrous” baritone voice in its AI-generated videos.

Tokyo district court said on Wednesday that voices should enjoy the same protection as publicity rights, at the end of a closely watched legal action brought against TikTok by Kenjiro Tsuda – best known for voicing the character Kento Nanami in the anime Jujutsu Kaisen.

But the court dismissed Tsuda’s request that the operator of TikTok remove the videos, noting that the user had deleted them soon after the suit was filed last November. “The unauthorised use of a performer’s voice … can be considered an infringement on publicity rights,” said the presiding judge, Aya Takahashi.

The lawsuit is believed to be the first in Japan seeking to defend an individual’s vocal identity against AI-generated copies. Japan’s voice actors, many of whom achieve star status through their “appearances” in anime, are increasingly worried that AI mimicry is threatening their livelihoods and the industry as a whole.

An actor’s voice “is the result of years of rigorous training and apprenticeship”, Yuko Sasaki, executive director of the Japan Actors Union said ahead of the ruling.

Tsuda, 55, claimed that the 188 TikTok videos uploaded on an anonymous account between July 2024 and September last year had been narrated by a “deep” and “lustrous” voice that could only be his. In response, the platform argued that the videos contained a “generic male voice” and that any perceived similarities to Tsuda’s voice were highly subjective.

The verdict is the first in which a Japanese court has declared that the human voice is protected under publicity rights, a reference to the ability to control and profit from aspects of an individual’s identity, in Tsuda’s case his distinctive voice.

The protection applies “if the purpose of using the voice is exclusively to take advantage of its commercial appeal”, Takahashi said, describing a voice to be “as symbolic of one’s personality as portraits are”.

The TikTok account, whose picture resembled Tsuda’s Jujutsu Kaisen character, combined images and AI-generated speech about urban legends, the occult and conspiracy theories.

At one point, the account had more than 200,000 subscribers and, according to the legal complaint, the clips would have earned its owner between ¥500,000 (£2,395) and ¥75,000 in monthly revenue, the Kyodo news agency said.

Describing the content as “sordid”, Tsuda’s legal team claimed the account had only attracted attention because it had cloned the “attractive voice of a popular actor”.

TikTok said in a statement it would “respect the court’s judgment while considering what steps to take after scrutinising [the ruling’s] details”. It added: “We will continue to sincerely work on the balance between technology development and rights protection.”

In 2024, actors in Japan launched a campaign called “No More” to oppose the unauthorised use of their faces and voices in AI-generated content.

With reporting by Agence France-Presse
