fullText:
Deepfakes and misinformation driven by artificial intelligence have become a point of deep concern for legislators, advocates and the public

An image of College Park, Georgia mayor Bianca Motley Broom kissing a man – who was not her husband – in a bar spread far and wide on Facebook. The fact that it’s fake is spreading faster, now, but only after it had been seen by thousands of people.

“I think this is a sad commentary about where we are in our democracy, and where we are in our political discourse,” Motley Broom said. “It also seeks to reinforce really tired stereotypes about women in leadership.”

Six years ago, when Motley Broom first took office in the Atlanta suburb, a political enemy might have needed at least rudimentary skill with image-editing software to forge an image of a politician in a compromising position. Today, all that is required is a computer and a prompt for an AI image generator.

The threat of deepfakes and misinformation driven by artificial intelligence has become a point of deep concern by legislators, advocates and the public.

A poll taken mid-June by Rad Campaign, a digital marketing agency, and Women Who Tech, an advocacy organization for female entrepreneurs, showed that about 71% of respondents worry about AI-generated deepfakes and disinformation affecting elections, while two in three respondents said they were concerned about AI being used to sexualize women.

“The findings show that Americans are more concerned about AI’s use in deepfakes, election disinformation, and the sexualization of women and children than its impact on jobs or the economy,” said Allyson Kapin, founder of the Rad Campaign and cofounder of Women Who Tech.

The Trump administration has a penchant for deploying AI imagery. In January, the White House’s official account on the social media platform X posted a digitally altered image of Nekima Levy Armstrong, who had been arrested in connection with a demonstration that disrupted church services in St Paul, Minnesota.

A picture of her calmly being escorted by a DHS agent was altered so that she appeared to be crying, and her skin had been darkened. Kaelan Dorr, the White House deputy communications director, later described the image as a “meme”.

Fake images of Zohran Mamdami, New York’s mayor, also began circulating from a “parody” account on X in February, falsely depicting him and his mother in the company of disgraced financier Jeffrey Epstein. Using Google’s SynthID tool, Reuters debunked the images, but not before other accounts had recirculated them as authentic, fueling conspiracy theories.

Despite significant apprehension around the potential economic consequences of AI, concern about deepfake images being used to sexualize women or children, or to influence elections, outstrips concern about AI affecting jobs by about three to one, Kapin said.

“The public is deeply concerned.”

Raphael Warnock, a Georgia Democratic senator, said in a video posted to Facebook that deepfake images had been circulating online falsely depicting him with health problems, with an armful of grandchildren he does not have – and with a full head of hair, which he said was funny, if problematic.

“As these tools become increasingly powerful, it will get harder and harder to distinguish fact from fiction, and there are already bad actors out there, who are doing everything they can to divide us and confuse us,” Warnock said. “This has huge implications for our democracy. What if hours before an election, someone created a page with AI, generated images, fake stories about the candidates, how will voters know what’s true, and what’s not true?”

Warnock is among a group of senate Democrats who have been war-gaming political responses to possible election interference scenarios. Chief among those scenarios: disinformation driven by fabricated images or videos circulated through social media.

Outgoing US senator John Kennedy, a Louisiana Republican, offered a bill last week requiring AI firms to install a “kill switch” for rogue AI. Senator Rand Paul of Kentucky blocked Kennedy’s bill, describing the effort as premature without additional industry input.

Hakeem Jeffries, the Democratic House minority leader, said in an interview earlier this month on SiriusXM that government should move “urgently” on AI regulations, broadly, calling for “guardrails to protect the American people from bad actors and bad behavior”, adding: “It should be a high priority.”

Jeffries noted that Republicans attempted to pass legislation preempting states from regulating AI last year, as part of the omnibus One Big Beautiful Bill. The amendment failed on a 99-1 vote in the senate.

State legislatures are also wrestling with AI regulation amid a widespread, bipartisan public backlash. Some states have legislation like Tennessee’s Ensuring Likeness Voice and Image Security Act – the Elvis Act – which protects politicians and residents alike from AI voice cloning and digital likeness replication, using the state’s robust right-of-publicity protections that are a product of Nashville’s recording industry.

Clear disclaimers are legally required in most states when a political campaign uses AI to manipulate the speeches, appearances or actions of officials or candidates. Georgia is not one of them.

While legislators in Georgia began debated deepfake protections in bills proposed in 2024 and 2025, they have not yet enacted legislation.

Motley Broom said she believes she was targeted by political opponents who objected to her role as a past president of the Georgia Municipal Association. “I have worked for my city to try to be the best advocate I can be on behalf of College Park,” Motley Broom said. “And I certainly won’t be deterred by internet trolls who think this carries weight.”

While she could consider legal action under existing defamation law in Georgia, Motley Broom paused for a moment when asked what legislators should be doing about this. The first amendment protection for speech has to be considered, she said.

“These types of attacks should not be without consequences,” she said. “I hope that lawmakers can address this in a way that balances not only first amendment protections, but the right of an individual not to have completely false accusations being levied. And I’m really hopeful that … that lawmakers on the state and federal level can think about that and think about it carefully, because this is the tip of the iceberg.”

title: Elmore and Grant named in Northern Ireland squad
description: Sparta Prague forward Kess Elmore is a surprise first call-up for Northern Ireland's 2027 Women's World Cup play-off with Portugal.
fullText:
Sparta Prague forward Kess Elmore is a surprise first call-up for Northern Ireland's 2027 Women's World Cup play-off with Portugal.

Elmore, 27, is a former England youth international and is one of five new call-ups in Michael McArdle's squad.

Galway United full back Lucy-Jayne Grant is included for the first time, as are the Irish Premiership trio Naomi McLaughlin, Jane McMaster and Charlotte Havern.

Havern has had a strong campaign for champions Cliftonville, while McMaster has stood out for Linfield and McLaughlin has impressed for Glentoran after a mid-season switch back to the league from Aberdeen.

There are several absentees through injury, including Kelsie Burrows, Laura Rafferty, Nadene Caldwell, Megan Bell, Joely Andrews, Danielle Maxwell and Caragh Hamilton.

Northern Ireland host Portugal at Inver Park on Friday, 9 October before the return leg in Portimao four days later.

The sides last met in Euro 2025 qualifying when Portugal ran out 4-0 winners in Liera before a narrow 2-1 victory at Mourneview Park.

If McArdle's side can upset Portugal, who are ranked 28 places higher than NI, then they would face Iceland or Croatia in the next play-off round.

While the majority of teams who win the second play-off round will progress to the finals in Brazil, Northern Ireland's ranking means they would likely face an additional inter-continental play-off round in February, as the lowest European side, if they are to make a first World Cup.

Goalkeepers: Jackie Burns (Burnley), Lauren Perry (Montrose), Maddy Harvey-Clifford (Cliftonville)

Defenders: Rebecca Holloway (Birmingham City), Rebecca McKenna (Birmingham City), Ellie Mason (Charlton), Natalie Johnson (Norwich City), Fi Morgan (Celtic), Abi Sweetlove (Linfield), Emily Cassap (Sunderland), Lucy-Jayne Grant (Galway United ), Jane McMaster (Linfield)

Midfielders: Aimee Kerr (Glentoran), Mia Moore (Glentoran), Brenna McPartlan (Burnley), Keri Halliday (Hearts), Connie Scofield (Sheffield United), Naomi McLaughlin (Glentoran), Charlotte Havern (Cliftonville).

Forwards: Lauren Wade (Hearts), Casey Howe (Celtic), Leyla McFarland (Rapperswil-Jona, Switzerland), Cora Chambers (Linfield), Kess Elmore (Sparta Prague).

title: How do teams deal with longer international window?
description: With the international window extended to four games, how do nations like Northern Ireland deal with the additional demands on players and staff?
fullText:
In years gone by, the final whistle would have blown in Northern Ireland's Nations League game with Hungary and the players would have been heading back to their clubs.

Instead, Michael O'Neill and his squad are back on the road to Slovakia to face Ukraine in the extended international window.

For 2026, the September and October breaks have been amalgamated into one 16-day window, with four fixtures instead of two.

Northern Ireland have made a strong start to the campaign with four points from two matches, but it isn't without its challenges.

But how does it impact a nation like Northern Ireland, who do not have the squad depth or resources of some of Europe's heavy hitters?

Szoboszlai's Hungary latest to draw blank in Belfast

O'Neill 'positive' as NI maintain unbeaten start

For Northern Ireland in particular, the schedule has been gruelling.

Their Nations League campaign started with a 5,000-mile round trip to Georgia, where Shea Charles' 99th-minute winner snatched a late victory.

For that game, O'Neill, his staff and players had stayed in the BST time zone instead of trying to adapt to the three-hour time difference.

With a short turnaround before Monday's game against Hungary - their first home match in 315 days - the squad flew back home overnight to arrive back in Belfast on Saturday morning.

While Northern Ireland kept Liverpool midfielder Dominik Szoboszlai quiet - as they did with Paris St-Germain star Khvicha Kvaratskhelia in Tbilisi - the players looked tired as the game progressed.

"Tiredness will be a big factor," O'Neill said.

"Logistics are a big factor as well in terms of your travel and how that works."

One other factor for smaller nations is injuries and suspensions.

Northern Ireland were already without key players such as Conor Bradley and Ali McCann before Sunderland defender Daniel Ballard injured his hamstring in Georgia, ruling him out of the rest of the window.

Unlike Germany boss Jurgen Klopp, who has the luxury of effectively selecting two different squads, O'Neill has to work with a smaller playing pool.

Of course, injuries are part of the game and can happen at any moment, but the condensed window only magnifies the issue.

"It's a massive factor in the game and if you look at some players who have been injured in the first game, like Dan, they are now out completely," O'Neill said.

"Other countries have had that as well, but you can miss four games of a six-game tournament."

Another factor to consider is an increase in yellow cards, with tired legs leading to a higher chance of picking up a second booking, which would lead to a suspension.

After two matches, seven Northern Ireland players are one card away from missing a match, and O'Neill admitted he found some of the yellows handed out to his side as "disappointing".

While this is the first iteration of the autumnal quadruple header, O'Neill says he would like to see consistency across the scheduling of matches.

Georgia, for example, have had their first two matches at home so have had limited travel and, by consequence, easier recovery from matches before they head to Hungary and Belfast for their final two games of the window.

"There are things in there that create a bit of an imbalance and I know it's difficult to get the fixtures all right," O'Neill said.

"The only thing I would like to see is we have an extra day's recovery now going into the third game.

"I would like to see the recovery periods between every game be consistent."

The consolation for Northern Ireland is that Ukraine will be making that same journey back from Tbilisi before the third game, but the caveat is they have an additional day to recover and have an hour less to travel with the time difference.

O'Neill added that he understands the logic behind the scheduling, but it has "high demands on players in that time".

"It might be difficult to do that [have consistent gaps between games] but I think that would help a lot of the teams, particularly the smaller nations," he said.

"Sixteen days is a long time and there's the travel as well, obviously.

"We're coping well with it, but I think it will be a tough game for us on Friday night."

While Europe's bigger nations have their own in-house resources, countries like Northern Ireland share staff with clubs, which can bring its own challenges in an extended window.

"We don't carry full-time doctors, full-time physios and full-time sports scientists," O'Neill added.

"Other countries are the same, but all our staff work at clubs and we need agreement from the clubs.

"That's a challenge to be able to staff it properly and keep the level of professionalism.

"The big countries don't have that, they have full-time staff and an army of staff to be able to do these things."

O'Neill also has to consider how much to rotate this squad. It's a fine balance between keeping key players fresh, but also how much exposure to give his young squad.

Of the 26-man squad, 17 of the players are aged 25 or under and only three - Josh Magennis (36), Paddy McNair (31) and Dion Charles (30) - are over the age of 30.

Arsenal's Ceadach O'Neill, Everton's Braiden Graham and Kieran Morrison, who is on loan at Sheffield Wednesday from Liverpool, are the three teenagers in the squad.

"I don't want to put too many young players on the pitch in a game like that where they're untried and untested at that level," O'Neill said.

"We want to bring the younger players in to give them the best chance to be able to do well and to build their confidence and to build their reputation. That's the challenge for us."

title: Fishlock set for Wales return - but not as player
description: Rhian Wilkinson says icon Jess Fishlock will be back with the national team if they reach a World Cup play-off final in December – but only as a coach.
fullText:
Rhian Wilkinson says in-form Wales icon Jess Fishlock will be back with the national team if they reach a Women's World Cup play-off final in December – but only as a coach.

Fishlock, Wales' most-capped footballer, called time on her international career last October.

But the 39-year-old continues to shine for Seattle Reign, having claimed two fine goals in last weekend's win over Boston Legacy to become the National Women's Soccer League club's all-time leading scorer.

Wales, meanwhile, are without a string of senior players for the World Cup play-off semi-final against Albania next month, but Wilkinson says she has turned down Fishlock's tongue-in-cheek offer to come out of international retirement.

"Jess could play forever, she's incredible," the Wales head coach said.

"There was never a doubt that Jess Fishlock could still do a job for us. [But] I think it was absolutely the right time for her to step away after that amazing qualification for the Euro [last year]."

Women's World Cup qualifying play-off semi-final

Live on BBC iPlayer, BBC Two Wales, BBC Sounds, BBC Radio Wales Extra, Radio Cymru, BBC Sport website and app, plus live text commentary.

Fishlock, who has said this will be her last year playing club football, will be on duty with Reign when Wales go to Albania on Friday, 9 October and then again in the return leg in Llanelli four days later.

Should Wales overcome a side who are 36 places in the Fifa rankings – and one they beat twice in the group phase of World Cup qualifying – they will play either Norway or Romania in a two-legged play-off final in December.

Wilkinson has revealed that another recently retired former player, Kayleigh Barton, will be part of her staff for the Albania ties and then Fishlock will have a role should Wales reach the final.

Fishlock previously worked as a technical assistant for Wales' opening game of this qualifying campaign, against the Czech Republic in March.

Wilkinson explained that Fishlock had been in touch before she named her semi-final squad on Tuesday, adding: "I didn't appreciate her saying 'call me up coach, I'm ready', which I thought was mean, but [she was] a wonderful player and a great leader for us.

"If we are able to get past Albania, she'll be coming in as a coach for us for the next round."

title: Sheedy surprised as header goes viral
description: Cardiff fly-half Callum Sheedy says he did not realise his "header" against Scarlets in the United Rugby Championship (URC) game would go viral.
fullText:
Cardiff fly-half Callum Sheedy says he did not realise his "header" against Scarlets in the United Rugby Championship (URC) game would go viral.

Sheedy headed the ball forward after chasing his own kick in the second half of the 21-15 victory against Scarlets on Saturday night.

The clip has had more than 800,000 hits across social media.

"I probably wasn't thinking at the time, that was the problem," said Sheedy.

"I remember the ball sitting up, and I could see Blair [Murray] coming towards me, and I thought it was going be an aerial contest.

"I thought there needed to be a way of me getting the ball past him, and there wasn't enough time to get it down to my foot, so the nearest body part was my head.

Sheedy said he was unaware of the appeal of the clip.

"I had a laugh, looking back at the video and the boys give me a bit of stick," said Sheedy.

"I didn't think of it at the time. After the game, I'd gone on my phone and my Instagram had blown up a bit. I'm glad people are enjoying it."

Sheedy says he was unsure whether using his head was allowed in rugby's laws, with former World Cup final referee Nigel Owens taking to social media this week stating he thought it was illegal if it was deliberate.

"I think it's a split 50-50 among the public," said Sheedy.

"I always thought it was legal, but enough people are telling me it's illegal, but who knows?

"Until the next person that does it, we'll never know."

Sheedy's exploits evoke memories of another former Cardiff maverick fly-half Mark Ring.

"I am waiting for Ringo [Mark Ring] to text me and I expect him to," said Sheedy.

"It would have been something he would have done."

Sheedy played his part in the victory in Llanelli before being replaced in the second half by Jarrod Evans, who has returned to Cardiff from Harlequins this season.

With Ioan Lloyd, who is currently injured, also in the Cardiff ranks, head coach Corniel van Zyl has three Wales fly-halves to call on.

"All I can do as a player is try my best and perform the best I can," said Sheedy.

"We all want to be number one, so how we go about that is going to be challenging because we're all going to want to play.

"I'm sure it'll be healthy competition."

Cardiff return to the Arms Park to face Zebre on Friday night, where they lost only one home game last season.

"It does make a big difference," said Sheedy.

"Hopefully we get a big crowd because I remember last season there were a lot of close games, and in the last 10 minutes, the crowd got us over the line.

"Corniel speaks a lot about making the Arms Park a fortress and we managed that last season."

There is also expectation on Cardiff this season after their sixth-place finish in the 2025-26 campaign and qualifying for the Champions Cup.

"You've got to welcome that expectation," said Sheedy.

"We got in the play-offs, but the good sides back it up.

"I am confident in the squad. We had a great pre-season and good start to the season, so let's see if we can kick on."

Cardiff will name their side to face Zebre on Thursday and have back three injury concerns with wing Mason Grady (head cut) and full-back Cameron Winnett (head) both major doubts.

Wales wing Josh Adams is still missing with a calf problem, while Iwan Stephens and Theo Cabango are long-term casualties.

Wing Tom Bowen is line to come into the starting side for Friday with centre Harri Millard another option on the other flank, with Jacob Beetham able to switch to full-back.

The Premier League footballers studying to become sporting directors
description: Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall, Taiwo Awoniyi and others have been juggling education with a football career - even studying on the team bus during away trips.
fullText:
The scene resembles an Oxbridge graduation ceremony, but those gathered in caps and gowns are in fact Premier League footballers or former players who have won major honours in Europe and around the world.

The 2026 cohort of graduates from the PFA Business School includes Everton midfielder Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall, Coventry City striker Taiwo Awoniyi and a host of well-known figures.

In the event at Arsenal's Emirates Stadium, Cesar Azpilicueta tells the group how studying on the morning of the 2021 Champions League final helped take his mind off the occasion before he captained Chelsea to a 1-0 win over Manchester City in Porto.

Dewsbury-Hall, 28, travelled by train from Merseyside to London to attend the ceremony and, despite being in the best form of his career, explains why he had completed a postgraduate diploma in global football sport directorship.

The former Leicester City and Chelsea player tells BBC Sport: "I hope I've got a long time left in football. But as a person, I'm always trying to learn and develop away from the pitch. I don't want to stop playing and then just sit around doing nothing.

"This was something that genuinely interested me. Whether I use it in the future, we'll see, but it's always good to do it now rather than wait until you've finished playing.

"If the time ever comes when an opportunity presents itself, luckily I've got something that can help me."

The assembled players are potential leaders in football's future.

Awoniyi, 29, joined Coventry from Nottingham Forest during the summer, and he remains part of Nigeria's squad as they attempt to qualify for the 2027 Africa Cup of Nations.

The striker has also continued his studies throughout his playing career.

"I've got a degree in business management and another diploma, so this is my third qualification," he says.

Awoniyi's father, Solomon, has previously spoken about his strict approach to education. At times it almost prevented his son from pursuing a career in football, but Awoniyi progressed from the Imperial Soccer Academy to Liverpool before making his name in German football with Union Berlin.

"I say to people I am a quiet dreamer," says Awoniyi, who was born in Ilorin, Nigeria. "I always felt education was important. It was a promise I made to my dad that if I played football, I would keep studying.

"That's what I have done and I am proud of it."

Awoniyi points to the "ups and downs" he has experienced as a footballer, referencing the serious injury he suffered in May 2025 when he was placed in a medically induced coma after rupturing an intestine in a collision with a goalpost when playing for Nottingham Forest against Leicester City.

To him, it is important to keep improving and to recognise there is more to life than football, which is where the Professional Footballers' Association course comes in.

Awoniyi says: "It's not like a 9-5 job in football. We go in and sometimes finish quite early and, although it's challenging, I think every footballer has time in the evening for something like this business school.

"Of course, it demands a lot from you and it's all about how willing you are to do it. I say to people there are a lot of things that are bigger than football.

"Yes, football is our passion, but we are normal human beings as well and maybe that's something the world doesn't always see."

The graduates certainly appear no different from anyone else celebrating an academic achievement, exhibiting their pride.

Awoniyi has brought members of his extended family to the ceremony, while Dewsbury-Hall seeks out former Everton midfielder Tim Cahill, now working in Qatari football, to discuss the art of scoring goals.

"Obviously there are stereotypes around footballers," Dewsbury-Hall says.

"But in every industry there are smart people and there are people who aren't so smart. You'd be surprised how many intelligent people there are in football.

"Maybe some players just don't want to do things like this, but they easily could. It's just not their passion.

"I'm not saying this is my passion, but it's something I've done to show that footballers can complete these kinds of courses while they're still playing. Who knows where it will lead?"

The course is designed to run alongside a football career. Seminars are scheduled to minimise clashes with matches and training sessions.

Players can study in their own time, although Dewsbury-Hall says he has had some "weird looks" while studying on an iPad during journeys home from away games.

Every graduate has a different story.

For Wycombe Wanderers defender Steve Cook, who captained Bournemouth in the Premier League earlier in his career, the course marked a return to formal education for the first time since his school days. Having already obtained coaching badges, he knows he is approaching the end of his playing career.

Some may not actively use their newly gained expertise for many years. All will benefit in some way, though, believes Azpilicueta.

"It's not only about preparing for life after football. It's about becoming a better version of yourself in your football career as well," the former Spain defender, who retired from playing at the end of last season, tells BBC Sport.

Education has been part of his life and is what helped him become a leader on and off the pitch.

Azpilicueta built a career after turning professional with hometown club Osasuna at the age of 17.

He had continued studying until that point and, after abandoning his degree when he became a professional footballer, he later returned to complete an MBA at Harvard University in the United States during his nine-year spell at Chelsea.

The desire to study before playing the biggest match of his club career, Chelsea's Champions League final triumph five years ago, indicates how he balanced his two interests.

"Normally I'd have a nap after lunch if the game was later in the day, but that day it was impossible. You could hear the fans and you knew a big game was coming up. Having my studies also helped me focus and improve myself away from football," he explains.

After ending his playing days with Atletico Madrid and Sevilla, Azpilicueta says he will not be rushing into his next role.

The PFA course includes sessions from prominent figures, such as Brighton chief executive Paul Barber, designed to help students understand how different areas of the football industry operate.

For now, many remain focused on playing football. But among this year's graduates might be future coaches, executives and sporting directors who go on to influence the game in different ways.

title: Tumultuous summer ends in success - what next for Stokes?
description: After concluding the county summer with Durham and the end of his England central contract, what is in store for Ben Stokes?
fullText:
As cricket prepares to go into hibernation for the winter after the usual summer slog, Ben Stokes' playing diary is a lot quieter than previously.

For the first time since 2014, there will be no central contract from the England and Wales Cricket Board as he begins the next chapter of his career.

The 35-year-old caused one of the sporting stories of the year when he announced in the middle of a Test decider against New Zealand that he was walking away from the England captaincy and international cricket as a whole.

Initial sanctuary has come at his own county, Durham, where he has been a wholehearted and willing contributor to their Division Two title success.

But it is a long six months before whites will be seen around English grounds again, and it means one of the greatest all-rounders the game has ever seen - and arguably the game's best player over the past decade - is now open to offers.

Tough chats and Three Peaks - Durham's road to the title

Campbell moves to Durham director of cricket role

As England's Test team start focusing on a Christmas tour to South Africa, Stokes is heading to Australia for the festive period.

That's because he has signed to play in the Big Bash for Adelaide Strikers as he plays in the T20 competition for the first time since 2015.

From there, Stokes has a variety of options as the gates of the franchise world are open to him.

But there are also complications. A global superstar like him would surely be of interest in India, but he did not take part in the IPL's mega auction in 2025 because of England commitments.

Overseas players who have previously played in the IPL - as Stokes has done for Chennai Super Kings, Rajasthan Royals and Rising Pune Supergiant - must register for the mega-auction that takes place every three years, or miss the subsequent two mini-auctions. As things stand, that makes him ineligible until the 2028 edition.

South Africa's SA 20 begins just before the Big Bash finishes, while the Pakistan Super League, which is expected to run concurrently with the IPL in the spring, would love a headliner like Stokes to bring some stardust and eyeballs to their tournament.

Head into the summer and there is Major League Cricket in the United States. But this is where another complication may arise.

If Stokes wants to play for Durham, or signs a contract that includes any white-ball cricket in the T20 Blast or One-Day Cup, he would need a special No-Objection Certificate (NOC) from the ECB to play in a franchise league that clashes with domestic competitions for which they are contracted.

And the ECB has previously refused NOCs to former England players who have wanted to pursue freelance T20 careers.

Retirement the best thing for me - Stokes

England captain Ben Stokes announces retirement

12 Dec 2026 - 26 Jan 2027: Big Bash (Australia)

17 Jan - 21 Feb: SA T20 (South Africa)

Mid-June - mid-July: Major League Cricket (USA)

And then there is his boyhood club, Durham.

It is where Stokes has wholeheartedly thrown himself into things away from the England spotlight.

After a family holiday, he returned to play in all 10 of their One-Day Cup games as they reached the semi-finals, before turning out in four of their remaining six Championship matches as the side romped to the Division Two title by 47 points, going unbeaten in the process.

There were plenty of highlights, too. He smashed an unbeaten 108 away to Derbyshire in his first game away from the international spotlight in the 50-over competition in July.

In the Championship, he hit four half-centuries in 10 innings and averaged 47.88 but it was with the ball in hand that the fireworks happened.

His rapid burst of 5-17 blew away Derbyshire again last month and, in a dead rubber at home to Worcestershire in the penultimate game, with the title already secured, Stokes produced one of his marathon spells to finish with 6-94 off 31.3 overs - the most wickets and overs of any bowler in the team.

His 25 wickets this season came at average of 20.36 and he demonstrated once again that he remains a fearsome and competitive animal when the match is on the line.

But Durham now need to discuss with Stokes how next summer will look, and it will be one of the first tasks for Ryan Campbell in his new role as director of cricket.

The Australian has spent the past four seasons as head coach, and enjoyed having Stokes in the dressing room and part of his team, and he believes that the all-rounder is keen to continue playing county cricket - and the red-ball stuff in particular.

"Yes, I do, I honestly do," Campbell told BBC Sport in an interview before his new role was announced.

"His love of the game, he talks about his bowling run-up and stuff that he can adapt to county cricket so he can bowl more. The playing, the batting, where he wants to bat, this sort of stuff, he's all-in I would have thought for the next couple of years at least."

When Stokes was suspended by the ECB for the second Test in June, it was Durham where he rediscovered his love of the game after the troubles of the Ashes in Australia last winter and the broken curfew post-Lords.

Being in and around the Riverside, singing the Blaydon Races after team victories and helping academy youngsters with practice is something that has not gone unnoticed.

"Ben's England through-and-through, but he is Durham through-and-through," said Campbell.

"He loves the club. The proudest thing I've ever had in relation to our work was when he said, 'I want to go back and play at Durham because the time there has been so amazing'. That's a big rap for our club and our environment that we've created."

But as Stokes contemplates his future, it's worth pointing out that he has not played a match in the short format of the game since appearing for Northern Superchargers in The Hundred in 2024.

While his appearances in the One-Day Cup this summer were his first in the 50-over format of white-ball cricket since the 2023 World Cup.

Of course, he has played starring roles in England winning the World Cup final in 2019 and then the World T20 final in 2022, but in the past few years he focused primarily on his commitments as England Test captain.

It is going to be a change of pace and Campbell is fascinated to see what unfolds.

"Ben will be quite wise with his decisions of where he goes, how long for, how many games he's going to play," he said.

"It's going to be a big test for him as he hasn't played T20 cricket for ages - trying to get back into the rhythm of white-ball bowling and batting.

"I hear Adelaide are going to open the batting with him. That's brilliant. That's where he belongs in T20 cricket. Where does he bowl? How are they going to use him? I'm intrigued to see that sort of stuff."

title: Will Pocognoli change keeper after loss to Switzerland?
description: Andy Burke ponders whether Scotland head coach Sebastien Pocognoli will change goalkeeper after Angus Gunn's performance in the 3-0 defeat by Switzerland.
fullText:
If it was a bad night for Jack Hendry, whose 11th-minute red card precipitated Scotland's demise against Switzerland, then it was hardly an evening Angus Gunn will look back on with any great fondness either.

"I've never been a big defender of goalkeepers and I'm looking for more from Angus Gunn," was the view of Sportsound pundit Andy Halliday on the Scotland keeper's performance.

The San Jose Earthquakes stopper, 30, was arguably at fault for the first and third of the three goals that hit the back of his net as the Swiss coasted to victory at Hampden in a deeply unsatisfactory first home match under Sebastien Pocognoli.

The opening goal came in the immediate aftermath of Hendry's red card for denying Dan Ndoye a goalscoring opportunity. Scotland thought they had been given a reprieve as referee Nenad Minakovic's original award of a penalty was changed after a VAR review to a free-kick on the edge of the box.

The let-off meant little as Ricardo Rodriguez smashed the set-piece past Gunn on the goalkeeper's side to open the scoring.

"Shoulder height and not a lot of pace," was Halliday's view. "For me I think it's so poor from Angus Gunn."

After Nico Elvedi turned home Ndoye's cross to double the Swiss lead, Zeki Amdouni rifled a shot that went through Gunn's arms and high into the net to make it 3-0.

"I know it's a powerful strike, but that's one that Angus Gunn can keep out," said former Scotland forward James McFadden.

Gunn started all three games at the World Cup in front of Liam Kelly and Craig Gordon. It was testament to Gordon's extraordinary longevity that he made the squad for the finals at the age of 43 - but also highlighted the lack of other quality options competing for the number one jersey.

Podcast: The Pocognoli report card

Falkirk's Scott Bain has replaced the retired Gordon in the squad for this Nations League campaign but there is a sense Scotland are not as blessed in the goalkeeping department as they have been in years gone by.

So, will Pocognoli be tempted to make a change in goals for the upcoming matches against North Macedonia on Saturday and Slovenia on Tuesday?

"I don't think there's somebody that's battering the door down to take his jersey because a lot of them aren't playing football," said Halliday.

"He probably is the number one deservedly but you never feel as confident with Angus Gunn between the sticks as you would have done a Craig Gordon, an Allan McGregor, a David Marshall, a Jim Leighton, an Andy Goram. They have been our goalies for the last 20-25 years.

"I'm looking at the first and the third goal - and I might be in the minority for the third goal, I think a lot of people will think it's been hit with such pace - but the goalies I mentioned there, do they save them? I think they do."

New coach, new players, but same old failings hamper Scotland

Hampden debut to forget but Pocognoli looks at bigger picture

Who 'battled impressively' for Scots? And how did you rate players?

Gunn made a couple of smart saves from Ndoye either side of half-time to prevent Switzerland killing the game off even earlier, but the keeper admitted he would look at the goals he conceded to see where he might have done better.

"They were good strikes but, as a goalkeeper, I'm always disappointed when I concede a goal," Gunn told media after the game.

"I'll look back and see what I could have done better and get better for the next game.

"[For the first goal] obviously when you've got a free-kick that close, you want to protect your side. I was holding as much as I could and saw it late. I'll probably look back at it.

"I'll probably be disappointed and try and get better for next time."

title: Ocon to leave Haas putting F1 future in doubt
description: Esteban Ocon is fighting to save his Formula 1 career after the Haas team announcement that they are splitting with the Frenchman at the end of the year.
fullText:
Esteban Ocon is fighting to save his Formula 1 career after the Haas team announced they would split with the Frenchman at the end of the year.

Ocon, who won the 2021 Hungarian Grand Prix for Alpine, joined Haas in 2025. He has been in F1 since 2016 and has also driven for the Manor and Force India teams.

There are no obvious berths for Ocon on the grid in 2027 but he insisted: "This is absolutely not the end of my Formula 1 career."

The 30-year-old added in a statement on social media: "I leave this project with my head held high and proud of my performances in what were not always the easiest of circumstances for various reasons and factors outside of my control.

"My immediate focus is the next race weekend. I will continue to work hard with the team, maximise every opportunity, and keep extracting every bit of performance from the car.

"There are still many races to go this season and, as always, I will give it my everything behind the wheel for myself and for my team.

"I am still motivated. I am still hungry."

Ocon has been outperformed by team-mate Oliver Bearman since joining forces with Haas last year.

This year, the Briton is 13th in the championship, three places and 13 points ahead of Ocon. Bearman has out-qualified Ocon 13-6 at an average advantage of 0.144 seconds.

Last year, Bearman finished 13th and Ocon 15th, separated by just three points, and in qualifying it was 18-7 at 0.175secs

Haas team principal Ayao Kumatso said: "Esteban's professionalism and commitment have proved valuable as we continue to grow as an organisation.

"Together this year we tackled the challenge of a major regulation change, where Esteban's driving experience and inputs were significant as we've worked hard to develop the VF-26 across the season."

title: Richards 'devastated' by Man City guilty verdicts
description: Former Manchester City defender Micah Richards felt "absolutely devastated" after reading the Premier League's "damning" verdict on the club's financial charges.
fullText:
Former Manchester City defender Micah Richards says he felt "absolutely devastated" after reading the Premier League's "damning" guilty verdict on the club's financial charges.

An independent commission found that City arranged "sham contracts" with a number of commercial partners as part of a scheme to disguise secret funding of more than £830m.

The league confirmed City have been found guilty of all charges related to breaches of financial rules between the 2009-10 and 2017-18 seasons, and all but one in relation to failure to co-operate with the investigation.

The club continue to deny any wrongdoing and have until 2 October to submit an appeal.

During that nine-year period the Sky Blues won the Premier League three times, with Richards part of their title-winning squad in 2011-12.

"The reports were troubling," he said on The Rest is Football podcast. "I saw the words which were used by the Premier League in 'sham contracts' and I felt absolutely devastated.

"I was at that club since I was 14 years old, I would die for that club. I achieved my dream at Manchester City, but then to hear these reports, and not only me as an ex-player, but the fans, what they have to go through, absolutely devastating."

While Richards was part of the City's youth academy he lived in 'digs' with a local family who are long-term supporters of the club.

The 38-year-old added: "My digs man, he rang me and he was literally in tears and asking me about information, which I don't know. I haven't got the answers to tell him.

"That's someone who's supported the club for 60-odd years and the uncertainty around it is just heartbreaking.

"To have a headline of this nature for a club that I love so much, it's been difficult. If you listen to the reports, they are damning.

"I feel saddened, I feel angry, I feel a little bit confused because, on the other side, you have City's side of the story."

City chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak said in a statement on Saturday that the club is still confident of proving its innocence, while on Tuesday chief executive Ferran Soriano said in a video message, external to staff and players that "irrefutable evidence" had been "ignored" by the commission.

City won their second Premier League title in 2013-14, overtaking Liverpool during the run-in to finish two points above the Reds.

Former Liverpool defender Jamie Carragher, who retired in 2013, said: "I feel for the players... they'll almost feel like a lot of their career is going to have an asterisk, or a lot of people will be calling it a sham.

"The players were told everything was fine. What the [City] hierarchy are coming out with now, they're just gaslighting.

"I think the titles should be taken off their list. Whether other clubs get them is probably slightly different. City have not just hurt their own players."

The 2013-14 season was the closest that Carragher's long-time team-mate Steven Gerrard came to winning the Premier League title.

"Those players will never get that feeling and it was robbed by Man City," Carragher added on Sky Sports News.

"No-one remembers the medal. Giving trophies or medals back, it doesn't mean anything. It's not about medals, it's about feelings."

title: 'Rock, paper, scissors' decides order of London Marathon races
description: A game of rock, paper, scissors is used to determine when the elite female and male races will take place at next year's two-day London Marathon.
fullText:
A game of rock, paper, scissors was used to determine when the elite female and male races will take place at next year's unique two-day London Marathon.

Men's world record holder Sabastian Sawe was beaten by women's wheelchair world record holder Catherine Debrunner - both 2026 London Marathon champions in their respective races - in the contest.

As a result, the elite men and men's wheelchair races are set for Saturday, 24 April, with the women's events taking place the following day on the traditional Sunday.

Hugh Brasher, chief executive of London Marathon Events, said: "Sabastian and Catherine's rock, paper, scissors battle was an entertaining way to decide which day would host each elite race.

"Splitting the elite races will allow us to shine an even brighter spotlight on the extraordinary athletes taking part."

Earlier this year, organisers of the event confirmed the London Marathon will be held across two days in what is said to be a momentous one-off edition of the event.

The decision was made to enable more people to take part, after a record 1.33 million people entered the ballot for next year.

In 2027 a record-breaking 100,000 participants will take part and it is estimated that more than £150m will be raised for charitable causes.

The women's championship categories will line-up behind the women's elite field for the first time in the London race.

"Our outstanding elite women's wheelchair field will begin the action just ahead of them, creating a true celebration of women's marathon racing," Brasher added.

The main events on both days will be a mixed field of male, female and non-binary participants.

title: £1.2bn on transfers with £830m inflated in sponsorships - Man City's 'asterisk era'
description: BBC Sport analyses Manchester City's dominance of English football during the period in which they were breaching financial rules.
fullText:
Outside Manchester City's Etihad Stadium is a lustrous silver statue of Sergio Aguero - mouth agape in ecstasy, kit swirling over his head - depicting his goal celebration after securing the club's first Premier League title.

It is the immortalisation of the most famous goal in English league football history, when City snatched the trophy away from Manchester United in the dying seconds of the 2011-12 season.

But what if the goal never happened? What if Aguero had never played for the club? What if City had opted to abide by football's financial rules instead of purposefully breaking them through a "disguised funding scheme"?

The revelation that the club has been found guilty of the charges brought against it by the Premier League three and a half years ago has left football fans around the world questioning the legitimacy of City's achievements between 2009 and 2018, when they were the most successful club in English football and cemented themselves among the global game's elite.

Some fans are referring to it as the asterisk era, and there is a possibility City could be retroactively stripped of the honours they earned during the period, with some clubs seeking legal advice over potential financial compensation.

So how exactly did City's "hugely overstated" income impact their actions in the transfer market, how key were the players who were brought in, and what does it all mean for both the past and the future?

Manchester City spent about £1.2bn on new players in the transfer windows between summer 2009 and January 2018.

In that time, the club won seven major trophies - three Premier Leagues, one FA Cup, and three EFL Cups - having previously gone without a significant honour since 1970.

The players they purchased during that time included some of the world's best, in all areas of the pitch. Multiple were signed for figures in the tens of millions every summer and made a huge contribution to the club's consistent success.

The graphic below demonstrates how much City spent in each summer and across the whole time period, and contrasts it with the amount of money that the commission which has found the club guilty determined had been falsely pumped into the club by its owners, under the guise of sponsorship income.

City did not only generate revenue from sponsorship funds in that time. And income is also spent on many things other than transfers, including player wages, utilities, insurance, infrastructure, marketing, foundations and more.

But the figures underline the fact that City would simply not have been able to purchase the quantity and quality of players they signed during their era of domination had they not been conducting what the commission described as a "concerted campaign to falsify" their financial accounts.

If City's financial power had been slashed by the extra £830m the commission says they falsely added to their books from sponsorships which were in large part funded by their owners, their transfer spend would surely have been massively reduced.

Add in money from falsely reported image rights and contracts and the total reaches £920m.

Chop the amount in half, say, and maybe they would only have brought in half the amount of players. Or the same amount, but heavily reduced in quality.

Which potentially means no Aguero, no David Silva, no Yaya Toure, no Kevin de Bruyne, or at least a significant reduction in the number or ability of the less glamorous players who were key cogs in the trophy-winning machine.

Would those successes have been achieved had the rule breaking not been going on in tandem? And what would the impact have been on all the other clubs who have played in the Premier League during that time?

Nobody will ever know. The seasons cannot be replayed. And so the outcomes exist in a kind of mixed reality where the world watched them happen, but isn't sure if they're really 'real'.

The era provided the foundation for City's ongoing success, too, meaning more trophies and TV income, and the chaos of the situation has also unleashed doubt about the present and future.

A quick quiz question - what do The Wizard of Oz, Super Mario Bros 2 and the ninth season of Dallas all have in common?

Feel free to grab yourself a hot drink and mull it over for a moment.

If you figured out that the plots of all three never really happened - because in their endings it was revealed that they existed only in the dreams of one of the lead characters - then very well done indeed.

So do the guilty verdicts mean the Premier League seasons between 2009-10 and 2017-18 should now be considered a figment of our collective imaginations too?

City have until Friday to mount an appeal. If that appeal is unsuccessful, then, at some point, the club will be given some sort of punishment.

Whether sanctions will retcon the past in any way is unknown.

And about moving forwards? Right now football fans, both of City and other clubs across the country, do not know whether the football they are watching is 'real' or not.

Are City actually top of the league and in a title challenge, or will they be docked points later in the season?

If they are linked with another team's star player, could that transfer happen or will they be unable to make deals at some point?

Will they be in the Premier League next season or will they be expelled and will there need to be a quite significant rejigging of the pyramid to accommodate them somewhere else?

And then there are questions about what comes later down the line.

Is anybody else breaking rules right now, which fans will only find out about in the future?

Does the potential for years of results to be retroactively kiboshed undermine the Premier League's popularity with fans, players and sponsors?

And can the action fans are watching week in, week out ever fully be trusted again?

The answers to those questions will determine the future of the biggest league in the world's most popular game.

title: Well, this is bad…
description: What’s the worst thing you would have imagined popping up on tonight’s MLB Gameday feed before the game started? Jarren Duran pops out to foul territory, caught by Marlins Man would be pretty bad. I wouldn’t want to see On-field injury delay, Payton Tolle overly aggressive hug either. But I don’t think I would have […]
fullText:
What's the worst thing you would have imagined popping up on tonight's MLB Gameday feed before the game started? Jarren Duran pops out to foul territory, caught by Marlins Man would be pretty bad. I wouldn't want to see On-field injury delay, Payton Tolle overly aggressive hug either.

But I don't think I would have imagined anything worse than this:

Yes. Andruw Monasterio — the last man on the Red Sox bench, the man who has just 2 hits in his last 32 at-bats, the man who many fans would have preferred be passed over on the roster in favor of Braiden Ward, who has never played in a Major League game in his life — pinch-hit for Roman Anthony. In the sixth inning.

The Red Sox have not yet said anything about Anthony's injury status. But we don't really need them to, do we? Anthony's career, young though it may be, has been defined by two things: (1) Precocious brilliance at the plate, (2) A gut-wrenching inability to stay on the field. Anthony struggled with a bizarrely stubborn hand injury for most of the season. He returned to put up an OPS just a tick under .800 over the last few weeks, but appeared to still be battling the injury as of Game 162:

This was Anthony’s last swing on Sunday. Check swing, immediately flexes hand. pic.twitter.com/RAXErsNhDV

His first two plate appearances against Cam Schlittler tonight both ended in awkward check-swing strikeouts. He may not get another one in this series.

title: Young U.S. men's soccer team has ups and downs in 4-2 victory over Chile
description: But all in all, it was another good result and fun outing for a program returning from the World Cup with the second of four friendlies over 11 days.
fullText:
ST. LOUIS — Amid all the excitement about his young U.S. soccer team, a wide-eyed crew that started the new World Cup cycle with an enlightening performance over the weekend, Mauricio Pochettino warned there would be ups and downs along the way.

After all, almost half the roster had never played at the senior level and, as a whole, the group hadn't spent much time together.

Tuesday's 4-2 victory over Chile at bubbly Energizer Park reinforced the coach's admonition.

The gorgeous build-up on the first goal.

Sebastian Berhalter and Gio Reyna putting their stamp on another match.

Teenager Julian Hall's second goal in two appearances, and teenager Mathis Albert scoring his first.

Chris Richards' 72nd-minute tiebreaking goal as part of a second-half comeback.

All in all, it was another good result and fun outing for a program returning from the World Cup with the second of four friendlies over 11 days. For the second time in four days, the Americans scored four goals and flexed their muscles against a South American foe.

There were troubling moments, as well, particularly in the first half, when the Americans conceded numerous scoring opportunities and made many mistakes. They were fortunate to be tied at intermission.

But they showed resilience in the second half and, coupled with the 4-1 thumping of Peru last Saturday in Orlando, continued building momentum heading into this Saturday's showdown with rival Mexico in greater Phoenix. They will also play Canada on Oct. 6 in St. Paul, Minnesota.

In a pregame ceremony in his hometown, World Cup captain Tim Ream was honored for 16 years and 86 appearances with the national team. The Charlotte FC center back, who will turn 39 on Friday, announced moments earlier that he has retired from international soccer and won't weigh his club future until after the MLS season.

"The kids are getting younger and younger," he said. Ream was talking about the U.S. roster, not his own three kids.

"I actually got a text message last night [that] I was a senior at Saint Louis University when [17-year-old forward Cavan Sullivan] was born," Ream said. "I was like, 'He's only four years older than my oldest.'"

Ream was not selected to the current roster.

The starting lineup Tuesday averaged just over 23 years old, including teenagers Hall, Neil Pierre and Adri Mehmeti. The other young starters were midfielder Brooklyn Raines, 21, and right back Frankie Westfield, 20.

At almost 6-foot-7, the 18-year-old Pierre was unmistakable on the backline. Like Sullivan, he is enjoying a breakout club campaign with the Philadelphia Union.

Reyna was the only holdover starter from the Peru match. Like Saturday, Pochettino started six 2026 World Cup players: Reyna, Berhalter, goalkeeper Chris Brady, wingers Antonee Robinson and Sergiño Dest, and center back Miles Robinson.

Brady, 22, made his first international start after debuting as a sub in a World Cup tuneup.

Chile — which has missed three World Cups since winning the 2016 Copa America — was without captain Gabriel Suazo and Lucas Cepeda, La Liga-based players red-carded in the 1-0 loss to Canada on Saturday in Toronto.

As they did against Peru, the Americans threatened early off a Reyna set piece. His free kick from 25 yards met Miles Robinson for a point-blank header that Lawrence Vigouroux slapped aside in spectacular fashion.

The U.S. was organized and energetic at the start but not always precise. In the 18th minute, a miscommunication between Berhalter and Mehmeti led to a Chilean threat. A minute later, Berhalter's tasty through ball sent Hall in alone, but after rounding Vigouroux, his off-balanced, angled bid missed high and wide.

Brady was shaky, sitting back when he should've come forward and allowing Victor Méndez to test him. Then, on shots a minute apart, he also got lucky as Ben Brereton's screamer dinged the crossbar and Darío Osorio's low bid hit the far post.

Against the run of play, the match took an unforeseen turn.

Two minutes after Osorio's scare, the Americans went ahead in the 37th on a wonderfully constructed goal. They won the ball in midfield. Dest and Reyna played a sharp combination. With quick and clever footwork, Dest danced into the box. He crossed to Hall, who dummied the ball with the smarts of a veteran, allowing Berhalter to bury a 12-yarder into the far post.

Brady's problems continued. On the last act of the half — a Chilean corner kick — he punched the ball up, then backward. A mad scramble ensued. Finally, from inside the six-yard box, Diego Ulloa's side-volley caromed off Westfield's arm and into the net.

Brady's night — or nightmare — was over. As he did against Peru, Pochettino changed his goalkeeper at halftime: FC Cincinnati's Brian Schwake made his first appearance, becoming the 12th debut in this camp.

He couldn't do much about Maxi Gutiérrez's go-ahead goal in the 49th minute. Westfield's misstruck header in midfield allowed Gutiérrez to glide into the U.S. end. Berhalter failed to shut him down, and the Chilean forward whistled a 23-yard shot into the far corner with pinpoint accuracy.

Two minutes later, the U.S. answered. Reyna lifted a gentle cross into the box, where Hall rose from eight yards and headed it into the far side.

Pochettino turned to his bench and made seven subs, including five veterans. Vigouroux made a fine foot save on Antonee Robinson, but on the ensuing corner kick, Berhalter delivered a perfect ball to Richards for a powerful header from the edge of the six-yard box.

Chile threatened to pull even. The U.S. extended the lead on Albert's stab off the underside of the crossbar from close range. The announced crowd of 21,680 loved it.

Just before the final whistle, a benches-emptying scuffle broke out after a Chilean player tapped the fallen Schwake on the arm with his foot. Play resumed, but at the final whistle, another brief incident broke out.

"Take Me Home, Country Roads" boomed over the speakers.

Winger Cole Campbell, a first-time camper held out of the Peru match for an undisclosed ailment, and goalkeeper Diego Kochen, who played the second half Saturday, were not in uniform. Kochen was healthy, but Pochettino chose to dress 26 players again.

In his 60th appearance, Antonee Robinson captained the team for the first time.

Sullivan replaced Berhalter in the 83rd minute.

The Americans are 11-1-3 in greater St. Louis, including 5-0-0 at Energizer Park, which sits 1.3 miles directly west of the Gateway Arch and opened before the 2023 MLS season.

title: OpenAI announces ‘dots’ agent after scrapping launch of new AI model over safety concerns
description:
Company’s product comes weeks after Meta introduced its own artificially intelligent agent Muse
Less than 24 hours after OpenAI announced it would scrap the launch of an artificial intelligence model over safety concerns, the company debuted a whole new suite of AI tools.
During its annual showcase for developers in San Francisco on Tuesday, Sam Altman, OpenAI’s CEO, enthusiastically unveiled an AI agent called “dots” that he said was “more ambitious” than ChatGPT and a “whole new way to work with AI”.
 Continue reading...
fullText:
Company’s product comes weeks after Meta introduced its own artificially intelligent agent Muse

Less than 24 hours after OpenAI announced it would scrap the launch of an artificial intelligence model over safety concerns, the company debuted a whole new suite of AI tools.

During its annual showcase for developers in San Francisco on Tuesday, Sam Altman, OpenAI’s CEO, enthusiastically unveiled an AI agent called “dots” that he said was “more ambitious” than ChatGPT and a “whole new way to work with AI”.

“It’s like an AI helper that always has your back,” Altman said, to loud applause from the developers attending the event. “In the future, if you like, you can work with a whole team of dots.”

OpenAI’s dots are colorful little blobs, donning berets or glasses, that appear on people’s phones or laptops, can be integrated into other apps and can follow commands. The agents can perform tasks without supervision such as schedule a meeting, book a flight or dole out assignments to colleagues. OpenAI says the “dots are an extension of you” and describes the tool as “frontier intelligence”.

Dots are powered by GPT-6 Astra, the company’s latest model. OpenAI said the previous evening it would halt the release of GPT-6.1 Astra because the updated model showed deceptive behavior during testing.

OpenAI’s dots will compete with Meta’s new AI agent, Muse, released two weeks ago. Meta’s product is aimed at everyday consumers more so than business customers, as OpenAI’s is, though Meta announced a small business offering Tuesday. The agent’s app, available in the US, has been downloaded more than 3m times.

OpenAI also apologized on Monday for one of its AI agents going rogue and hacking an Australian government website. The apology came after the company has been plagued by reports and admissions that its AI systems have been acting independently and gaining access to various company and government websites.

During OpenAI’s event on Tuesday, Altman touted the power of Astra and introduced similar potent AI tools. One model, called GPT-6.1 Sol, is cheaper and “smarter than Astra in many ways”, the CEO said. Altman also previewed a new “Ultrafast” mode for its AI coding models, which can generate outputs up to eight times faster than what’s available now.

“People often talk about AI as a new industrial revolution, I find that quite off-putting,” Altman said at the end of his presentation. “There are some parts of life that we cannot and should not automate. I believe that the future, if we get this right, can be more like a new Renaissance than a new industrial revolution.”

title: Sculptures honoring N. Korean soldiers to be erected in Vietnam
description: Sculptures honoring North Korean soldiers who fought in the Vietnam War are set to be installed in Hanoi, Pyongyang's state media reported Monday....
fullText:
Sculptures honoring North Korean soldiers who fought in the Vietnam War are set to be installed in Hanoi, Pyongyang's state media reported Monday.

A ceremony unveiling the monument's foundation plaque was held Friday at the Vietnam Military History Museum in Hanoi, the Korean Central News Agency (KCNA) said.

North Korea is believed to have sent close to 400 soldiers to Vietnam during the war, including 90 pilots between 1966 and 1969.

The plaque, inscribed "Feelings of Friendship between Vietnam and DPRK," notes that the two countries established diplomatic relations in January 1950 and that North Korea "rendered material and moral assistance" during Vietnam's "anti-U.S. resistance to national salvation."

DPRK is the acronym for North Korea's official name, the Democratic Republic of Korea.

"The combat spirit and self-sacrificing spirit displayed by Korean soldiers are a noble and beautiful symbol of the good international unity and contributed to the consolidation of the friendly relations between Vietnam and the DPRK," the accompanying text read, according to the KCNA.

The unveiling ceremony was attended by North Korea's Vice Defense Minister Ryo Chol-ung and his Vietnamese counterpart, Nguyen Truong Thang, along with North Korean Ambassador to Vietnam Ri Sung-guk, embassy staff and Vietnamese defense officials.

The North Korean delegation also visited a memorial in Bac Ninh City, north of Hanoi, honoring fallen Korean People's Army soldiers and laid a wreath there.

Led by Ryo, the delegation has been in Vietnam since Sept. 22.

The trip comes as Pyongyang and Hanoi have stepped up efforts to deepen bilateral relations.

Early this month, North Korean leader Kim Jong-un wrote to Vietnamese President To Lam, pledging to strengthen ties, marking the country's 81st founding anniversary.

Relations between the two nations have warmed steadily since last October, when Lam became the first Vietnamese president to visit North Korea in 18 years.

In May, Vietnamese Foreign Minister Le Hoai Trung visited the North for talks with his North Korean counterpart, Choe Son-hui.

The following month, the two countries' security ministers held talks in Pyongyang to discuss ways to expand cooperation on public security and law enforcement.

title: 'Paying attention in age of clickbait' – 2027 World Communications Day theme
description: The Vatican Dicastery for Communication releases the theme for the 2027 World Communications Day, which is “A New Gaze: Paying Attention in the Age of ...
fullText:
On the feast of St. Gabriel the Archangel, the Holy See’s Dicastery for Communication released the theme for the 61st World Communications Day.

The theme will be “A New Gaze: Paying Attention in the Age of Clickbait,” according to a press release published on Tuesday by the Dicastery (our parent organization).

This year’s theme invites Christians to open ourselves to “a conversion of our gaze: to look again, with attention and with love.”

“The attention economy, with its struggle for a few moments of interest amid the rapid and endless flow of content, is transforming not only our cognitive abilities but also the depth of our interpersonal communication,” it noted.

Only by paying attention to others with love can we see the “world, others, even ourselves, as Christ sees us: called by name and loved.”

“Our communication changes when our gaze chooses to encounter others rather than judge them,” said the statement.

People are inundated every moment of every day with expectations of rapid reactions and superficial relationships, resulting in a lack of genuine attention fueled by digital culture, it added.

“Yet attention is a precious form of generosity: the word ‘attention’ comes from ad-tendere—to reach out toward the other and toward the truth,” said the press release. “Christian communication can rediscover attention as both a gift and a way of seeing—the gaze of Jesus, who saw and allowed Himself to be touched.”

Rather than seeking to capture attention, communicating is about safeguarding attention “as a precious resource for relationships.”

In our modern age of “clickbait,” Christians are invited to pay attention and rediscover a healthy form of attention to one another.

“Communication is not just about words,” concluded the press release. “It involves the entire person and asks us to look, hear, and feel again in order to answer Christ’s call.”

World Communications Day 2027 takes place in many parts of the world—including the United States, England and Wales, France, Spain, Poland, and Italy—on May 9, but is celebrated on different days in various parts of the world, as set by the national Bishops’ Conferences.

title: Crossing the Computer-Use Chasm
description: Crossing the Computer-Use Chasm
fullText:
I have been working with our customers @browserbase for over a year now. It feels like living through a cambrian explosion, and I have collected a whole book worth of stories. There’s unbounded creativity in how the world adopts new technology, and it is in full effect with computer-use. Every week, I’m surprised by something that our customers have built with @browserbase , and I’m excited to share some of those stories with y’all!

We are seeing computer-use cross the chasm in real time, as more of the early majority is exposed to this voodoo magic. But before we get carried away too far into the future, I want to recap and share about how this all started.

October '24: Anthropic published about their newest ability: computer-use in Sonnet 3.5

I remember seeing this release, and wondering how this will spread like wildfire in 3 months. But, when I started tinkering with it, I realized it was terrible at doing anything meaningful yet.

Fast forward, Jan 2025: OpenAI releases a research preview of Operator.

Operator got people taking attention at computer-use, and I was so excited when I got access to this on my 200$ Pro plan. I told Operator to join a Google Meet with my friends, and it started commenting in the meeting. Black magic.

Two days later, Browserbase shipped Open Operator.

This is when I started following Browserbase closely, and I remember thinking how this is the beginning of a new modality of AI interaction. In my mind, it was inevitable that this technology will have lasting implications on knowledge work, where almost all my daily work is done inside a browser.

In early '25, coding agents had gone exponential and developers started to realize how this would translate to better computer-use. Websites are basically code (HTML & Javascript), and you could let a coding agent manipulate a website by writing more code.

A lot of signs were pointing me towards this being the the most fun next big thing, and so I joined Browserbase in June '25.

Mid '25: Browser Agents started to become a category of its own. Customers would come up to us in zoom calls and show off their latest demos. After a day of customer conversations, I would leave brimming with ideas on how our infrastructure will power this new wave of applications.

I saw enterprise customers using @Stagehanddev to power their "agentic crawling" efforts for KYC.

I saw healthcare companies automating insurance claims using browser automation.

I saw developers building full-scale behavior simulation and UI-testing suites using different "personas".

I saw an agent that would login to critical software and ensure that all configurations were compliant.

Everyday, it was something new.

Meanwhile, claude-code was absolutely ripping, and the models were getting much better at computer-use. All the labs started publishing their computer-use benchmarks on Mind2Web, WebVoyager and OSWorld.

^^Gemini 2.5's model card shows its benchmark performance, as measured on Browserbase.

2026 came around, and Openclaw took everyone by surprise. We all realized how important a good harness is to building an agent.

And then a few people started to notice, if you took this harness and gave it access to a browser, it could start doing "work" for you.

I setup my Openclaw on a VM, and started using it as my personal trainer. It would use a browser session to pull relevant YouTube videos, and prepare my workout for the next day. I started planning my trips and date nights with openclaw. I was obsessed, and so were many others!

Somewhere in mid-2026, models and harnesses started to get really really good with computer-use. In fact, people (👀 @danshipper) started giving Codex their email access.

Developers stopped testing their apps, and let their Codex run wild testing everything in its browser.

Something very interesting started happening in the last couple months.

Instinct, which went live in August, has been the most viral invite-only product launch in recent history.

Meta went live with Muse in September. It is currently on a faster growth curve than ChatGPT in 2022.

Now millions of people across the world can feel that black magic I felt with OpenAI Operator. They could all see the power of an agent planning out their travels, using a browser to book their tickets. These agents are now making e-commerce transactions with credit cards, which is a strong sign of the user's trust in these systems.

At Browserbase, we have seen many tailwinds to our business, but this has been the strongest by far. It seems like the average internet user can just download an app from the App Store, and use state-of-the-art computer-use out of the box. The packaging of these personal agents is extremely appealing and will spread very far.

However, even after all these improvements, I'd argue that we haven't yet crossed the computer-use chasm. Most people are willing to let an agent run some errands for them, but haven't yet offloaded mission-critical workloads.

My taxes haven't been filed by an agent. My investments aren't being managed by an agent. My insurance is not supervised by an agent. Payroll for my company is not being run by an agent.

Geoffrey Moore’s central argument in Crossing the Chasm is that early adopters will tolerate an incomplete product because they want an advantage. The early majority will not. They want something reliable, proven, and safe enough to become part of normal work.

One of the biggest challenges with agents is that of identity. How do you delegate your identity and permissions to your agent. How do you configure your agent to have all your passwords, and what about 2FAs.

Even if we solve the problem of delegating identity, the bigger question arises: what about permissions? Should an agent have the same permissions as the human, and if not, where do you draw the line. For critical decisions, agents ask their human for explicit approval, but if not designed well, this can lead to approval fatigue.

One of the biggest friction points with the broader adoption of computer-use is security. For agents to perform economically valuable work, they are going to have access to sensitive information like health records, bank accounts, and personally identifiable information. The big question for our industry is how we ensure these agents browse the web without leaking any information to honeypots or vulnerabilities. Additionally, how do we ensure the world wide web doesn't inject my agent's context.

In addition to the challenges of agent identity & security, you have the challenge of working within the current incentive structure of the internet. Antibots and CAPTCHAs, which originally existed to prevent bad bots from doing bad things, are now blocking good-intentioned agents.

All of these are challenges that get solved at an infrastructure and ecosystem level. We should enable our agents to have emails, phone lines, IP addresses, credentials, credit cards, securely governed within isolated sandboxes and browsers.

As the agents build more distribution leverage, it forces the ecosystem to change its incentive structure. The internet economy will start to open itself to agents, and WebMCP is a promising direction to the future.

At Browserbase, we say that we're in the diffusion business, and these are all problems that we're wrestling with everyday. Just a matter of time till we cross into the majority.

title: Llms.txt: agent-optimization wishful thinking
description: Can't remember where I stumbled upon a SEO-type guide that was suggesting agent-optimization via a robot.txt-like file llms.txt which lives in the web root and helps agents use your site. Perfect, I thought, my sightread.org has a zillion options, all bookmarkable.
fullText:
Can't remember where I stumbled upon a SEO-type guide that was suggesting agent-optimization via a robot.txt-like file llms.txt which lives in the web root and helps agents use your site. Perfect, I thought, my sightread.org has a zillion options, all bookmarkable. I imagined a world where someone asks ChatGPT for a sight reading exercise or maybe even a teachable gradual sequence of exercises, and said ChatGPT creates the URLs and send the person to the correct exercise. Wonderful! So I dully created my sightread.org/llms.txt

I guess something was still bothering me, mainly how do I even know it's useful and do the agent's crawlers are finding it ok. Asked Gemini back then, 6-7 months ago. It told me to link to it from my robots.txt like

Next time Gemini (3-pro) told me this is invalid and wrong and not even a sitemap. Agh!

I also monkey-see-monkey-do'd a link to it from my HTML head, like so:

Recently I asked Claude about opinions and it told me that no one cares. Agent crawlers ignore it. My coding agent might find it useful in the absence of agents.md, but no SEO/Agent-O at all. Ditch it, it said. Write a public facing HTML instead. And I did.

Lo and behold, Lighthouse now has an "agenting browsing" audit. I ran it, it complained about my missing llms.txt. I restored it, LH complained it has no links. My markdown had URLs but not formatted as links. Fine. Fixed. Bye. Now the HTML meta is like described by the docs:

I am ready! Come to me my agents!

Still something was bugging me. Does llms.txt matter or not at all? One company that knows crawling and has an agent and a browser and developer tools in the browser says YES! It's WRONG if it's missing. Another agentic company says meh! Who cares?

What to do but look at server logs to see who's crawling my llms.txt

First I compared number of requests to robots.txt to the number of requests to llms.txt. In terms of percentage it's 1 - 1.2% in the last 5 days. That's it? Not impressed. For every 100 requests to robots.txt I get 1 request for llms.txt.

Next - who is requesting it? Here are the top user-agents (or should we say agent-agents?)

There's some Claude, no GPT, no Gemini... Meta + Googlebot total of 0.08%

One UA is responsible for 66%. Running latest Chrome on Linux, not identifying itself. Just one poorly vibecoded crawler going rogue on my poor server? Maybe.

Is it me? My syntax was wrong? I dunno. I'm inclined to to say llms.txt doesn't matter, whatever Lighthouse says. Until I see googlebot/gemini in the logs, I don't trust it.
